title: Probabilistic Focal Search: Accelerating Bounded-Suboptimal Search via Lower-Bound Advancement
summary: Bounded-suboptimal search seeks a solution within a factor $w$ of optimal while reducing search effort. Focal Search (FS) uses heuristic guidance within FOCAL, the frontier nodes eligible under the threshold $w f_{\min}$, but its deterministic policy may leave $f_{\min}$ unchanged for many expansions. We introduce Probabilistic Focal Search (PFS), which follows the FS guided choice with probability $p$ and expands a minimum-$f$ OPEN node with probability $1-p$. The latter branch encourages the lower bound to advance, enlarging FOCAL and admitting nodes that may lead to feasible solutions. By balancing guidance and lower-bound advancement, this mechanism can reduce time to a bounded solution when progress is limited by delayed FOCAL admission. As a secondary transfer experiment, we apply the same scheduler to Dynamic Potential Search, yielding Probabilistic Dynamic Potential Search (PDPS). We benchmark PFS against FS on N-Puzzle, Pancake Sorting, and the Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP), and evaluate its anytime extension on the Generalized Covering TSP (GCTSP), using multiple $w$ and $p$ values. Across these benchmarks, the largest gains occur when long $f_{\min}$ plateaus delay useful FOCAL admissions; in such settings, the probabilistic factor may reduce node expansions by about 90\% or more (e.g., on N-Puzzle and TSP). For the anytime algorithm family, Anytime Probabilistic Focal Search (APFS) outperforms all tested algorithms in evaluating anytime methods on GCTSP. We also observe that the benefit is smaller when the deterministic search already advances efficiently (e.g., Pancake Sorting), indicating that the probabilistic factor is most useful when FOCAL admission is a search bottleneck. The PDPS transfer shows that the mechanism also transfers to potential guidance, although its common-success effects remain domain- and bound-dependent.

AI.tldr: They introduce a probabilistic variant of Focal Search that occasionally expands the global best node to break f_min plateaus, greatly reducing node expansions in domains where FOCAL admission is the bottleneck, and show it transfers to a related algorithm and anytime settings.
AI.motivation: Classical bounded-suboptimal search algorithms like Focal Search use a deterministic expansion policy inside the FOCAL list, which can cause long plateaus where the best f-value in OPEN (f_min) does not increase for many expansions. During such plateaus, the set FOCAL of nodes within the suboptimality bound remains small, delaying the admission of promising nodes that could lead quickly to a w-bounded solution and causing unnecessary node expansions. There is a need for mechanisms that maintain heuristic guidance but also proactively advance the f_min lower bound when it is stagnant, thereby enlarging FOCAL earlier and improving efficiency, ideally in a way that is simple and transferable across related search algorithms and anytime variants.
AI.method: They propose Probabilistic Focal Search (PFS), a modification of Focal Search. At each step, PFS chooses between two expansion policies: with probability p it behaves like standard FS, expanding a node from FOCAL according to the usual heuristic guidance; with probability 1−p it expands a node with minimum f from OPEN (i.e., the global best f node). Expanding the minimum-f node tends to increase f_min more quickly, which in turn raises the FOCAL threshold w f_min and admits more nodes into FOCAL. This probabilistic scheduler is also applied to Dynamic Potential Search, creating Probabilistic Dynamic Potential Search (PDPS). They empirically evaluate PFS vs FS on N-Puzzle, Pancake Sorting, and TSP for multiple suboptimality bounds w and probabilities p, and study an anytime extension, Anytime Probabilistic Focal Search (APFS), on the Generalized Covering TSP. They measure node expansions and performance across problem domains and parameter settings to characterize when and how much the probabilistic factor helps.
AI.result: Experiments show that PFS can dramatically reduce search effort compared to standard FS in domains where f_min stays on long plateaus, which delay the admission of useful nodes into FOCAL. In N-Puzzle and TSP, the probabilistic mechanism sometimes reduces node expansions by around 90% or more for suitable choices of w and p. APFS, the anytime version, achieves the best performance among all tested anytime algorithms on the GCTSP benchmark. For Pancake Sorting, where deterministic search already advances f_min efficiently, the benefit of PFS is small, demonstrating that the gain is domain- and structure-dependent. Applying the same scheduling idea to Dynamic Potential Search (PDPS) shows that the mechanism is transferable to potential-based guidance, though its success still depends on the specific domain and suboptimality bound.
AI.conclusion: Introducing a simple probabilistic scheduler that occasionally expands the global minimum-f node can mitigate f_min plateaus in bounded-suboptimal search, allowing FOCAL to grow sooner and significantly reducing node expansions when FOCAL admission is the main bottleneck. Probabilistic Focal Search and its anytime variant can outperform their deterministic counterparts and other baselines on several domains, especially N-Puzzle, TSP, and GCTSP, while offering limited additional benefit where deterministic progress is already good. The same idea can be transferred to Dynamic Potential Search, indicating that probabilistic lower-bound advancement is a generally useful design principle for heuristic search, although its practical impact is domain- and parameter-dependent.

title: Automating Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) Formulation Generation from Natural Language
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on AI as a Tool for Mathematics, Computer Science, and Machine Learning (AI4Research)
summary: Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) is a central formulation for combinatorial optimization and has gained increasing attention due to its compatibility with quantum, hybrid quantum-classical, and quantum-inspired solvers. However, translating natural-language problem descriptions into correct QUBO formulations remains difficult, requiring the identification of binary variables, constraints, objective functions, penalty terms, and suitable penalty weights. This process is time-consuming and often demands substantial domain expertise. To address this challenge, we propose an end-to-end multi-agent framework that automatically generates QUBO formulations from natural-language problem descriptions, supported by structured or unstructured test cases. To evaluate its performance, We also introduce QUBOBench, a benchmark containing 100 combinatorial optimization problems across 12 application domains, curated from peer-reviewed literature, competitions, and canonical NP-hard problems. Experimental results show that our framework achieves 68% accuracy on QUBOBench, outperforming a direct single-call baseline by 22%. Further analysis identifies iterative self-repair as the most important component contributing to improved performance. The data and code are open-sourced at https://quitttcat.github.io/QuantumQUBOAgent.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an automatic, multi-agent system that converts natural-language descriptions of combinatorial optimization problems into QUBO formulations, together with a new benchmark (QUBOBench) to evaluate such systems.
AI.motivation: Formulating real-world combinatorial optimization problems as QUBOs is crucial for using quantum, hybrid, and quantum-inspired solvers, but the translation from natural language to correct QUBO form is difficult, slow, and requires significant expertise. There is also a lack of standardized benchmarks to systematically evaluate automatic QUBO formulation methods.
AI.method: The authors design an end-to-end multi-agent framework where multiple specialized agents collaborate to: (1) parse natural-language problem descriptions, (2) identify binary variables, constraints, and objectives, (3) construct QUBO formulations with appropriate penalty terms and weights, and (4) iteratively repair and refine formulations based on structured or unstructured test cases. They also construct QUBOBench, a benchmark of 100 diverse combinatorial optimization problems from 12 application domains, collected from literature, competitions, and classic NP-hard problems, to evaluate the framework against a direct single-call baseline.
AI.result: On the QUBOBench benchmark, the proposed multi-agent framework achieves 68% accuracy in producing correct QUBO formulations, which is a 22% absolute improvement over a direct single-call baseline. Ablation and component-wise analyses show that iterative self-repair is the key factor driving the performance gains.
AI.conclusion: Automatic translation from natural-language problem descriptions to QUBO formulations is feasible and can be significantly improved using a multi-agent, self-repairing approach. The new QUBOBench benchmark enables systematic evaluation of such systems. The open-sourced data and code provide a foundation for further research on automated QUBO modeling for quantum and quantum-inspired optimization.

title: A Multi-Stage Rule-Chaining Framework for Compositional and Interpretable Cognitive Reasoning
summary:
The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) benchmarks cognitive generalization, the ability to infer and apply abstract rules from limited examples. This paper presents a multi-stage rule-chaining framework that performs compositional reasoning across symbolic, structural, and conceptual levels. The framework integrates three complementary solvers:
  (1) a deterministic rule discovery module that induces atomic transformations through geometric, color, and object-based analysis;
  (2) a pattern-composition engine that reconstructs outputs via block merging, repetition, and spatial heuristics; and
  (3) a structural abstraction layer that infers hierarchical and nested relationships across grids.
  These solvers operate sequentially within a progressive fallback hierarchy, where each stage reuses prior reasoning traces to enhance interpretability and generalization. Training passed for 995 tasks out of 1000, further evaluated on 105 tasks out of 120 and solved 230 test tasks out of 240 ARC-AGI-2 tasks. The system achieved strong coverage across deterministic, compositional, and abstract categories, demonstrating an overall accuracy exceeding 95 percent. The proposed architecture bridges symbolic reasoning and pattern synthesis, providing interpretable insight into cognitive generalization. The results suggest that rule chaining and hierarchical composition can advance machine reasoning toward transparent, human-aligned abstraction without relying on task-specific tuning.

AI.tldr: A multi-stage, rule-chaining framework for ARC that combines symbolic rule discovery, pattern composition, and structural abstraction to achieve >95% accuracy with interpretable, human-aligned reasoning.
AI.motivation: To improve cognitive-style generalization on ARC by creating a system that can infer abstract, compositional rules from very few examples, while remaining interpretable and not relying on task-specific tuning or brute-force search.
AI.method: Introduce a three-stage framework: (1) a deterministic rule discovery module that induces atomic geometric, color, and object-based transformations; (2) a pattern-composition engine that builds outputs via block merging, repetition, and spatial heuristics; and (3) a structural abstraction layer that infers hierarchical and nested grid relationships. These solvers are arranged in a progressive fallback hierarchy, where later stages reuse reasoning traces from earlier ones to enhance interpretability and generalization.
AI.result: On ARC-AGI-2, the system successfully trained on 995/1000 tasks, was further evaluated on 105/120 tasks, and solved 230/240 test tasks, achieving over 95% overall accuracy with strong coverage on deterministic, compositional, and abstract task categories.
AI.conclusion: Rule chaining combined with hierarchical, compositional reasoning can yield highly accurate and interpretable performance on ARC. This architecture effectively bridges symbolic reasoning with pattern synthesis and advances transparent, human-aligned abstraction without task-specific tuning.

title: Understanding LoRA Rank Trade-offs in Diffusion Model Fine-Tuning
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at CSCE 2026
summary: Selecting LoRA rank for diffusion fine-tuning requires balancing quality and compute cost. We present a controlled study on CIFAR-10 using a DDPM U-Net with ranks {2,4,8,16,32}, fixed optimization settings, and a reproducible local-folder pytorch-fid protocol. We report FID, trainable parameters, runtime, and GPU memory, then validate trends with extended-budget DDPM runs (20 epochs; ranks 4/8/16) and a Tiny DiT backbone (10 epochs; ranks 4/8/16). Results show moderate ranks are most efficient: rank 4 achieves the best DDPM FID (124.1380), rank 8 is close (124.2136), and higher ranks provide limited gains despite larger adaptation cost. These findings support small-to-moderate ranks as practical defaults under fixed training budgets.

AI.tldr: Study on how LoRA rank affects diffusion model fine-tuning efficiency on CIFAR-10; finds small-to-moderate ranks (4–8) best balance FID and compute.
AI.motivation: LoRA is widely used to adapt diffusion models efficiently, but practitioners lack clear guidance on what rank to choose to balance model quality and computational cost. Existing reports are often anecdotal, use inconsistent setups, or focus on language models rather than image diffusion. This paper aims to provide a controlled, reproducible comparison of several LoRA ranks for diffusion fine-tuning, quantifying the quality–efficiency trade-offs.
AI.method: Use a DDPM U-Net trained on CIFAR-10 and fine-tune it with LoRA at different ranks {2,4,8,16,32}. Keep optimization hyperparameters, training schedule, and dataset fixed. Measure Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), trainable parameter counts, wall-clock runtime, and GPU memory footprint, using a local-folder pytorch-fid protocol for reproducibility. Validate observed trends by running longer-budget DDPM experiments (20 epochs, ranks 4/8/16) and by repeating the study with a Tiny DiT backbone (10 epochs, ranks 4/8/16).
AI.result: Across tested settings, moderate LoRA ranks give the best efficiency–quality trade-off. On DDPM with CIFAR-10, rank 4 attains the best FID (124.1380) and rank 8 is nearly as good (124.2136), while higher ranks (16, 32) do not yield commensurate FID improvements despite notably increasing the number of trainable parameters, runtime, and memory consumption. The validation experiments with extended training and with a Tiny DiT backbone show consistent trends, reinforcing that very high ranks provide diminishing returns.
AI.conclusion: Under fixed training budgets for diffusion model fine-tuning, using LoRA with small-to-moderate ranks (around 4–8) is a robust, practical default. Such ranks achieve competitive or best FID scores while substantially reducing trainable parameters and compute compared to higher ranks, and these findings appear stable across both DDPM and Tiny DiT backbones and across different training durations.

title: Data-Efficient Language Modeling: From Frontier Advancement to Principle-Guided Model Improvement
summary: Learning from limited text requires models to use context, generalize to new inputs, and retain useful capabilities. Qiushi Engine conducted a long-horizon, end-to-end autonomous research program on BabyLM 2026 Strict-Small, within 10 million corpus words and 100 million cumulative word presentations. Three stages connected frontier advancement, principle discovery, and principle-guided model improvement. Stage I combined compact restatements, budget reinvestment, and residual incremental learning to build a frontier model. Stage II found that exact repetition and aligned restatement produce different patterns of context use, depending on target relations and prediction windows. In controlled tasks, recovering familiar performance did not ensure that unseen inputs could still use learned computations. These findings support a testable data-efficient learning principle: organize experience around the contextual dependencies needed for prediction; separately design visible information, supervision, and preservation; test learning, generalization, and retention. Stage III retained source text, masked more local clues, supervised selected targets, and preserved predictions on ordinarily masked inputs. Two continuation seeds from the same parent outperformed ordinary continuation on the complete nine-metric aggregate. Overall rose from 42.02 to 42.25 across two generations; the second achieved the highest Overall in the public Strict-Small snapshot of 8 September 2026. Further studies addressed compression, relational anchors, shared representations, and measurement. Models are available on Hugging Face; code and research records accompany the GitHub repository. Together, these stages illustrate Research RSI: recursive self-improvement of the research process. Scientific understanding and method innovations change subsequent questions and designs; new experiments test and refine them.

AI.tldr: This paper reports an autonomous, multi-stage research program that develops compact language models under strict data limits, discovering principles for data-efficient learning and using them to recursively improve both models and research methods.
AI.motivation: Understand how to train language models that learn effectively from very limited text, while also exploring how an autonomous research system can iteratively improve its own methods and understanding over multiple generations.
AI.method: Run a three-stage, long-horizon autonomous research pipeline on the BabyLM 2026 Strict-Small benchmark: (I) build a strong frontier model using techniques like compact restatements, budget reinvestment, and residual incremental learning; (II) design controlled experiments contrasting exact repetition vs aligned restatement to probe context use, generalization to unseen inputs, and retention of learned computations; (III) apply the discovered principles to redesign training data and objectives—keeping source text, increasing masking of local clues, selectively supervising targets, and preserving predictions on normally masked inputs—then compare ordinary and principle-guided continuation runs across nine evaluation metrics.
AI.result: Stage II experiments showed that different forms of data presentation (exact repetition vs aligned restatement) lead to distinct context-usage patterns and that restoring familiar-task performance does not guarantee preserved generalization for novel inputs. From these, the authors formulated a principle for data-efficient learning centered on structuring experience around prediction-relevant dependencies and decoupling information visibility, supervision, and preservation. Applying this in Stage III yielded two continuation models from a shared parent that both surpassed baseline continuation, improving the nine-metric Overall score from 42.02 to 42.25, with the second model achieving the best publicly reported Strict-Small score as of 8 September 2026. Additional analyses explored model compression, relational anchors, shared representations, and evaluation methodology, and released models and code.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that an autonomous research system can not only improve models under strict data constraints but can also recursively refine its own research methodology—termed Research RSI. By iteratively linking frontier model building, principle discovery, and principle-informed redesign, the system develops and tests a concrete, testable principle for data-efficient learning, showing that carefully organized experience and decoupled training signals can yield measurable gains and guide future experimental design.

title: Quantifying the Memorization-to-Generalization Transition: Scaling Laws and Phase Structure in Grokking
summary: Neural networks trained past memorization frequently undergo a delayed transition to generalization, a phenomenon known as grokking. Despite theoretical progress on \emph{why} this transition occurs, the quantitative structure of \emph{when} it occurs in hyperparameter space remains uncharacterized. We map the memorization-to-generalization boundary across 384 configurations of two-hidden-layer MLPs on modular arithmetic, fitting a power-law scaling relation for generalization onset time: $T_{\mathrm{grok}} \propto H^{-0.27}\, D^{-2.04}\, η^{-0.50}\, λ^{-0.64}$ ($R^2 = 0.732$; $0.821$ with interactions). The exponent hierarchy reveals that data complexity ($D^{-2.04}$) is the dominant driver of regime transition, not model capacity ($H^{-0.27}$): doubling data accelerates generalization by ${\sim}4\times$, while doubling width yields only ${\sim}1.2\times$. A sharp phase boundary at weight decay $λ\gtrsim 1.0$ separates grokking from non-grokking configurations, and weight norm trajectories show monotonic compression during the transition, consistent with implicit regularization selecting low-complexity solutions. These results provide a quantitative foundation for predicting and controlling regime transitions in overparameterized networks.

AI.tldr: The paper quantitatively characterizes when grokking (a delayed transition from memorization to generalization) occurs in neural networks, finding a power-law relation between grokking time and key hyperparameters, with data complexity as the dominant factor.
AI.motivation: Although prior work has explained why grokking can occur, there is little quantitative understanding of where in hyperparameter space the transition from memorization to generalization happens or how long it takes. This paper aims to systematically map that boundary and derive predictive scaling laws for the onset of grokking.
AI.method: The authors train two-hidden-layer MLPs on modular arithmetic tasks across 384 hyperparameter configurations, varying model width, dataset size, learning rate, and weight decay. They measure the time (in training steps) to transition from memorization to generalization and fit a power-law scaling relation between this grokking time and the hyperparameters, also examining interaction terms and weight norm trajectories.
AI.result: They find a power-law scaling for the grokking onset time: T_grok ∝ H^{-0.27} D^{-2.04} η^{-0.50} λ^{-0.64}, with R^2 = 0.732 (0.821 including interactions). Data complexity (dataset size D) has the strongest influence, while model width H has a relatively weak effect. Doubling data speeds up generalization by about 4x, but doubling width only yields about 1.2x speedup. They identify a sharp phase boundary at weight decay λ ≳ 1.0 separating grokking from non-grokking regimes, and observe monotonic weight norm compression during the transition.
AI.conclusion: Grokking onset time in overparameterized MLPs follows a robust power-law with respect to key hyperparameters, with data complexity as the main driver of the memorization-to-generalization transition and model capacity playing a secondary role. A critical weight decay threshold separates grokking from non-grokking behavior, and weight norm dynamics support the view that implicit regularization favors low-complexity solutions. These findings enable more systematic prediction and control of regime transitions in overparameterized neural networks.

title: NCP-ArchPreview Technical Report: Moving towards Latent Space Language Models through Next Concept Prediction
summary: We introduce NCP-ArchPreview, a latent-space language model that pushes autoregressive pretraining beyond standard next-token prediction (NTP). Alongside NTP, the model learns through Next Concept Prediction (NCP) to predict discrete concepts that span multiple tokens, introducing an explicit and more challenging concept-level objective while preserving standard token-level autoregressive generation. NCP-ArchPreview builds a latent space by constructing a product-quantized concept vocabulary directly from its hidden states, and subsequently learns to predict future concepts via a dedicated Concept Module. These predicted concepts are then fed back to the token level to guide subsequent generation, with NTP and NCP trained jointly end-to-end. We scale this architecture to 8.9B parameters and train it on 5.73T tokens from the Dolma-3 dataset, marking the largest demonstration of a latent-space language model to date. Remarkably, by consuming only 51.3% of the total training tokens, NCP-ArchPreview achieves the final pretraining loss of OLMo-3-7B. Following full pretraining, it outperforms OLMo-3-7B by 2.45 points on the downstream macro-average, including a notable 5.99-point gain on GSM8K. Controlled experiments isolate a clear progression of performance gains stemming from both the latent architecture and the NCP objective. Furthermore, utilizing only 85% of the standard computation, NCP-ArchPreview approaches the training loss of a strictly parameter-aligned 8.9B baseline. The learned latent space remains highly valuable after the pretraining stage: updating just the 17M-parameter VQ module yields a novel, lightweight interface for domain adaptation, while a simple injection of concept representations into a DFlash2 drafter improves the mean accepted length by 4.17% with negligible overhead.

AI.tldr: The paper presents NCP-ArchPreview, a large latent-space language model that augments next-token prediction with next-concept prediction, leading to faster and more efficient pretraining and strong downstream gains over comparable baselines.
AI.motivation: Standard autoregressive language models optimize next-token prediction, which may underutilize higher-level structure and concepts present in text. The authors want to explore whether adding an explicit concept-level prediction objective and latent space can improve training efficiency, final performance, and provide new capabilities like lightweight domain adaptation and better drafting, all at large scale.
AI.method: They build NCP-ArchPreview, an 8.9B-parameter model trained jointly on Next Token Prediction (NTP) and a new Next Concept Prediction (NCP) objective. A product-quantized concept vocabulary is constructed directly from the model’s hidden states to form a discrete latent space. A dedicated Concept Module predicts future concepts in this space, and these predicted concepts are then fed back into the token-level model to guide subsequent generation. Training is end-to-end on 5.73T Dolma-3 tokens. They also evaluate controlled baselines, a parameter-matched 8.9B model without the latent architecture, and conduct post-hoc experiments where only the 17M-parameter VQ module is updated for domain adaptation and where concept representations are injected into a DFlash2 drafter.
AI.result: NCP-ArchPreview, trained on only 51.3% of the tokens used for OLMo-3-7B, matches OLMo-3-7B’s final pretraining loss and ultimately surpasses it by 2.45 points on a macro-average of downstream benchmarks, including a 5.99-point improvement on GSM8K. With 85% of the standard compute, it approaches the training loss of a strictly parameter-aligned 8.9B baseline. Controlled experiments show that both the latent architecture and the NCP objective contribute to the performance gains. The learned latent space is shown to be reusable: updating only the 17M-parameter VQ module enables effective domain adaptation, and injecting concept representations into a DFlash2 drafter increases mean accepted length by 4.17% with minimal overhead.
AI.conclusion: Explicit next-concept prediction over a learned discrete latent space can be integrated with standard next-token training at scale, yielding better training efficiency and downstream performance than comparable pure-token baselines. The latent space is not only helpful during pretraining but also offers a compact handle for domain adaptation and can be reused to improve drafting systems, suggesting latent-space language models are a promising direction for more efficient and adaptable LMs.

title: An Open Recipe for IMO Gold: Training Nemotron for Olympiad Mathematics
summary: We study how model post-training and test-time inference design affect natural-language proof generation for hard olympiad mathematics. Starting from Nemotron 3 Ultra, we train two specialist checkpoints using supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, and evaluate checkpoint choice, verification, and refinement. Based on these findings, we present an open-model test-time-compute pipeline. The system operates entirely in natural language, with no formal prover, external tools, or internet access. Three Nemotron 3 Ultra checkpoints - the general-availability model and two post-trained specialists - power an iterative search that generates, verifies, and refines candidate proofs; a separate high-compute stage then selects each final submission. The system scored 30 out of 42 points at IMO 2026, reaching the gold-medal threshold. We release the two post-trained checkpoints as well as the training data, the training and inference code, the submitted solutions, and Nemotron-IMO-Bench, a new benchmark of 200 novel olympiad-level problems.

AI.tldr: They build and analyze a natural-language-only system (based on Nemotron 3 Ultra) that generates, verifies, and refines proofs for very hard olympiad math problems, reaching gold-medal performance at IMO 2026 and releasing models, code, and a new benchmark.
AI.motivation: Olympiad-level math problems are challenging tests of deep reasoning and proof-writing, and existing systems often rely on formal provers or external tools. The authors want to understand how post-training (SFT, RL) and test-time inference strategies affect natural-language proof generation on these hard tasks, and to build a strong, fully open, tool-free system that performs competitively on real IMO problems.
AI.method: Starting from the base Nemotron 3 Ultra, they train two specialized models via supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. They then design and evaluate a test-time pipeline in which three checkpoints (the base plus two specialists) are used in an iterative search process that generates candidate proofs, verifies them, and refines them, all in natural language without formal tools. A separate high-compute selection stage then chooses the final answer. They also systematically study checkpoint choice, verification, and refinement design decisions.
AI.result: Their system, using this multi-checkpoint, multi-stage natural-language pipeline, achieved 30/42 points on IMO 2026—meeting the gold-medal cutoff. They also created Nemotron-IMO-Bench, a dataset of 200 new olympiad-level problems, and prepared the post-trained checkpoints, training data, code, and submitted solutions for public release.
AI.conclusion: Carefully designed post-training (SFT and RL) together with a compute-intensive, multi-checkpoint test-time pipeline can produce high-quality natural-language proofs on very challenging olympiad mathematics problems, reaching gold-medal performance on a real IMO. Openly releasing the models, code, and a dedicated benchmark should facilitate further research on advanced mathematical reasoning and proof generation in language models.

title: CMNIE: An Information Extraction Benchmark for Chinese Military News
summary: Structured extraction from Chinese military news supports intelligence analysis, decision-making, and knowledge base construction. However, existing resources provide limited support for joint informa?tion extraction in this domain, especially when events, event arguments, entities, and relations must be modeled together. We present CMNIE, an information extraction benchmark for Chinese military news. Extend?ing military-domain resources beyond document-level event annotations, CMNIE jointly annotates event triggers, event arguments, named enti?ties, and entity relations under a unified domain schema. The dataset contains 13,000 instances collected from public Chinese military news, with manual annotations for 7 event types, 10 argument roles, 7 entity types, and 8 relation types. We evaluate supervised IE models, zero-shot large language models, and fine-tuned LLM-based extraction methods on a shared test set. Experimental results show that CMNIE remains chal?lenging, especially for relation extraction and exact matching of event?argument spans; zero-shot LLMs often identify relevant semantic units but fail to match gold span boundaries exactly. CMNIE provides a stan?dardized benchmark for studying schema adherence, exact span match?ing, and joint structured extraction in specialized Chinese news.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CMNIE, a benchmark dataset for joint information extraction from Chinese military news, covering events, arguments, entities, and relations.
AI.motivation: Existing information extraction resources for Chinese military news are limited, especially for joint modeling of events, event arguments, entities, and relations under a unified schema. There is a need for a standardized benchmark to support intelligence analysis, decision-making, and knowledge base construction in this specialized domain.
AI.method: The authors construct CMNIE, a manually annotated dataset of 13,000 instances from public Chinese military news. They design a unified domain schema including 7 event types, 10 argument roles, 7 entity types, and 8 relation types, and jointly annotate event triggers, event arguments, named entities, and entity relations. They then evaluate different information extraction approaches, including supervised IE models, zero-shot large language models, and fine-tuned LLM-based extraction methods, on a shared test set.
AI.result: CMNIE is shown to be challenging for existing methods. In particular, relation extraction and exact matching of event-argument spans yield relatively low performance. Zero-shot LLMs can often recognize semantically relevant information but frequently fail to match the exact gold-standard span boundaries required by the benchmark.
AI.conclusion: CMNIE serves as a standardized benchmark for research on schema adherence, precise span matching, and joint structured extraction in specialized Chinese news, highlighting current limitations of both traditional supervised IE models and LLM-based methods in this domain.

title: Finishing the Task Is Not Enough: Evaluating Agent Resilience and Considerate Participation under Accumulating Challenge
summary: Sustained deployment of generative AI agents requires more than isolated task success. Agents must remain useful across repeated interactions, changing conditions, and dependencies on people within shared workflows, especially as technical, human, and operational disruptions accumulate over time. We propose operational resilience and considerate participation as two complementary aspects of evaluating such agents: the former captures how agents recover from blocked work while preserving progress and communicating their limits, and the latter captures how their adaptation accounts for affected people, role boundaries, and the surrounding workflow. Yet both remain underexplored under accumulating challenge. We study 120 simulated healthcare trajectories across two generative AI models and twelve stakeholder-derived tasks under light, medium, and heavy challenge. We compare textual action plans, prompted internal assessments, and quantitative structured workload and affect reports to examine how agent behavior and reported state change as challenge accumulates. Regarding operational resilience, agents shift from self-directed recovery toward greater human dependence, while reporting increasing workload and negative affect in structured reports but seldom expressing strain in textual responses. Regarding considerate participation, agents broaden from task-focused adaptation toward task reframing, attention to others, role-boundary adjustment, and wider coordination, with distinct patterns across actions and internal assessments. From these findings, we derive five deployment dilemmas involving persistence, attention, role boundaries, state disclosure, and escalation that require stakeholder specification, further informing technical implications for learning, situated evaluation, and embodied adaptation.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates generative AI agents not just on one-off task success but on how they remain useful and responsible over time under accumulating disruptions in complex workflows.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of generative AI agents focus mainly on isolated tasks and static conditions. In real deployments, agents must operate over many interactions, in dynamic environments, alongside humans, and under various disruptions. There is little understanding or measurement of how such agents maintain usefulness, recover from problems, and interact considerately with people as challenges accumulate, particularly in sensitive domains like healthcare.
AI.method: The authors introduce two evaluation lenses—operational resilience and considerate participation—and design a simulation study in a healthcare context. They simulate 120 care trajectories using two generative AI models and 12 tasks derived from healthcare stakeholders. Each trajectory is run under light, medium, and heavy levels of challenge (i.e., disruptions or complications). They collect and compare three types of data: (1) the agents’ textual action plans, (2) their prompted internal self-assessments, and (3) quantitative structured reports of workload and affect. They then analyze how both behavior and reported internal state evolve as challenges accumulate across conditions and models.
AI.result: For operational resilience, as challenges increase, agents move from trying to recover and continue on their own toward relying more on humans for help and intervention. Their structured reports indicate rising workload and more negative affect, but this strain is rarely visible in their natural-language outputs. For considerate participation, agents’ strategies expand beyond direct task completion: they increasingly reframe tasks, show more explicit concern for others, adjust role boundaries, and coordinate more widely with additional actors in the workflow. The patterns of these adaptations differ between their observable actions and internally prompted assessments.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that generative AI agents’ resilience and social participation patterns change substantially under accumulating disruption, revealing tensions between what they do, what they say, and what they report in structured form. From these observations, the authors articulate five key deployment dilemmas—around persistence, attention allocation, respecting role boundaries, disclosing internal state, and escalation to humans—that cannot be settled purely technically and instead require explicit stakeholder decisions. These dilemmas motivate new technical work on learning mechanisms, context-sensitive evaluation methods, and forms of embodiment that better support long-term, socially aware deployment of AI agents in real workflows.

title: Think Before You Link: Rarity, Reasoning, and Retrieval in Multilingual Entity Linking
summary: Multimodal entity linking grounds entity mentions in text and images to knowledge-base entries. These systems degrade on rare entities, but prior work measures rarity primarily through popularity-based metrics such as pageviews. We broaden this view using knowledge-graph structural metrics that capture how well an entity is documented and connected. These metrics identify many rare entities that popularity metrics miss. Across the resulting rare-entity slices, state-of-the-art accuracy drops by 15.4-39.9%, showing that different rarity definitions expose different failure modes. To address these failures, we introduce a simple, training-free framework in which a reasoning-capable vision-language model iteratively searches and reasons over Wikipedia, gathering evidence dynamically. Controlled experiments show that reasoning and retrieval are complementary. Reasoning alone does not significantly improve accuracy on rare entities. Retrieval without reasoning improves rare-entity accuracy but can hurt overall accuracy. Their combination performs best. On MERLIN, a multilingual multimodal entity linking benchmark over five languages (Hindi, Indonesian, Japanese, Tamil, Vietnamese), our best system improves over the state of the art by 6.9% overall and by up to 23.3% on rare-entity slices. We release MERLIN-Rare, rare-entity test slices for targeted evaluation, with our framework.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how multimodal entity linking systems fail on rare entities, introduces richer graph-based rarity metrics, and proposes a training-free retrieval + reasoning framework that significantly improves performance on a new multilingual benchmark MERLIN, especially for rare entities.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal entity linking systems perform poorly on rare entities, but rarity has been measured mainly by popularity metrics like pageviews, which miss many under-documented or sparsely connected entities. The authors want to better characterize and evaluate rare-entity performance and to design methods that can robustly link such entities across multiple languages and modalities without expensive retraining.
AI.method: 1) Define new rarity metrics based on structural properties of entities in a knowledge graph (e.g., documentation and connectivity) and show they surface rare entities missed by popularity-based metrics. 2) Build MERLIN, a multilingual multimodal entity linking benchmark in five low/medium-resource languages. 3) Propose a training-free framework that uses a reasoning-capable vision–language model to iteratively retrieve and reason over Wikipedia pages: the model searches, inspects evidence, and updates its hypotheses over multiple steps. 4) Conduct controlled ablations comparing reasoning-only, retrieval-only, and combined retrieval+reasoning settings, and evaluate especially on carefully constructed rare-entity slices (MERLIN-Rare).
AI.result: State-of-the-art multimodal entity linking accuracy drops by 15.4–39.9% on rare-entity slices defined by the new structural rarity metrics, demonstrating distinct failure modes compared to popularity-based rarity. In experiments on MERLIN, the proposed framework combining retrieval and reasoning yields the best performance: reasoning alone does not help much on rare entities, retrieval alone boosts rare-entity accuracy but harms overall accuracy, while their combination improves both. The best system improves over previous state of the art by 6.9% overall and up to 23.3% on rare-entity subsets. MERLIN-Rare, a collection of rare-entity test slices, is released for targeted evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Rarity in entity linking should not be defined solely by popularity; structural metrics over knowledge graphs reveal additional classes of rare entities and uncover different system weaknesses. Multimodal entity linking on such entities benefits most from a combination of dynamic retrieval and explicit reasoning within a vision–language model, rather than either component alone. The authors provide both a stronger, training-free baseline and new multilingual benchmarks (MERLIN and MERLIN-Rare) to spur further work on robust rare-entity grounding across text and images.

title: Towards a Deterministic Math Solver for Clinical Language Models
summary: Large language models are unreliable at arithmetic, which is a problem for clinical calculators where a single numerical error changes the recommendation. The standard response is to hardcode each calculator as a validated function, one at a time. We test an alternative: the model does not calculate. Instead, it writes case-specific Python that a restricted local executor runs as a deterministic solver, and the model's task reduces to deciding how to use it. We evaluate this Program-Solve interface on MedCalc-Bench Verified (1,100 cases, 55 calculators) against direct model arithmetic and a hand-written 22-calculator library, using Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-32B-AWQ, after auditing the benchmark's formulas against current clinical guidelines and flagging 16 of 55 with version, use or coefficient concerns. With formulas and gold variables supplied and both routes reading the whole note, handing off to the solver is not a reliable advantage at 7B (75.31% against 72.02%, a paired +3.29 points with a 95% calculator-cluster interval of [-3.49, 10.38]) but is one at 32B (90.53% against 83.47%, +7.05 [0.47, 14.60], clear of zero). The hand-written library is exact on its 440 supported cases but abstains elsewhere (40.0% overall). Adding an executor thus helps some open-weight models more than others even under matched formula, variable and note access, and is not a substitute for verified formulas or reliable variable extraction either way.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates using large language models to generate Python programs that a local executor runs to perform clinical calculator arithmetic, comparing this approach to direct model computation and a fixed calculator library.
AI.motivation: Large language models often make arithmetic mistakes, which is risky in clinical decision support where a single numerical error can change treatment. Existing practice is to implement each clinical calculator as a separate, validated function, which does not scale easily. The authors want to know whether offloading calculation to a deterministic program executor that LLMs control can provide safer, more accurate results across many calculators, without hardcoding each one.
AI.method: The authors propose a Program-Solve interface where the language model does not compute directly but instead writes case-specific Python code that a restricted local executor runs deterministically. Using the MedCalc-Bench Verified dataset (1,100 cases spanning 55 clinical calculators), they audit the benchmark formulas against current guidelines, then compare three approaches: (1) direct arithmetic by Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-32B-AWQ reading the entire clinical note; (2) the same models using the Program-Solve interface to call a solver with supplied formulas and variables; and (3) a hand-written library of 22 calculators that returns exact outputs where supported and abstains otherwise. Performance is measured as accuracy with confidence intervals clustered by calculator.
AI.result: At 7B model size, delegating computation to the solver yields only a small, statistically uncertain improvement over direct model arithmetic (75.31% vs. 72.02% accuracy, a +3.29 percentage point gain with a 95% calculator-cluster confidence interval of [-3.49, 10.38]). At 32B size, the Program-Solve interface gives a clear advantage (90.53% vs. 83.47%, +7.05 points with a 95% interval of [0.47, 14.60]). The hand-written 22-calculator library achieves perfect accuracy on the 440 cases it covers but abstains on all others, leading to only 40% overall coverage. The authors also identify that 16 of the 55 calculators in the benchmark have issues related to formula versioning, usage, or coefficients relative to current clinical guidelines.
AI.conclusion: Using an LLM-controlled program executor can substantially improve arithmetic reliability for some larger open-weight models but offers limited or uncertain benefits for smaller ones when formulas and variables are already provided. This approach does not replace the need for carefully validated calculator formulas or robust variable extraction from clinical notes, and a limited hand-written library, while exact where applicable, cannot provide broad coverage. Overall, adding an executor is a useful but incomplete solution to safety and accuracy issues in clinical LLM applications.

title: Multilingual in Name Only? Cultural and Linguistic Weaknesses of LLMs in Urdu
summary: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for open-ended text generation, yet their behaviour in low-resource languages remains poorly understood. In this work, we question how correct and reliable is the generation of multilingual LLMs when used for the task of story generation. We consider Urdu language as a representative low-resource language. We generate Urdu-Stories, a corpus of 93 stories generated using three contemporary LLMs (GPT-5.1, Qwen-3-Max, DeepSeek-3.1). We manually annotate the errors present in them under a nine-label linguistic, semantic, and cultural taxonomy. Our notable findings suggest that LLMs often make basic errors of grammar and semantics. The stories lack coherence, have unnatural repetition and show pervasive cultural shallowness. We further show using few-shot prompting that the cultural and context errors largely remain unresolved. Our findings highlight the limitations of current LLMs as a reliable source of content generation and information retrieval for low-resource languages.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how well multilingual large language models generate stories in a low-resource language (Urdu) and finds frequent grammatical, semantic, and cultural errors, showing these models are unreliable for such tasks.
AI.motivation: Although multilingual LLMs are widely used for open-ended generation, their performance in low-resource languages is not well understood. The authors aim to systematically study correctness, reliability, and cultural adequacy of LLM-generated stories in Urdu, a representative low-resource language, because users may rely on these models for content creation and information in such languages.
AI.method: The authors construct Urdu-Stories, a corpus of 93 Urdu stories generated by three state-of-the-art multilingual LLMs (GPT-5.1, Qwen-3-Max, DeepSeek-3.1). They manually annotate the errors in these stories using a nine-category taxonomy covering linguistic (e.g., grammar), semantic (e.g., coherence), and cultural aspects. They also experiment with few-shot prompting to see whether providing better context and examples can reduce cultural and contextual errors.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that all tested LLMs frequently produce basic grammatical and semantic errors in Urdu. The generated stories often lack coherence, contain unnatural repetitions, and exhibit superficial or shallow cultural content. Few-shot prompting does not substantially mitigate cultural and context-related errors, indicating that such issues are persistent rather than easily fixable with prompt engineering.
AI.conclusion: Current multilingual LLMs, even state-of-the-art ones, are not reliable for story generation or information-related content creation in low-resource languages like Urdu. Their limitations span grammar, semantics, discourse coherence, and cultural depth, and are not easily addressed by simple prompting strategies. This calls for more targeted research and development to improve LLM capabilities and evaluation in low-resource languages.

title: Studying Without a Syllabus: Task-Agnostic Environment Preprocessing
summary: Before an LLM agent tackles tasks in a new environment, it can inspect available corpora and tools and construct reusable resources such as indices, scripts, or procedural guidance. Most automated adaptation methods, however, rely on task examples, trajectories, or evaluation feedback to decide what to build. Existing task-agnostic approaches avoid this supervision but commit in advance to a preparation strategy for a particular type of environment. We study a more open-ended setting: can an agent study an unfamiliar environment without a syllabus, i.e. before test time and without knowledge of the downstream task distribution, and choose how to prepare it? We formalize task-agnostic environment preprocessing, in which a studying system explores an environment under a budget and produces artifacts for a frozen solver. We compare unaided and archive-equipped meta-agents with fixed synthetic-practice and corpus-processing methods across six heterogeneous benchmarks. A meta-agent variant achieves the highest Avg@3 reward on five benchmarks, while fixed corpus processing remains best on the largest corpus benchmark. Larger study budgets do not reliably improve downstream reward. Nevertheless, studied artifacts reduce the test-time sampling needed to reach a given score, demonstrating how reusable preparation can shift computation from repeated test-time attempts to a pre-task study phase.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how LLM agents can pre-study an unfamiliar environment in a task-agnostic way and build reusable artifacts to help a separate solver perform better later, without knowing future tasks.
AI.motivation: Most current methods for adapting LLM agents to new environments require supervision such as task examples, trajectories, or evaluation feedback, or they hard-code a single preparation strategy per environment type. There is little understanding of whether and how an agent can autonomously study an environment in advance, without knowing the downstream task distribution, and decide what useful resources to construct. The authors aim to formalize and evaluate this more open-ended, task-agnostic environment preprocessing setting.
AI.method: They formalize “task-agnostic environment preprocessing,” where a studying system explores an environment within a fixed budget and produces artifacts (indices, scripts, guidance, etc.) that will later be used by a frozen solver at test time. They instantiate and compare several approaches: unaided meta-agents, archive-equipped meta-agents that can store and reuse artifacts, and fixed strategies like synthetic-practice generation and static corpus processing. They evaluate these approaches across six heterogeneous benchmarks and measure performance using metrics like Avg@3 reward and sample efficiency at test time.
AI.result: Across the six benchmarks, a particular meta-agent variant (which adaptively decides how to study and what artifacts to build) attains the highest Avg@3 reward on five benchmarks, indicating strong overall performance. However, on the largest-corpus benchmark, a fixed corpus-processing strategy still performs best. Increasing the study-time budget does not consistently lead to higher downstream rewards, but the artifacts produced during study reliably reduce the number of test-time samples needed to achieve a given score.
AI.conclusion: Task-agnostic environment preprocessing is a viable way to shift computation from repeated test-time attempts to a pre-task study phase. Adaptive meta-agents can often outperform fixed preparation strategies across diverse environments, though simple corpus processing may remain competitive on very large corpora. While more study time does not guarantee better final performance, precomputed artifacts improve test-time efficiency and show that reusable preparation is a powerful complement to standard LLM agent design.

title: Analyzing Traditional and Neural Approaches to Multilingual Readability Assessment
summary: Transformer-based models excel at Automatic Readability Assessment (ARA), yet feature-based models remain in active use because their predictions tie back to linguistic properties. This matters because readability labels are subjective and rater-dependent, so high accuracy on noisy ground truth may reflect surface patterns rather than the linguistic structure that defines difficulty. We test whether transformers internalize the same features as traditional models across Arabic, English, French, Hindi, and Russian using the ReadMe++ dataset. Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) identify the features driving traditional classifiers, which we then use as TCAV concept sets to probe multilingual XLM-R and language-specific encoders. Transformers recover surface-length, syntactic, and lexical-diversity signals, and reflect the ordinal CEFR structure of the traditional models. Alignment varies by model family, language, and layer, with language-specific encoders tracking traditional models more clearly than XLM-R. High linear separability does not always imply directional influence, limiting linear probing for count-based readability features.

AI.tldr: The paper compares transformer-based readability models with traditional feature-based models across multiple languages, probing whether transformers implicitly capture classic linguistic readability features.
AI.motivation: Although transformers achieve strong performance on Automatic Readability Assessment, their decisions are hard to interpret, while traditional feature-based models are explicitly tied to linguistic properties like syntax and lexical diversity. Because readability labels are subjective and noisy, there is a need to understand if transformer performance truly reflects meaningful linguistic structure or just surface correlations, and how their internal representations relate to established readability features across languages.
AI.method: Using the multilingual ReadMe++ dataset (Arabic, English, French, Hindi, Russian), the authors train traditional feature-based classifiers and transformer encoders (multilingual XLM-R and language-specific models). They apply SHAP to the feature-based models to identify the most influential linguistic features, then convert these features into concept sets for TCAV to probe the transformer representations layer by layer. They also analyze linear separability versus directional influence for count-based readability features.
AI.result: Transformers encode signals corresponding to surface length, syntactic complexity, and lexical diversity and mirror the ordinal CEFR level structure learned by traditional models. However, the strength and clarity of this alignment depends on the model family, language, and network depth; language-specific transformers align more closely with feature-based models than XLM-R. The study further finds that features that are linearly separable in the representation space do not always exert a strong directional influence on the model’s predictions.
AI.conclusion: Transformer-based ARA models do internalize several classic readability-related features and the CEFR difficulty ordering, but this alignment is uneven across languages and architectures. Language-specific models appear more faithful to traditional feature-based signals than multilingual XLM-R. Moreover, simple linear probes can be misleading because linear separability does not guarantee causal or directional importance, so more careful concept-based probing is needed when interpreting readability features in transformers.

title: When Validation Stops Learning: Auditing Update Admission for Continual Embodied Agents
summary: Independent evaluation can reject harmful policy updates yet also prevent useful continual learning. We argue that update admission must be assessed through both error control and retained learning opportunities at a stated interaction budget. We identify a concrete failure: a range-based confidence gate cannot certify unchanged old-task behavior within otherwise substantial budgets. A standard paired-binomial construction reduces this burden when outcome disagreements are rare. We also specify certified historical-reference promotion and a round-level missed-opportunity metric. In a constructed one-step pushing diagnostic with 32 seeds, fresh paired checks admit 31.6% of a common update stream at 2,000 episodes per stage, versus zero for the range-based gate; unconditional replay nevertheless learns better in closed-loop runs. A separate learned-dynamics stress test distinguishes model bias from feedback-selection error. The contribution is an admission-audit protocol with analytical and synthetic evidence; physical-robot and VLA validation remain open.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and analyzes a protocol for auditing which policy updates are admitted during continual learning, balancing safety against missed learning opportunities.
AI.motivation: Independent evaluation mechanisms for policy updates can block harmful changes, but they may also be overly conservative and stop beneficial continual learning. Existing gates based on confidence ranges fail to guarantee preservation of previous-task performance without excessively large interaction budgets. The authors aim to design an update-admission framework that both controls errors and quantifies lost learning opportunities, within realistic budget limits.
AI.method: They formally define update admission as a joint problem of statistical error control and opportunity retention under a fixed interaction budget. They analyze a standard range-based confidence gate and show its limitations in certifying unchanged behavior on old tasks. They then introduce a paired-binomial test construction that lowers the sample burden when disagreements between old and new policies are rare. Additional components include rules for promoting historical references and a round-level metric of missed opportunities. They validate these ideas in a synthetic one-step pushing diagnostic task with multiple random seeds, comparing different gating schemes and unconditional replay, and perform a separate learned-dynamics stress test to separate model bias from feedback-selection error.
AI.result: In the one-step pushing diagnostic with 32 random seeds and 2,000 episodes per stage, the proposed paired-check admission admits 31.6% of the candidate updates from a common update stream, while the baseline range-based gate admits none under the same budget. However, in closed-loop performance, simple unconditional replay still outperforms the gated schemes in terms of learning quality. The learned-dynamics stress test successfully distinguishes between errors arising from model bias and those from how feedback is selected.
AI.conclusion: The work contributes an admission-audit protocol for continual-learning policy updates that explicitly trades off error control against lost learning opportunities, backed by both analytic arguments and synthetic experiments. While their paired-binomial mechanism substantially improves admission rates over range-based confidence gates at realistic budgets, it does not yet dominate simpler baselines in end-to-end learning performance. The authors highlight that further work is needed, especially validation on physical robots and large-scale real-world environments (VLA), to establish the protocol’s practical value.

title: Larger Context Window, Fewer Overcorrections: Optimizing Prompts and Batching for Minimal-Edit Grammatical Error Correction
summary: Minimal-edit Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) is a challenging task for zero- and few-shot prompted Large Language Models (LLMs), which systematically overcorrect and degrade $F_{0.5}$ by rewriting well-formed spans. While fine-tuning provides an effective solution, it imposes substantial infrastructure demands. We introduce a prompt-based approach that closes the gap to fine-tuned models through three advances in GEC prompting methodology. First, we introduce taxonomy-based instructions to enforce minimal-edit constraints with a comprehensive list of grammatical error rules, equipping the LLM with a bounded, metric-aligned scope of correctable edits, which benefits the strongest models while remaining model-dependent overall. Second, we show that batching multiple uncorrected sentences into a single input context acts as a targeted regularizer against overcorrection, systematically reducing the edit rate across diverse LLM families; we hypothesize this arises from attention dilution effect induced by the bounded capacity of self-attention scores. Finally, LLM-assisted Prompt Optimization refines these instructions. Powered by Gemini 3.1-Pro, our prompt achieves $F_{0.5}=78.32$ on the BEA-2019 test set - establishing a new prompt-based SOTA while shrinking the gap to the fine-tuned single-model SOTA (Staruch et al., 2025) to a mere $0.38$ points. Code, prompts, and outputs are publicly available.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a prompt-based method that greatly reduces overcorrection in prompt-only grammatical error correction with LLMs, achieving near fine-tuned performance on BEA-2019.
AI.motivation: Prompted LLMs tend to overcorrect grammatical error correction inputs, hurting the F0.5 score, and fine-tuning—while effective—is resource intensive. The authors want a low-infrastructure, prompt-based solution that approaches fine-tuned performance and enforces minimal edits.
AI.method: They design taxonomy-based instructions listing concrete grammatical error types to constrain edits, use batched inputs (multiple sentences per prompt) to regularize against overcorrection via an attention dilution effect, and apply LLM-assisted prompt optimization (using Gemini 3.1-Pro) to iteratively refine the prompts.
AI.result: The resulting prompt, when used with Gemini 3.1-Pro, attains F0.5=78.32 on the BEA-2019 benchmark, setting a new state of the art among prompt-only methods and reducing the difference to the best fine-tuned single-model system to 0.38 F0.5 points.
AI.conclusion: Carefully engineered prompts—combining error taxonomies, batching strategies, and automated prompt optimization—can nearly match fine-tuned GEC systems, mitigating overcorrection in LLM-based minimal-edit grammatical error correction without the cost of model fine-tuning.

title: Decoupling Readiness from Release for Tail-Aware Scheduling of Agentic LLM Workflows
summary: Agentic LLM workflows consist of sequences of model turns interleaved with tool interactions, so their end-to-end completion time depends not only on inference speed but also on when ready turns are released. Most runtimes release each turn immediately upon readiness. Under contention, this eager release policy can accumulate released but unfinished work; once submitted, those turns can no longer be reordered by the workflow-level policy, increasing tail latency. We present a tail-risk-aware turn release scheduling method that jointly decides which ready turn to release next and how much released but unfinished work to maintain. The method uses a mean--Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) objective to capture the evolving tail risk of unfinished workflows, incorporates online estimates of turn work when prioritizing ready turns, and adapts the released work budget to observed queue pressure. We evaluate the method using real agent execution traces from software engineering tasks across multiple LLMs and workflow arrival rates. The method performs comparably to eager release under light load and substantially reduces the P95 of workflow flow time under contention, achieving up to a \(3.50\times\) speedup.

AI.tldr: They propose a scheduling method for releasing LLM agent turns that reduces tail latency in multi-turn, tool-using workflows, especially under high load.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent runtimes eagerly release each ready turn for inference. Under contention this leads to many in-flight turns that cannot be reordered, inflating tail latency for workflows that are already long or unlucky. There is a need for a workflow-aware release policy that explicitly controls tail risk and overall flow time, rather than just pushing work to the model as soon as it is ready.
AI.method: They formulate turn release as a scheduling problem over ready turns and a budget of released-but-unfinished work. They optimize a combined mean and Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) objective to represent both average and tail latency risk. The policy estimates the remaining work per turn online, prioritizes which ready turn to release next based on these estimates and risk, and dynamically adapts the budget of in-flight work according to observed queue pressure.
AI.result: Using real software-engineering agent traces, across different LLMs and workflow arrival rates, their method matches eager release performance at low load but significantly improves performance under contention, reducing 95th-percentile workflow completion time by up to a 3.5x factor.
AI.conclusion: Tail-risk-aware scheduling of LLM agent turn release, using a mean–CVaR objective and adaptive control of in-flight work, can substantially improve tail latency of multi-turn agentic workflows without hurting performance under light load.

title: Detectable Only Where It Is Confounded: What Verified Duplication Counts Say About Membership Evidence in Language Models
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures. Code, data, and sentence banks: https://github.com/IamArmanNikkhah/detectable-only-where-confounded
summary: When a language model finds a sentence unusually cheap to predict, it is tempting to conclude that the sentence was in its training data. Almost every published test of that inference has had to guess which sentences were in the training data, the members, and which were not. This paper removes the guessing. Two model families, OLMo-2 and Pythia, publish their pretraining corpora, and a public index over those corpora returns the exact number of times any sentence appeared in each. Those counts make three questions answerable directly. The answers form a pincer, closing from two sides. At the duplication levels ordinary text actually has, five models from 1B to 13B parameters carry at most a faint trace of their own exposure. We measure that trace with a design that reads the same sentence through two models, which cancels fluency and quality by construction, and it comes to a rank correlation near -0.08, where -1 would be a perfect relation and 0 none. Where the trace does become strong, above roughly a thousand copies, the two corpora agree on which sentences those are, because they are the famous ones, so exposure can no longer be told apart from fame. Two further measurements show how apparent membership signal gets manufactured. A common way to build a non-member is to change one word of a member. The model does prefer the original, but the gap is the same whether the original appeared once or a hundred times, so what the model is rewarding is the author's word choice, not memory. Above a thousand copies the gap grows with model size on the twelve sentences we can test there, at the same boundary where the pincer closes. And swapping the controls for sentences that differ from the members in register moves a detector from 0.83 to 0.94 AUC, on a scale where 0.5 is a coin flip and 1.0 is perfect separation. We release the sentence banks, counts, and code.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically studies whether language models’ higher likelihood for a sentence indicates that the sentence was in their training data, using models whose full pretraining corpora and duplication counts are known.
AI.motivation: Membership inference for language models is important for privacy, copyright, and safety. Prior work often assumes that if a model assigns unusually high probability to a sentence, that sentence was seen during training, but these studies typically lack ground truth about actual training membership or duplication counts. The authors want to rigorously test whether model preference truly reflects memorization versus more general linguistic competence, using settings where training data and its duplication are fully observable.
AI.method: They use two model families, OLMo-2 and Pythia, that publish their pretraining corpora and allow exact counting of how many times each sentence appears. They build sentence banks with known duplication frequencies, then evaluate multiple models (1B–13B parameters) on these sentences. They compare model behavior across two independently trained families, using a paired design that reads the same sentence through both, which cancels generic fluency/quality effects. They compute rank correlations between duplication counts and model preference, and analyze membership-style tests where non-members are generated by minimal edits (e.g., single-word changes) or by register changes, measuring how AUC changes. They also investigate how effects vary with duplication levels, especially above ~1000 copies.
AI.result: For realistic duplication levels found in normal text, the five evaluated models show only a very weak relationship between training duplication and model preference, with rank correlations around -0.08, close to zero. A strong trace of training exposure appears only for sentences duplicated roughly a thousand times or more, but these highly duplicated sentences are largely famous across both corpora, making it impossible to disentangle mere exposure from general fame. The model’s preference for original vs. single-word-perturbed variants is almost independent of duplication count between 1 and 100, indicating that the preference stems from linguistic appropriateness, not memorized training exposure. Above about a thousand copies, the original-vs-perturbation gap grows with model size for the small set of testable sentences. When they swap controls to use sentences differing mainly in register, a membership detector’s AUC jumps from 0.83 to 0.94, showing that apparent membership signals can arise from stylistic mismatches rather than true memorization.
AI.conclusion: Under realistic duplication, current language models from 1B–13B parameters encode little directly exploitable signal about whether a specific sentence was in their training data, and strong membership signals appear only for highly duplicated, typically famous text where exposure is confounded with public prominence. Many membership inference successes can be explained by stylistic and word-choice effects rather than literal memorization. The work suggests that raw model likelihood is a poor indicator of training membership except for extremely overrepresented content, and provides resources (sentence banks, counts, code) to support more grounded future studies of memorization and membership inference.

title: Demystifying the Privacy-Utility Trade-off in LLM Interactions
summary: The integration of Large Language Models into daily tasks relies on context-rich instructions, inevitably exposing sensitive user information. Current privacy-preserving methods typically employ context-agnostic static rules, causing severe utility degradation. However, the specific mechanisms governing how sanitization impacts downstream performance remain largely underexplored. To address this, we conduct a systematic analysis to deconstruct the privacy-utility trade-off, uncovering three underlying mechanisms: (1) Context-Dependent Utility, which first establishes when to sanitize by revealing that data value shifts from critical constraints to dispensable noise based on user intent; (2) Strategic Adaptation, which subsequently determines how to sanitize by dictating that the choice between removal and replacement depends on the task's reliance on factual integrity versus structural coherence; and (3) Combinatorial Interplay, which finally extends the protection scope by demonstrating that attributes form a semantic web of synergistic dependencies or antagonistic redundancies. Guided by these insights, we introduce an intent-driven local protection framework. By distilling a lightweight model Veilmind-4B to drive a dynamic extraction-sanitization-restoration pipeline, our approach reaches a low-leakage privacy point while preserving substantially higher response utility than existing privacy-oriented baselines, advancing the privacy-utility trade-off toward the Pareto frontier.

AI.tldr: They analyze how different ways of sanitizing prompts for LLMs affect both privacy and task performance, identify three key mechanisms behind the privacy-utility trade-off, and propose an intent-aware sanitization framework with a distilled 4B model that better balances privacy and utility than prior methods.
AI.motivation: Using LLMs in real tasks requires feeding them rich, personal context, which risks leaking sensitive information. Existing privacy protections are mostly static and context-agnostic, often harming usefulness, and we lack a principled understanding of exactly when and how sanitization hurts or preserves downstream performance.
AI.method: They conduct a systematic, mechanism-focused study of the privacy-utility trade-off in LLM prompt sanitization. They decompose it into three mechanisms—context-dependent utility, strategic adaptation (removal vs. replacement), and combinatorial interplay of attributes—then design an intent-driven local protection framework. They distill a lightweight 4B model, Veilmind-4B, to operate a dynamic pipeline that extracts sensitive info, sanitizes it according to task intent and attribute relations, and later restores non-sensitive parts as needed.
AI.result: Their framework achieves a low-privacy-leakage operating point while maintaining substantially higher task utility compared to existing privacy-preserving baselines. Empirically, they show improved balance between protection and performance, approaching the Pareto frontier of the privacy-utility trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Understanding context dependence, sanitization strategy, and attribute interactions is crucial for designing privacy mechanisms that do not overly sacrifice utility. An intent-aware, dynamic extraction–sanitization–restoration pipeline driven by a small local model like Veilmind-4B can significantly improve the practical privacy-utility balance for LLM-based applications.

title: Does Linguistic Structure Enrichment Enhance Coherence Assessment? Not With Current Architectures
summary: Recent advances in large language models have transformed human-computer interaction. Despite their fluency, these models often produce texts that are grammatically correct but semantically incoherent, containing contradictions or disruptions in logical flow. This work investigates whether enriching text with syntactic and rhetorical information can improve incoherence prediction. Our experiments and analysis show that plain texts achieved higher accuracy because the added information was structurally and syntactically incompatible with the language model's architecture. Additionally, to demonstrate the practical importance of coherence assessment, we performed zero-shot experiments on a Brazilian disinformation dataset, suggesting that textual coherence can serve as a proxy for detecting misleading content. Code and models are available at https://github.com/ittozzamV/cohereclassifier.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether adding syntactic and rhetorical annotations helps large language models detect incoherent text, finding instead that plain text works better, and shows coherence can help flag misleading Brazilian content.
AI.motivation: Although large language models generate fluent text, they frequently produce outputs that are logically inconsistent or semantically incoherent. There is a practical need to automatically detect such incoherence, both to improve model outputs and to support downstream tasks like identifying misleading or disinformative content.
AI.method: The authors enrich texts with additional syntactic and rhetorical information and train language-model-based classifiers to predict textual incoherence, comparing performance against models that use plain text only. They conduct experiments to see how these different input representations affect incoherence detection and further run zero-shot experiments on a Brazilian disinformation dataset to test whether coherence scores can proxy for detecting misleading content.
