AI.result: Models using only plain text outperform those augmented with syntactic and rhetorical annotations, indicating that the added structure is not well aligned with the underlying language model architecture. In zero-shot tests on Brazilian disinformation data, coherence-based measures show promise as indicators of misleading content.
AI.conclusion: Enriching inputs with explicit syntactic and rhetorical structures does not necessarily improve incoherence prediction for current language-model architectures and can even hurt performance. Nonetheless, coherence assessment itself is useful and can act as a proxy signal for identifying misleading or disinformative texts, as demonstrated on Brazilian content.

title: Defining AI Agents: A Compendium of Criteria, Metrics, and Benchmarks
summary: The term agent in artificial intelligence lacks a standard definition, complicating the evaluation, comparison, and reproducibility of AI agent research. We address this ambiguity through a survey organized around five dimensions of agenticness: environmental interaction, learning and adaptation, autonomy, goal-directed behavior, and temporal coherence. For each dimension, we examine how the underlying capability has been conceptualized across prior work and synthesize the metrics, benchmarks, and evaluation frameworks used to assess it. This review provides a structured account of the current landscape of agent evaluation, highlighting both established approaches and areas where evaluation remains limited or inconsistent. We additionally introduce the Agent Compendium, a public-facing digital resource that organizes and extends the evaluation methods identified through this review. Together, the survey and compendium provide a common structure for evaluating and comparing agent capabilities across AI systems, supporting more reproducible research, clearer communication, and more systematic study of artificial agents.

AI.tldr: The paper surveys how AI agents are defined and evaluated, organizing existing work into five core dimensions of “agenticness” and providing a digital compendium of evaluation methods to standardize comparison and improve reproducibility.
AI.motivation: The notion of an “agent” in AI is used widely but inconsistently, which makes it hard to compare systems, assess capabilities rigorously, and reproduce results. Different papers emphasize different properties (e.g., autonomy vs. learning) without a shared framework, leading to fragmented evaluation practices. The authors aim to resolve this by clarifying what constitutes an AI agent and by bringing structure to how agent capabilities are measured.
AI.method: The authors conduct a structured survey of prior work on AI agents, organizing the literature around five dimensions of agenticness: environmental interaction, learning and adaptation, autonomy, goal-directed behavior, and temporal coherence. For each dimension, they analyze conceptual definitions in the literature and collect existing metrics, benchmarks, and evaluation frameworks. They then build the Agent Compendium, a public digital resource that categorizes and extends these evaluation tools.
AI.result: The survey yields a taxonomy of agent capabilities along the five dimensions and maps existing evaluation methods to each. It identifies which areas have mature, widely used benchmarks and which suffer from sparse, inconsistent, or ad-hoc evaluation. The Agent Compendium is released as a structured repository that aggregates and organizes these evaluation methods for community use.
AI.conclusion: By providing a clear, multidimensional framework for understanding agenticness and a curated compendium of evaluation tools, the work standardizes how AI agents can be characterized and compared. This structure is intended to enable more reproducible experiments, clearer reporting of agent capabilities, and more systematic, cumulative research on artificial agents across different AI systems and paradigms.

title: LLM-Anchored Paralinguistic Enrichment for Alzheimer's Disease Detection
summary: Speech-based automatic detection of Alzheimer's disease (AD) provides a non-invasive and scalable approach to early cognitive screening. AD affects both lexical-semantic organization and speech production, including atypical pauses and word elongations. However, existing methods have yet to fully integrate these paralinguistic cues with linguistic content. We propose LLM-Anchored Paralinguistic Enrichment (LAPE), which enriches LLM-derived linguistic representations with paralinguistic cues through three coordinated innovations. The first is prosodic event textualization, which enables the LLM to model pauses and elongations jointly with lexical content by encoding them as explicit markers with bounded duration-aware repetition. The second is lexico-prosodic unitization and chunking, which preserves event identity and magnitude in both modalities by pooling only consecutive word units. The third is text-anchored paralinguistic fusion, which integrates local and utterance-level speech features by using NormGate to normalize and dynamically scale them relative to text. We evaluate LAPE on ADReSS and ADReSSo using participant-level cross-validation and leave-one-subject-out evaluation. LAPE achieves state-of-the-art performance across all four primary settings. Code will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: They propose a method (LAPE) that combines prosodic/paralinguistic cues with LLM-based text features to improve automatic Alzheimer’s detection from speech, achieving state-of-the-art results on ADReSS and ADReSSo.
AI.motivation: Existing automatic Alzheimer’s detection from speech usually focuses on textual/linguistic content or uses prosodic features separately, but does not tightly integrate prosodic/paralinguistic cues (like pauses and elongations) with large language model (LLM) representations of text. Since Alzheimer’s affects both what people say (lexical-semantic organization) and how they say it (speech production and timing), leveraging both jointly should yield better detection. The authors seek a principled way to encode, align, and fuse these two modalities so that LLMs can model them together effectively.
AI.method: They introduce LLM-Anchored Paralinguistic Enrichment (LAPE), composed of three innovations: (1) Prosodic event textualization: encode pauses and word elongations directly into the text stream as special markers, with repetition patterns representing their (bounded) durations, so LLMs can process them jointly with words. (2) Lexico-prosodic unitization and chunking: align and group consecutive word units so that each chunk preserves both the lexical identity and the associated prosodic event type and magnitude; pooling is constrained to neighboring units to maintain local structure. (3) Text-anchored paralinguistic fusion: use a mechanism called NormGate to normalize utterance-level and local acoustic/prosodic features and dynamically scale them relative to the LLM text representations, enabling multi-scale speech–text fusion anchored on the textual backbone.
AI.result: On the ADReSS and ADReSSo benchmarks for Alzheimer’s detection from speech, under both participant-level cross-validation and leave-one-subject-out evaluation, LAPE delivers state-of-the-art performance across all four primary experimental settings, outperforming previous approaches that use only text, only paralinguistic cues, or simpler fusion schemes.
AI.conclusion: Encoding prosodic events as text markers, carefully chunking lexico-prosodic units, and fusing normalized speech features with LLM-based text representations yields a more informative joint representation for Alzheimer’s detection from speech. This integrated LAPE framework better captures both lexical-semantic and speech-production abnormalities characteristic of Alzheimer’s disease and sets a new performance bar on standard benchmarks, indicating that LLM-centered but paralinguistically enriched modeling is a promising direction for non-invasive cognitive screening systems.

title: The Agent Incident Registry: Toward Preventing Repeated AI Agent Failures
summary: AI agents increasingly act through tools and delegated authority, but general incident repositories rarely capture the mechanisms needed to compare public failures with agent-security evaluations. We present the Agent Incident Registry (AIR), a source-linked catalog containing \N{} records of agent-related events disclosed from \Yfirst{} through \Ylast{}. Each record includes supporting evidence, a stable identifier, and missingness-aware labels for causal role, disclosure class, mechanism, and outcome. Among the \Nprimary{} generative-system records in which the agent acted, \Rprimary{} involved realized harm (\Pprimary\%). Realized outcomes concentrate in in-the-wild and safety-failure records, while responsible disclosures and research demonstrations are overwhelmingly demonstrated; the aggregate share therefore characterizes collection composition rather than deployment risk. After initial curation, a second human reviewer checked all \N{} records and their existing labels for completeness and correctness. In a deployment-analogue audit, InjecAgent's \NInjecAgentCases{} cases occupy three of AIR's twelve surfaces and are all attacker-triggered, whereas AIR contains \Nsafety{} no-adversary safety failures. AIR supports source-grounded case retrieval and evaluation-scope auditing, not failure-rate or control-efficacy estimation.

AI.tldr: They introduce AIR, a structured registry of real-world AI agent incidents, enabling consistent comparison and analysis of agent failures and evaluations.
AI.motivation: Existing incident databases for AI do not capture the specific mechanisms and context needed to meaningfully compare failures of AI agents that use tools or act with delegated authority, especially against lab-based security and safety evaluations. This gap makes it hard to understand how evaluation results relate to real-world agent deployments and incidents.
AI.method: They build the Agent Incident Registry (AIR), a source-linked catalog of agent-related incidents collected over a defined time period. Each entry includes evidence links, stable identifiers, and carefully designed, "missingness-aware" labels covering causal role, disclosure type, mechanism, and outcome. Records are curated by one annotator and then fully reviewed by a second human annotator for quality. They also perform an audit-style comparison between AIR records and InjecAgent’s evaluation cases, mapping InjecAgent’s scenarios onto AIR’s incident “surfaces” and contrasting attacker-triggered incidents with no-adversary safety failures captured in AIR.
AI.result: AIR currently contains N total records, with N_primary generative-system records where the agent actively acted; R_primary of these involved realized harm, corresponding to P_primary%. Realized-harm outcomes are concentrated in in-the-wild events and safety failures, whereas responsible disclosures and research demos mostly show only demonstrated, not realized, harm. InjecAgent’s N_InjecAgentCases cases map onto 3 of AIR’s 12 defined incident surfaces and are exclusively attacker-triggered, while AIR also includes N_safety incidents that are safety failures without any adversary. These results illustrate how AIR’s structure can be used to analyze where evaluations do and do not match real-world incident profiles.
AI.conclusion: AIR provides a structured, source-grounded registry for AI agent incidents that enables more precise retrieval of cases and auditing of what kinds of incidents are in scope for various evaluations. It is explicitly not intended to estimate real-world failure rates or the effectiveness of controls, but rather to support better alignment between evaluation designs and the diversity of real agent failures observed in practice.

title: SearchAtlas: Analyzing Agentic Search Strategies via Evidential Query Graphs
comment: Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026. 30 pages, 9 figures, including appendices
summary: LLM search agents are often evaluated on final-answer accuracy, overlooking the process. Analyzing a search strategy requires understanding how credible evidence is retrieved to address question constraints. This valuable information is buried in raw search trajectories that are long and difficult to parse. We introduce SearchAtlas, a framework that converts search trajectories into structured graphs whose edges represent how evidence is propagated across the reasoning trace, from the query that retrieves it to the final answer. Our automated parsing pipeline achieves a mean edge F1 of 86.0% against human-annotated graphs and remains consistent across repeated runs. We analyze five search agents on three benchmarks, revealing systematic differences in search scale and evidence aggregation. SearchAtlas exposes fragmented answer support, question constraints that do not reach the answer, and unverified parametric knowledge entering the response. These process failures are strongly associated with incorrect answers, even more so than an LLM judge given either the raw trajectory or the ordered query list, suggesting that the constructed graphs provide useful interpretability. Moreover, an audit of cases in which process-diagnostic scores disagree with final-answer correctness shows that they capture information not reducible to answer accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SearchAtlas, a framework that transforms LLM search trajectories into structured evidence-propagation graphs to better evaluate and interpret search agents beyond final-answer accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM-based search agents focus largely on whether the final answer is correct, ignoring how the answer was obtained. Raw search trajectories are long, complex, and hard to interpret, making it difficult to understand whether credible evidence was retrieved, how it was used, and where reasoning broke down. There is a need for a systematic way to inspect and compare search strategies, identify process failures (like missing constraints or unverified knowledge), and link them to answer quality.
AI.method: The authors design SearchAtlas, a framework that automatically converts an LLM search agent’s trajectory (queries, retrieved evidence, intermediate reasoning steps, and final answer) into a structured graph. In this graph, nodes represent elements such as queries, evidence, and answer components, and edges capture how evidence is propagated from retrieval to final answer. They build an automated parsing pipeline to construct these graphs from raw trajectories and evaluate its accuracy against human-annotated graphs using edge-level F1. They then apply SearchAtlas to five different search agents across three benchmarks, computing process-diagnostic scores and analyzing patterns in search scale, evidence aggregation, and constraint handling.
AI.result: The automated parsing pipeline achieves a mean edge F1 of 86.0% versus human-annotated graphs and is stable across repeated runs, indicating reliable graph construction. Analysis of five search agents on three benchmarks uncovers systematic differences in how they search and aggregate evidence. SearchAtlas highlights issues such as fragmented answer support, question constraints that fail to influence the final answer, and unverified parametric knowledge being injected into responses. These process-level failures correlate strongly with incorrect answers—more strongly than an LLM judge provided only the raw trajectory or the ordered query list—showing that the graph representation adds interpretive value. Additionally, in cases where process-diagnostic scores and final-answer correctness disagree, the diagnostics still capture meaningful information not reducible to accuracy alone.
AI.conclusion: SearchAtlas offers a structured, graph-based way to interpret and evaluate LLM search agents by focusing on the evidence-propagation process rather than just final-answer correctness. Its parsing is accurate and consistent, and the resulting graphs reveal process failures that are tightly linked to incorrect answers and not fully captured by conventional evaluations or LLM judges. This suggests that process-aware diagnostics are a valuable complement to answer-based metrics, enabling deeper auditing, comparison, and improvement of search agents.

title: Grounding Agent Memory: Environment-Probing Curation for Enterprise Agents
summary: Persistent memory is entering production-oriented agent platforms to help long-horizon agents accumulate experience across sessions. Yet a post-task curator agent restricted to completed trajectories can preserve errors, overgeneralize partial evidence, or retain stale knowledge. We introduce environment-probing curation, a deployment-compatible extension that gives an existing asynchronous curator agent least-privilege, read-only world tools to check, scope, and refresh candidate memories. It requires no model retraining and leaves the task agent, retriever, memory representation, and production write authority unchanged. In a production-like GitHub Copilot (GHCP) harness built on its SDK, we compare stateless execution, full in-context learning, GHCP + Mem, and GHCP + Mem (w/ Env Probing) on CLBench database exploration and 90 adapted APEX management-consulting tasks. On CLBench, probing raises pass rate from 39% to 73% and pass-discounted reward from 8.60 to 22.60 while reducing queries from 8.8 to 4.7 per question and task-agent cost from \$3.38 to \$1.68. Across six APEX worlds, all 18 memory-versus-baseline mean reward comparisons are positive and task-agent tool calls fall by 16--75%; probing gives the best task-agent reward gain per dollar in five worlds. Probing also attains higher mean reward than GHCP + Mem on both Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.7 without schema drift. Environment probing therefore turns existing agent-memory curation into an environment-informed, auditable process while preserving a compact task-time interface.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes environment-probing curation for persistent memory in production-like agent systems, enabling a curator agent to verify and update memories via read-only environment interactions, substantially improving performance and efficiency on realistic benchmarks without retraining models or changing task-time interfaces.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon AI agents now use persistent memory to accumulate experience across sessions, but current post-hoc curation processes only see completed trajectories. This constraint can cause persistent errors, overgeneralization from limited evidence, and outdated knowledge to be stored. The authors are motivated to design a way to make memory curation more accurate, up-to-date, and trustworthy in real production-like systems, while minimally disturbing existing components and without expensive retraining.
AI.method: They introduce environment-probing curation: a least-privilege, read-only extension for existing asynchronous curator agents. The curator, when deciding what to store, can call world tools and query the environment to check the validity, scope, and freshness of candidate memories. The method is deployment compatible: it requires no retraining and does not change the task agent, retriever, memory representation, or write authority. The approach is instantiated in a GitHub Copilot (GHCP) harness, where variants are compared: stateless execution, full in-context learning, GHCP with memory, and GHCP with memory plus environment probing.
AI.result: In a production-like GHCP SDK harness, environment probing significantly boosts performance and efficiency. On CLBench database exploration, probing raises pass rate from 39% to 73% and pass-discounted reward from 8.60 to 22.60, while nearly halving queries per question (8.8 to 4.7) and task-agent cost ($3.38 to $1.68). On 90 adapted APEX management-consulting tasks across six worlds, all 18 comparisons of memory vs. baseline show higher mean reward, and task-agent tool calls drop by 16–75%. Probing yields the best task-agent reward gain per dollar in five of six worlds and outperforms GHCP + Mem on both Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.7 models, without schema drift.
AI.conclusion: Environment-probing curation converts existing memory curation into an environment-informed and auditable process, while keeping the task-time interface simple and compact. By allowing a curator agent to verify and refresh candidate memories via read-only world tools, the approach mitigates error preservation, overgeneralization, and staleness, and delivers large gains in performance and cost-efficiency on realistic benchmarks without retraining or major system changes.

title: Auto-RecSys: Harnessing Autonomous Research Agents for Industry-Scale Recommender System
summary: Auto-research agents have shown the potential to automate hypothesis generation, experiment execution, and iterative refinement. However, scaling this paradigm to industry-scale recommendation models introduces two challenges: (1) long feedback loops, where model training can take days, making serial iteration prohibitively slow and requiring parallel exploration across multiple research directions; and (2) system complexity, where large configurations, fragile infrastructure dependencies, and multi-day GPU jobs require robust and recoverable execution. We present Auto-RecSys, an autonomous research system for long-horizon experimentation on industry-scale recommendation models. Auto-RecSys addresses these challenges through three harness designs: (1) distributed asynchronous execution for running multiple experiments in parallel across servers, (2) centralized cross-server memory for persistent and recoverable execution across sessions and failures, and (3) cognitive-procedural separation, where natural-language skill files guide LLM reasoning while deterministic scripts enforce operational correctness. Auto-RecSys further employs a dual-loop self-evolving architecture: an Execution Evolution Loop in which model-specific playbooks accumulate operational knowledge by recording failed attempts and crystallizing successful pipelines, and an Idea Evolution Loop in which experimental outcomes inform subsequent ideation. Evaluated on recommendation models, Auto-RecSys significantly reduces the human time required per experiment cycle and improves execution reliability as its playbooks mature.

AI.tldr: Auto-RecSys is an autonomous system that runs large-scale recommendation experiments reliably and in parallel, reducing human effort and improving robustness over time via self-evolving playbooks.
AI.motivation: Existing auto-research agents work on short, simple ML workflows, but industry-scale recommendation models have long training cycles and complex, fragile infrastructure. This makes sequential experimentation slow and error-prone, and failures costly, so a more robust, parallel, and recoverable autonomous system is needed.
AI.method: The authors design Auto-RecSys around three execution harnesses—(1) distributed asynchronous execution to run many experiments in parallel, (2) centralized cross-server memory to persist state and recover from crashes or restarts, and (3) cognitive–procedural separation, where LLMs use natural-language skill files for reasoning while deterministic scripts ensure correct low-level operations. On top of this, they implement a dual-loop self-evolving architecture: an Execution Evolution Loop that builds model-specific operational playbooks from past failures and successes, and an Idea Evolution Loop that uses experimental results to guide new hypotheses and experiment designs.
AI.result: On large-scale recommendation model workloads, Auto-RecSys cuts down the human time needed per experiment cycle and increases execution reliability, with performance improving as its accumulated playbooks grow richer.
AI.conclusion: An autonomous research framework tailored for long-horizon, industry-scale recommendation systems can make experimentation more efficient and reliable. By combining robust distributed infrastructure, persistent memory, procedural safeguards, and self-evolving playbooks, Auto-RecSys effectively scales auto-research to complex real-world RecSys settings.

title: Fork Where the Model Changes Its Mind: Belief-Shift Branching for Tree-Structured Reinforcement Learning
summary: Tree-structured rollouts give critic-free reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) step-level credit: fork a chain at an intermediate point, and sibling outcome differences estimate step value. Each fork adds sampling cost, so realistic budgets typically allow only a few forks per chain. A fork placed where the outcome is already largely settled yields siblings that mostly agree and provide almost no credit signal; hence, for a given tree size, where forks are placed largely determines how much step-level RL can gain. Most existing mainstream methods place forks by structure, such as fixed lengths, midpoints, and delimiters, or by next-token entropy. We formalize fork placement as locating the \emph{pivots} of the chain's value curve, where the expected outcome turns. We propose \emph{belief-shift branching}: read the model's answer belief at candidate boundaries and fork just before the step where consecutive beliefs diverge most. Three instantiations, none needing step-level supervision, span access levels: a black-box probe, a logit-lens depth profile, and a learned activation direction, which is fit offline and therefore used only in the validation before RL training. The signal only \emph{places} forks, and the probe costs about $1\%$ of step compute on mathematics and under $5\%$ on code when it runs inside the rollout engine. In that validation, against Monte-Carlo value curves, a belief-shift signal ranks first in each of the eight model$\times$benchmark panels, ahead of entropy, structural, and LLM-judge baselines. In RL across three model families and two domains, belief-shift forking leads every mathematics aggregate, on OLMo-3-7B by $+2.6$ aggregate and $+2.9$ on AIME 2026 over the strongest baseline, and sweeps every OLMo code column, by $+6.5$ on LiveCodeBench-medium.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a method, belief-shift branching, to optimally place forks in tree-structured rollouts for critic-free reinforcement learning, improving step-level credit assignment and downstream performance in math and code tasks.
AI.motivation: In tree-structured RL with verifiable rewards, each additional fork in a rollout is expensive, so only a limited number can be used. If forks are placed at points where the final outcome is already mostly determined, sibling trajectories provide little information for credit assignment, weakening the benefits of step-level RL. Existing fork placement heuristics (fixed structural positions or next-token entropy) do not explicitly target the points where the model’s belief about success is actually changing, potentially wasting compute. There is a need for a principled, low-cost way to identify the most influential steps—pivots—along a trajectory where branching yields maximal learning signal.
AI.method: The authors formalize fork placement as identifying pivots on the trajectory’s value curve—points where the expected outcome shifts. They introduce belief-shift branching: the model’s belief in success is measured at candidate boundaries, and forks are inserted just before the step with the largest consecutive belief change. They provide three implementations that do not require step-level supervision and vary by access level: (1) a black-box probe that queries the model’s answer belief at boundaries; (2) a logit-lens-based depth profile that reads internal logits as a proxy for belief; and (3) a learned activation direction that maps activations to success belief, trained offline and used only in validation prior to RL. The belief-shift signal is used solely to choose fork locations; rollout and RL proceed as usual. The probe overhead is small (≈1% extra compute on math, <5% on code) when integrated into the rollout engine. They evaluate fork-placement quality via Monte Carlo value curves and then test RL performance across multiple model families and benchmarks in math and code.
AI.result: In validation against Monte Carlo value curves, the belief-shift signal best identifies high-impact pivot locations, ranking first across all eight model×benchmark settings and outperforming baselines based on entropy, structural rules, and LLM-judge assessments. In end-to-end RL experiments across three model families and two domains (math and code), belief-shift branching improves final task performance over the strongest existing fork-placement baselines. On OLMo-3-7B for math, it yields a +2.6 aggregate improvement and +2.9 on AIME 2026. For code, it achieves gains across all OLMo code benchmarks, including a +6.5 improvement on LiveCodeBench-medium. These results show that better fork placement alone, without changing the RL objective or rewards, significantly boosts learning efficiency and capability.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing where to branch in tree-structured rollouts is crucial for effective step-level credit assignment in critic-free RL with verifiable rewards. By targeting pivots in the model’s evolving belief—rather than structural positions or entropy alone—belief-shift branching more efficiently allocates limited branching budget. The proposed belief-based signals are inexpensive, require no step-level labels, and generalize across models and domains. Empirically, they consistently outperform existing baselines in both proxy pivot-detection metrics and actual RL performance on math and code, indicating that belief-aware fork placement is a powerful and practical lever for improving RLVR-style training.

title: Structurally Speaking: Motif-Oriented Graph Captioning through Bidirectional Graph-Text Translation
summary: Graph captions should help readers understand graph structure, rather than simply translate adjacency matrices into long textual edge lists. A useful graph caption abstracts connectivity into recognizable motifs, such as hubs, paths, cycles, cliques, and bridges, because these motifs provide compact structural units that are easier to read, compare, and recover. In this paper, we study motif-oriented graph captioning as a bidirectional graph-text translation task, where captions must both preserve enough topology for graph recovery and express the graph through concise motif-level descriptions. We show that direct prompting of GPT-5.1 often produces graph-recoverable captions by enumerating node-to-node connections, but these captions are verbose and can contain inconsistent motif interpretations. To address this gap, we introduce Structurally Speaking, a lightweight structured prompting protocol that guides translation between explicit connectivity and motif-level abstraction. Experiments on a synthetic motif-based dataset show that structured prompting produces shorter and more motif-consistent captions while maintaining comparable graph recovery. These results suggest that explicit topology-to-motif reasoning guidance can make LLM-generated graph captions more interpretable without model fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a structured prompting protocol to generate concise, motif-based graph captions that remain detailed enough to reconstruct the original graph.
AI.motivation: Traditional graph captions often degenerate into verbose edge lists that are hard to read and fail to highlight important structural patterns like hubs, cycles, and cliques. There is a need for captions that both preserve recoverable topology and provide high-level, human-interpretable summaries.
AI.method: The authors frame graph captioning as a bidirectional graph-text translation problem, where captions must allow graph recovery and convey motif-level abstractions. They evaluate direct prompting of GPT-5.1 and then introduce a lightweight, structured prompting protocol called Structurally Speaking that explicitly guides the model from raw connectivity to motif descriptions and back.
AI.result: On a synthetic dataset built from known motifs, Structurally Speaking yields captions that are shorter and more consistent in their use of motifs than captions from direct GPT-5.1 prompting, while achieving similar performance in reconstructing the original graphs from the captions.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly guiding LLMs to reason from topology to motifs via structured prompting improves the interpretability and conciseness of graph captions without sacrificing graph recoverability, and this can be done without any model fine-tuning.

title: MOSAIC: Query-Aware Exploration Policy Adaptation for GraphRAG
summary:
Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) can connect evidence distributed across a corpus graph, but most systems use largely shared exploration procedures across queries. This creates a structural mismatch: direct facts may need compact local neighborhoods, comparisons need balanced coverage of multiple targets, and mediated questions may require deeper paths through weakly related connectors. We present Mosaic, a training-free framework that formulates GraphRAG retrieval as a per-query control problem. An LLM analyzer converts query-specific evidence requirements into a bounded policy over seed selection, graph traversal, stopping, and evidence selection, while the corpus graph, indexes, scoring functions, grounding procedure, and answer generator remain shared.
  On GraphRAG-Bench, Mosaic achieves query-weighted Answer Correctness of 76.97 on Medical and 64.33 on Novel, improving over the strongest previously reported overall results by 5.13 and 4.43 points. On Medical, it reaches 95.1 Evidence Recall and 86.1 Context Relevancy. Controlled comparisons on an identical graph and generator show that no fixed narrow, medium, or wide policy is consistently optimal; Mosaic improves by 9.96 points over the strongest canonical fixed policy. Relative to Fixed Wide, it evaluates 81.9% fewer paths and retains 47.2% fewer evidence items. Transfer experiments on HotpotQA, MuSiQue, and 2WikiMultiHopQA further show that the policy interface can be applied without benchmark-specific retriever training.

AI.tldr: Mosaic is a training-free GraphRAG framework that dynamically adapts graph retrieval policies per query using an LLM, substantially improving answer correctness, evidence recall, and efficiency over fixed retrieval policies and prior systems.
AI.motivation: Existing GraphRAG systems largely use one-size-fits-all exploration policies for all queries, causing a mismatch between query needs (local facts vs comparisons vs multi-hop mediated reasoning) and retrieval behavior, which harms accuracy and efficiency.
AI.method: Formulate GraphRAG retrieval as a per-query control problem. An LLM "analyzer" interprets each query and outputs a bounded control policy specifying seed node selection, traversal width/depth, stopping criteria, and evidence selection strategy over a shared corpus graph and retrieval stack. This policy is then executed without any additional training.
AI.result: On GraphRAG-Bench, Mosaic achieves 76.97 and 64.33 query-weighted Answer Correctness on Medical and Novel, surpassing previous best by 5.13 and 4.43 points. On Medical it attains 95.1 Evidence Recall and 86.1 Context Relevancy. Under controlled conditions with identical graph and generator, Mosaic beats the best fixed (narrow/medium/wide) policy by 9.96 points, while reducing evaluated paths by 81.9% and retained evidence by 47.2% compared to Fixed Wide. It transfers successfully to HotpotQA, MuSiQue, and 2WikiMultiHopQA without retriever retraining.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, LLM-driven per-query control over graph retrieval policies is more accurate and efficient than any fixed policy, works in a training-free setup, and transfers across multi-hop QA benchmarks, demonstrating that query-specific retrieval control is key to unlocking GraphRAG’s potential.

title: Using Semantic Uncertainty to Estimate Transition Relevance in Turn-taking
comment: Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026. 21 pages, 4 figures, 9 tables
summary: Turn-taking is a fundamental mechanism that governs when interlocutors speak and listen. Although Spoken Dialogue Systems (SDS) exploit a range of linguistic, acoustic, and non-verbal cues, they produce ill-timed responses in unscripted interaction. A central challenge is anticipating Transition Relevance Places (TRPs), or opportunities, not obligations, for a listener to take the floor. Human listeners do not wait for turn endings; as an utterance unfolds, they use expectations about its developing meaning to anticipate TRPs and decide whether to take the floor. We examine whether these evolving expectations can be modeled through semantic uncertainty -- an LLM-derived measure of how strongly a turn so far constrains what may plausibly come next. To do so, we sample possible continuations of an ongoing turn and use changes in semantic dispersion to identify TRPs within turns. We evaluate this account on a dataset with TRP labels derived from real-time listener responses, rather than retrospective annotation. Our approach substantially outperforms prompt-based and fine-tuned text-only baselines, providing empirical support for the view that evolving semantic constraints inform perceived turn-taking opportunities in unscripted interaction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a method to predict conversational turn-taking points (TRPs) by modeling semantic uncertainty with LLMs, and shows it outperforms text-only baselines.
AI.motivation: Spoken Dialogue Systems struggle with timing their responses correctly in unscripted conversations, largely because they fail to anticipate natural opportunities for turn-taking (TRPs) as humans do. Understanding and modeling how humans anticipate these opportunities can help build more natural interactive systems.
AI.method: The authors define a measure of semantic uncertainty using a large language model: they sample multiple possible continuations of an ongoing turn and compute semantic dispersion among these continuations. They track changes in this dispersion over the unfolding utterance and use them to detect likely Transition Relevance Places. They then test their approach against prompt-based and fine-tuned text-only baselines on a dataset where TRPs are labeled based on real-time listener behavior.
AI.result: The semantic-uncertainty-based model identifies TRPs within turns more accurately than prompt-based and fine-tuned text-only baselines on the evaluated dataset with real-time listener-derived TRP labels.
AI.conclusion: Evolving semantic constraints during an utterance, as captured by changes in LLM-based semantic uncertainty, provide a strong signal for perceived turn-taking opportunities in unscripted dialogue, and can substantially improve turn-timing in spoken dialogue systems.

title: Benchmark Radar: A Living Database and Search Engine for AI Benchmarks and Evaluation
summary: Benchmark researchers and developers of large language models (LLMs) and other AI systems need to find relevant evaluations, locate their benchmark datasets and code, and understand the settings behind reported scores. We present Benchmark Radar, a living database and search engine for retrieval and discovery of AI benchmarks, covering LLM evaluation, agentic and tool-use benchmarks, coding, reasoning, safety, and domain-specific evaluations. The system combines daily discovery of benchmark papers, repositories, datasets, and releases with a searchable benchmark catalog, mentions in model cards and technical reports, and score histories. It retains source identities and citations so readers can inspect candidate benchmarks and their evaluation evidence. Daily discovery draws on 37 sources: 13 direct connectors and 24 first-party research and engineering feeds. The catalog contains 1,283 source records drawn from 4 benchmark catalogs and 12,916 numeric observations on 790 records. We describe collection and retrieval, audit the full catalog, and examine benchmark saturation, adoption trends, and the limits of score comparisons. A worked example walks through a complete prior-art search, showing how to query the catalog and inspect benchmark evidence when designing a new evaluation. We release the web dashboard with a benchmark leaderboard, a Pareto frontier view of score against measured use, saturation and trend views, daily feeds, downloadable evidence, a command-line interface (CLI) for offline queries, and reproducible analysis.

AI.tldr: Introduces Benchmark Radar, a searchable, continuously updated database of AI benchmarks, their datasets, code, and reported scores, to help researchers systematically find, assess, and compare evaluations for LLMs and other AI systems.
AI.motivation: Researchers and developers working on LLMs and other AI systems struggle to discover relevant benchmarks, locate their data and code, and understand the conditions behind published scores. Existing information is scattered across papers, repositories, model cards, and reports, making it hard to perform thorough prior-art searches, assess benchmark saturation, and interpret score comparisons. A centralized, structured, and up-to-date resource is needed to organize this growing landscape of benchmarks and their usage.
AI.method: The authors build Benchmark Radar, which automatically performs daily discovery of benchmark-related artifacts (papers, repositories, datasets, releases) from 37 sources, including 13 direct connectors and 24 first-party research and engineering feeds. They aggregate this into a unified, searchable catalog that preserves source identities and citations, links to mentions in model cards and technical reports, and tracks numeric score observations over time. They then audit the catalog and analyze it to study benchmark coverage, saturation, adoption trends, and the reliability of score comparisons. They also implement user-facing tools: a web dashboard with multiple views (leaderboard, Pareto frontier, saturation and trends), daily feeds, a CLI, and downloadable evidence for offline analysis.
AI.result: Benchmark Radar currently contains 1,283 source records aggregated from four existing benchmark catalogs and other sources, with 12,916 numeric score observations across 790 benchmark records. The system can surface benchmark usage in model cards and technical reports, maintain score histories, and support complex queries over benchmarks and their evidence. The authors’ audit and analyses reveal patterns of benchmark saturation and adoption trends, and highlight limitations in how benchmark scores can be compared across models and settings. The worked example demonstrates that the system can support a complete prior-art search for designing new evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark Radar provides an extensible, continuously updated infrastructure for discovering and analyzing AI benchmarks across LLMs and related areas. By centralizing benchmark metadata, score histories, and usage evidence, it makes it easier to conduct systematic prior-art searches, evaluate benchmark saturation and trends, and reason more carefully about score comparisons. The released web dashboard, CLI, and reproducible analyses aim to support both researchers designing new evaluations and practitioners seeking to understand and choose among existing benchmarks.

title: Robust Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Incomplete Modalities via Semantic-aware Completeness based Reconstruction
comment: Accepted to the Findings of EMNLP 2026
summary: Recent multimodal sentiment analysis studies increasingly adopt text-centric fusion approaches to exploit the rich sentiment information inherent in the textual modality. However, these approaches often suffer from performance degradation during inference due to partially missing or noisy data in real-world scenarios, especially when sentiment-related cues are missing. To address this issue, we introduce a new completeness estimation approach that quantifies the degree of sentiment-relevant information preserved in incomplete data to guide the reconstruction of missing semantics. Furthermore, we propose a training strategy that stabilizes multi-task learning while jointly optimizing sentiment prediction and completeness estimation. Extensive experiments and in-depth analyses on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach enables more accurate semantic reconstruction, leading to more precise sentiment prediction.

AI.tldr: They propose a multimodal sentiment analysis method that estimates how complete the sentiment-relevant information is in partially missing/noisy inputs and uses this estimate to better reconstruct missing semantics, improving sentiment prediction.
AI.motivation: Text is usually the strongest modality for sentiment, so recent work uses text-centric fusion. But in real applications, some modalities or sentiment cues can be missing or noisy, which degrades performance, especially if critical sentiment-related signals are absent. There is a need for models that can recognize and compensate for incomplete sentiment information.
AI.method: They introduce a completeness estimation module that quantifies how much sentiment-relevant information remains in incomplete multimodal data. This estimate then guides the semantic reconstruction process for missing parts. In addition, they design a joint training strategy that treats sentiment prediction and completeness estimation as related tasks in a multi-task learning framework, with techniques to stabilize this joint optimization.
AI.result: On three standard multimodal sentiment analysis benchmarks, their method yields more accurate reconstruction of missing semantic information compared to baselines, which translates into better sentiment classification performance. They also report detailed analyses validating the effectiveness of completeness estimation and the training strategy.
AI.conclusion: Estimating the completeness of sentiment-relevant information and using it to guide reconstruction is an effective way to make multimodal sentiment analysis more robust to missing or noisy data, resulting in more accurate sentiment predictions in realistic, imperfect-input settings.

title: KuaiRP Series Role-playing Models Technical Report
summary: This paper introduces the complete technical solution for the KuaiRP series of role-playing models. We aim to achieve four core objectives for a dedicated role-playing model: simplified prompt engineering, highly stable output quality, built-in domain world knowledge, and high-efficiency deployment with a small parameter size. However, effectively injecting deep domain knowledge often leads to a severe catastrophic forgetting of the model's general agent capabilities. To overcome this trade-off, we propose a multi-stage training pipeline. First, we design a standardized character template and construct an SFT data pipeline based on user behavior simulation and reverse profile filtering. Next, we utilize a rule-based composite reward function during the Reinforcement Learning (RL) phase to eliminate common degradation phenomena like length expansion and repetitive generation. Finally, to recover the general capabilities compromised during SFT and RL, we propose a novel self-distillation paradigm using Two-stage On-Policy Distillation (OPD) equipped with Cumulative-Divergence Decay (CDD). By using the domain-adapted model as the teacher and the original base model as the student, we effectively balance deep domain knowledge injection with the preservation of general agent capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate that the KuaiRP models not only match the current state-of-the-art proprietary models in role-playing fidelity within our target domains, but also successfully recover general agent capabilities, maintaining extremely low deployment costs.

AI.tldr: Presents KuaiRP role-playing LLMs and a training pipeline that injects strong domain role-play skills while preserving general capabilities and keeping models small and efficient.
AI.motivation: Dedicated role-playing models often need rich, specific world/character knowledge and stable in-character behavior, but naively injecting deep domain knowledge via fine-tuning harms the model’s general agent capabilities and increases complexity and deployment cost. The authors want a method that yields high-fidelity, stable role-play in specific domains with simple prompting, while still retaining broad usefulness and being lightweight to deploy.
AI.method: They design a multi-stage training pipeline. (1) Define a standardized character template and build supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data using simulated user behaviors and reverse profile filtering to get consistent, high-quality role-play data. (2) Apply reinforcement learning with a rule-based composite reward to suppress common degeneration issues such as overly long outputs and repetition, improving response stability and quality. (3) Introduce a Two-stage On-Policy Distillation (OPD) self-distillation method with Cumulative-Divergence Decay (CDD), where the domain-adapted model (teacher) transfers its role-play skills to the original base model (student) in a way that gradually relaxes divergence penalties, aiming to re-align with the base model’s general capabilities while retaining the specialized knowledge.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations show that KuaiRP models reach role-playing fidelity comparable to state-of-the-art proprietary models in their target domains. At the same time, their general agent abilities, which were degraded by earlier SFT and RL stages, are substantially recovered through the OPD+CDD distillation process. The resulting models also maintain low parameter counts, enabling cost-efficient deployment.
AI.conclusion: A carefully designed multi-stage pipeline—SFT with structured character data, RL with rule-based rewards to control degeneration, and novel OPD with CDD for self-distillation—can successfully combine deep domain role-playing expertise with preserved general capabilities in relatively small models. This demonstrates that the usual trade-off between strong domain role-play and general-agent performance can be mitigated while keeping deployment efficient.

title: Distribution-aware Language Neuron Identification in Multilingual Large Language Models
summary: Multilingual large language models (mLLMs) contain a small fraction of feed-forward neurons that are sensitive to particular languages, commonly termed language-specific neurons. Existing work measures language specificity using the entropy of each neuron's language-wise probabilities of being active, where a neuron is considered active when its activation value is positive. However, this approach may not fully capture the multilingual nature of mLLMs, where language representations are distributional and mutually related. We propose Distribution-aware Language Neuron selection, which leverages pairwise relationships between per-language activation distributions over the full activation range, including negative values. Specifically, we quantify each neuron's language specificity by clustering languages using pairwise overlap coefficients between their activation distributions. Across two mLLMs and two held-out corpora, our identifier more effectively isolates language-specific causal effects, yielding up to 4.9$\times$ higher on-target language damage per neuron while preserving off-target language performance.

AI.tldr: They propose a better way to find language-specific neurons in multilingual LLMs using distribution-aware clustering of activation patterns, leading to stronger, more targeted causal effects on individual languages.
AI.motivation: Existing methods detect language-specific neurons by using entropy of the binary ‘active vs not’ status per language, but this ignores that (1) activations are full distributions, including negative values, and (2) languages are related and should be compared distributionally. This can mischaracterize how multilingual representations are organized and limit our ability to causally intervene on language behavior.
AI.method: They define Distribution-aware Language Neuron selection. For each neuron and each language, they collect the full activation distribution (positive and negative). They compute pairwise overlap coefficients between languages’ activation distributions, then cluster languages based on these overlaps to see whether a neuron separates one or a small set of languages from the others. This clustering-based measure is used to score language specificity and select neurons. They evaluate this on two multilingual LLMs and two held-out corpora.
AI.result: Their distribution-aware metric selects neurons that, when intervened on, produce more language-specific causal effects than the entropy-based baseline. Concretely, they achieve up to 4.9× higher performance damage on the target language per intervened neuron, while keeping performance on non-target languages largely intact.
AI.conclusion: Considering full activation distributions and inter-language relationships yields a more faithful notion of language-specific neurons in multilingual LLMs than simple entropy over binary activations. This improves our ability to identify and causally manipulate language-specific components without harming other languages, suggesting that more nuanced, distribution-aware interpretability metrics are valuable for analyzing mLLMs.

title: Same Day, Same Story; One Day Ahead, a Different Signal: The Dual Validity of Financial Sentiment
summary: Financial NLP has a standard workflow: validate a sentiment tool against human labels, then trust it to extract market signal. This assumes the two evaluations measure the same thing. We test that assumption in a setting where both can be measured at once: a corpus of securities class actions (2002-2025) linking 70,500 X messages to abnormal stock returns, with a single-annotator human labelled gold sample. Running five instruments (VADER, Loughran-McDonald, FinBERT, Twitter-RoBERTa, and an LLM annotator) through one identical pipeline, we find that the relationship between construct and predictive validity depends on the sampling convention and score representation. Under conventional method-specific sampling, human agreement aligns more closely with graded same-day associations than with one-day leads. On a fixed-n panel, however, agreement has similar graded rank correlations at both horizons, while the coarse ordering remains weak. Benchmark agreement therefore establishes semantic validity but does not by itself determine predictive rankings. In a conversation that is 17.6% spam, message volume predicts neither market damage nor settlement size.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether human-labeled sentiment scores and market-predictive sentiment metrics actually measure the same construct in financial NLP, using a large dataset of securities class action messages linked to stock returns.
AI.motivation: In financial NLP, sentiment tools are typically validated by comparing them to human labels and then used to predict market movements, implicitly assuming that higher agreement with human annotations implies better predictive power. The authors question this assumption, noting that construct validity (agreement with human sentiment judgments) and predictive validity (ability to forecast returns) may diverge and have not been tested jointly on the same data at scale.
AI.method: They compile a 2002–2025 corpus of 70,500 X (Twitter) messages associated with securities class actions, each linked to abnormal stock returns, and create a single-annotator human-labeled gold sample. Five sentiment instruments—VADER, Loughran-McDonald dictionary, FinBERT, Twitter-RoBERTa, and an LLM-based annotator—are run through a unified evaluation pipeline. They compare construct validity (agreement with human labels) and predictive validity (association with same-day and next-day abnormal returns) under different sampling schemes (conventional method-specific sampling vs. a fixed-size panel) and different ways of representing sentiment scores (graded vs. coarse). They also analyze the impact of message volume and spam prevalence on measures of market damage and settlement size.
AI.result: They find that the relationship between construct validity and predictive validity is not stable: it changes depending on how the sample is drawn and how scores are represented. Under conventional method-specific sampling, human agreement tracks graded same-day return associations better than next-day predictive power. In a fixed-n panel, however, the rank correlation between agreement and predictive performance is similar for same-day and next-day horizons, but the overall ordering of tools by predictive power remains weak. They also find that in a message set where 17.6% of content is spam, the sheer volume of messages does not predict either the extent of market damage or the size of legal settlements.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that benchmark agreement with human annotators primarily establishes semantic or construct validity of financial sentiment tools, but it cannot be relied upon alone to infer which tools will perform best in predicting market outcomes. Predictive rankings are sensitive to sampling and score representation choices. Additionally, conversational volume—especially in noisy, spam-laden environments—does not serve as a reliable proxy for economic impact, implying that both practitioners and researchers should be cautious when using human agreement or raw message counts as stand-ins for predictive or economic relevance.

title: Rethinking Verbalized Confidence for LLM-as-a-Judge: A Compatibility Shift on Post-2025 Proprietary Models
summary: Verbalized confidence, long dismissed as overconfident, coarse, and prone to round-number clustering, is now the more robust soft-scoring mechanism for LLM-as-a-Judge on top-tier proprietary models. Across SummEval, AggreFact, and HelpSteer2, spanning up to 18 LLMs, we show that the standard advice to prefer log-probabilities no longer holds on post-2025 models, where verbalized confidence is the better signal. We call this a compatibility shift. On top of a standard verbalized-confidence baseline, we introduce two new ingredients: an overconfidence advisory and self-debate. Together they improve calibration, score-distribution spread, and robustness to task subjectivity. We further observe a generation effect: post-2025 models accommodate these two additions with little balanced-accuracy cost, whereas pre-2025 models pay a measurable penalty. Compared with logprob-based G-Eval, verbalized confidence is the more subjectivity-robust soft signal on GPT-family top-tier releases. The shift is invisible under accuracy-only reporting. Rather than defaulting to hard predictions, we recommend broader use of soft scoring in LLM-as-a-Judge. More broadly, verbalized confidence has moved from a weaker substitute for logprobs to a practical soft-scoring mechanism for contemporary LLM judges.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that for modern (post-2025) LLMs acting as judges, asking the model to state its confidence in words works better than using log-probabilities as a soft score, especially on subjective evaluation tasks.
AI.motivation: Traditional advice for LLM-as-a-Judge systems is to rely on token log-probabilities as a calibrated, fine-grained soft score and to distrust verbalized confidence, which is seen as overconfident, coarse, and biased. However, LLMs and prompting methods have changed rapidly. The authors want to re-evaluate this assumption on contemporary top-tier models and understand whether verbalized confidence has become a more reliable signal, particularly for tasks with subjectivity where robust soft scoring is important.
AI.method: They compare two soft-scoring mechanisms—log-probabilities (e.g., as used in G-Eval) and explicit verbalized confidence—across several benchmarks (SummEval, AggreFact, HelpSteer2) and up to 18 different LLMs, both pre- and post-2025 generations. Starting from a baseline where the model provides a verbal confidence score, they add two techniques: (1) an overconfidence advisory that warns or nudges the model to avoid unjustified high confidence, and (2) self-debate, where the model argues with itself before committing to a confidence score. They then measure calibration, distribution spread of scores, robustness to subjectivity, and accuracy/balanced accuracy across models and generations.
AI.result: For top-tier post-2025 GPT-family and similar models, verbalized confidence becomes a more robust soft-scoring signal than log-probabilities, especially for subjective or noisy evaluation tasks. The overconfidence advisory and self-debate further improve calibration, widen the score distribution (reducing clumping), and increase robustness to task subjectivity, while incurring little to no cost in balanced accuracy for newer models. In contrast, older (pre-2025) models do suffer an accuracy penalty from these additions. The superiority of verbalized confidence over logprobs is not visible if one only looks at accuracy metrics; it emerges clearly in calibration and robustness analyses.
AI.conclusion: The conventional wisdom that log-probabilities are the preferred soft-scoring mechanism for LLM-as-a-Judge no longer holds for state-of-the-art post-2025 models. There has been a "compatibility shift": modern models now handle verbalized confidence, plus overconfidence advisories and self-debate, in a way that yields better-calibrated, more informative, and more subjectivity-robust soft scores than logprob-based methods like G-Eval. Practitioners should favor soft scoring via verbalized confidence rather than relying on hard decisions or logprobs alone when building contemporary LLM-judge systems.

title: The Oligarch Barely Steers Model Collapse in Multi-Model Ecosystems
summary: AI-generated text is flowing back into the training corpora of the next generation of models. Recursive training on it drives model collapse, and recent work extends the setting to many models feeding one another -- but almost always with the market split evenly, while real generative AI is an oligopoly. Concentration raises two worries: fewer, more uniform sources may make collapse faster, and later models may be dragged toward the oligarch's output. We test both in controlled ecosystems: 13 open 1--4B models form natural ecosystems of 3 to 13 players, plus an injected probe that pushes the top share to 90%; each generation, every model's output is mixed into a shared pool by market share and every model is retrained on that pool from clean base weights, for five generations. Yet within the range we test, neither worry materializes; what emerges instead is an invariance. Making the split more unequal barely changes the speed of collapse. Destinations move even less: the share and identity knobs shift five-generation endpoints by only a few percent of the drift common to all arms -- the ecosystems collapse to nearly the same place. An extreme share paired with the strongest injected bias still does not guarantee steering, and the topic shifts it does produce leave only a faint trace on the ruler that measures collapse. What sets the speed is who supplies the pool and how readily those suppliers are carried along: with every share held fixed, swapping the members of a K=3 ecosystem changes five-generation drift by 2.8x; a share-weighted index of each member's susceptibility explains the speed differences across nineteen arms with R^2 = 0.68; and replacing half the pool with human text roughly halves drift without changing its course. Within the tested range, concentration sets neither the destination nor the pace of collapse; the pace follows whose text fills the pool.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how market concentration among AI text generators affects model collapse when models are recursively trained on each other’s outputs, and finds that concentration neither significantly accelerates nor steers collapse within tested ranges; instead, the collapse speed depends on which models supply the training pool and how susceptible they are to drift.
AI.motivation: As AI-generated text increasingly contaminates training data for new language models, “model collapse” – degradation from recursive training on synthetic data – becomes a serious concern. Prior work mainly assumes multiple models contribute equally to the data pool, but in reality generative AI markets are oligopolistic with a few dominant providers. This raises two key questions: (1) Does having a few large, homogeneous sources accelerate collapse compared to a more diverse market? (2) Can dominant models steer the behavior and outputs of newer or smaller models toward their own biases and style? Understanding these effects is important for both theory and policy around training data curation, ecosystem design, and long-term model reliability.
AI.method: The authors build controlled “ecosystems” of 13 open-source language models (1–4B parameters), forming multiple arms with 3–13 models each, and also introduce a probe model whose output can be given an extreme market share (up to 90%). In each generation, every model produces synthetic text; all outputs are mixed into a shared training pool weighted by each model’s market share; and then every model is retrained from its clean base weights on that mixed pool. This is repeated for five generations. They vary (a) the market concentration (distribution of shares among models), (b) which specific models populate the ecosystem, and (c) the degree of injected topical or stylistic bias from the high-share probe model. They then measure collapse (drift and degradation) and directional steering effects across these different configurations, and compare against conditions where part of the pool is replaced by human-written text.
AI.result: Within the tested regimes, increasing market concentration (making the share distribution more unequal or pushing one model’s share to ~90%) has little impact on either the speed or the endpoint of model collapse. Ecosystems with very different share distributions converge to very similar collapsed states, and the final destination is only weakly affected by which model is dominant or how biased its outputs are. Even with strong injected bias at extreme share, steering effects on the final behavior are modest and mostly limited to small topic shifts. By contrast, which specific models constitute the ecosystem strongly affects collapse speed: holding shares fixed but swapping members in a 3-model ecosystem changes five-generation drift by a factor of 2.8. A share-weighted index of each model’s susceptibility to drift explains about 68% (R^2=0.68) of the variation in collapse speed across 19 experimental arms. Mixing in human-generated text (replacing half of the synthetic pool) roughly halves the rate of drift while leaving its direction mostly unchanged.
AI.conclusion: The main driver of model collapse under recursive synthetic training is not market concentration per se, but the characteristics and susceptibilities of the models whose text populates the training pool. Within the studied range of oligopolistic conditions, skewing market shares toward a few large providers neither substantially changes the endpoint of collapse nor reliably allows a dominant model to steer the ecosystem’s behavior. Instead, the pace of collapse is governed by how prone contributing models are to drift when exposed to their own and others’ synthetic outputs. Introducing human-authored text can significantly slow collapse, though it does not alter its direction. Policy and engineering efforts should thus focus less on concentration alone and more on controlling the composition and quality of the training pool and on monitoring model susceptibility to recursive-training drift.

title: K/V-Cache Interventions Dissociate Representation Alignment from Persona Expression in Decoder-Only Language Models
summary: We study K/V-cache interventions -- transplanting a target-conditioned K/V trajectory into a source-persona generation -- as a structured surface for persona control in decoder-only language models. Across 13 intervention configurations applied to Llama-3.1-8B for a fixed source-to-target persona pair, we report two consistent dissociations between representation-level alignment and behavioral expression, plus a common failure under position perturbations. First, all layer-band K/V replacements (early, mid, late) achieve strong local V-space alignment (V-gap 0.91, 0.89, 0.84), but only mid-layer replacement (layers 9-20) combines substantial target-marker expression with preserved lexical diversity. Second, full and mid-layer replacement induce comparable alignment (V-gap 0.94 vs. 0.89) yet produce different lexical-diversity profiles (TTR 0.65 vs. 0.77). Third, position perturbations (lag and shuffle) apply distinct operations yet uniformly suppress target-persona expression -- a common behavioral failure rather than a strict dissociation. Representation-level similarity metrics alone are thus not sufficient predictors of downstream persona expression in the regimes we study; the K/V cache emerges as a controllable but structurally constrained intervention surface. Because the transplanted trajectory carries the target's own generated token history, we characterize the intervention as trajectory-level transplantation rather than isolated persona-representation injection; a same-token-sequence control, decoding an identical token sequence under source vs. target conditioning, reproduces the sign and layer localization of the L28 representational shift, indicating the shift is not explained solely by imported token history. These findings characterize representation-behavior dissociation in a high-signal setting rather than establishing universality across models or persona pairs.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates using K/V-cache interventions—specifically, transplanting key/value trajectories from a target persona into a source persona’s generation—as a structured method to control personas in decoder-only language models.
AI.motivation: To understand whether manipulating internal representations (K/V caches) can reliably control persona in language models, and to test if representation-level similarity metrics actually predict observable persona behavior.
AI.method: Apply 13 configurations of K/V-cache interventions to Llama-3.1-8B for a fixed source-target persona pair, including early/mid/late layer-band replacements, full vs. partial replacements, and position perturbations (lag, shuffle). Measure representation-level alignment (e.g., V-gap), behavioral persona expression (target-marker expression), and lexical diversity (TTR). Use a same-token-sequence control to disentangle effects of imported token history from persona representation shifts.
AI.result: (1) Early, mid, and late K/V replacements all show strong local V-space alignment, but only mid-layer (layers 9–20) replacement yields substantial target persona expression while preserving lexical diversity. (2) Full-layer and mid-layer replacement have similar representation alignment but different lexical diversity (TTR 0.65 vs. 0.77). (3) Position perturbations, despite being different operations, consistently suppress target persona expression. A same-token-sequence control replicates the representational shift at layer 28, indicating it is not solely due to the imported token history.
AI.conclusion: Representation-level similarity metrics (like V-gap) are not reliable stand-alone predictors of persona behavior in the studied regimes. The K/V cache is a powerful but structurally constrained surface for persona control, and persona interventions operate at the trajectory level rather than as simple static representation injections. The reported dissociations are characterized in a specific high-signal setting and are not claimed to generalize universally across models or persona pairs.

title: Autonomous Chemical Mechanistic Discovery through Agentic Reasoning and Validation
comment: This paper has been submitted to Nature Communications
summary: Unraveling reaction mechanisms is central to modern chemistry, yet automating these investigations remains challenging because computational workflows still rely heavily on expert intervention. Here we introduce ARCHE, an autonomous agentic system that integrates a general-purpose reasoning model, a domain-specialized computational chemistry model, and a structured tool registry to transform mechanistic inquiry into a scalable, self-validating process. ARCHE interprets scientific questions, generates and prioritizes mechanistic hypotheses, orchestrates computational workflows, and iteratively refines conclusions based on computed evidence within a closed loop. We validate its capabilities across three increasingly demanding scenarios: reconstructing stereocontrolling transition states and validating the corresponding reaction mechanism in a previously reported asymmetric catalytic reaction; proposing and validating a plausible radical pathway through iterative hypothesis refinement for a recently discovered but unpublished $α$-iodoboronate C-I cleavage reaction; and identifying a chemically interpretable descriptor that governs selectivity in nickel-catalysed migratory cross-coupling reactions. By coupling agentic reasoning with rigorous computational validation, ARCHE advances autonomous mechanistic discovery and establishes a foundation for broader machine-assisted chemical research. The code for ARCHE is publicly available at https://github.com/JetAstra/Arche-Harness.

AI.tldr: Introduces ARCHE, an autonomous agent system that automates mechanistic studies in computational chemistry by combining a general reasoning model, a chemistry-specialized model, and a tool registry, and validates it on several challenging reaction case studies.
AI.motivation: Reaction mechanism elucidation is crucial in chemistry but current computational workflows require significant expert input, making them hard to scale, reproduce, and automate. There is a need for systems that can autonomously generate, test, and refine mechanistic hypotheses using computational tools with minimal human intervention.
AI.method: Develop ARCHE, an autonomous agentic framework composed of: (1) a general-purpose reasoning model to interpret scientific questions and plan strategies; (2) a domain-specialized computational chemistry model to handle chemistry-specific reasoning; and (3) a structured registry of computational tools and workflows. ARCHE operates in a closed loop: it parses a mechanistic question, proposes and ranks mechanistic hypotheses, orchestrates appropriate quantum-chemical/computational workflows, evaluates computed results, and iteratively refines hypotheses and conclusions based on this evidence.
AI.result: Demonstrated ARCHE on three escalating testbeds: (1) reconstructed stereocontrolling transition states and validated the accepted mechanism of a known asymmetric catalytic reaction; (2) proposed and validated a plausible radical mechanism, via iterative refinement, for an unpublished α-iodoboronate C–I bond cleavage reaction; and (3) discovered a chemically interpretable descriptor that controls selectivity in nickel-catalyzed migratory cross-coupling reactions.
AI.conclusion: ARCHE successfully couples agentic reasoning with rigorous computational chemistry tools to autonomously perform mechanistic studies, offering a scalable and self-validating approach to reaction mechanism discovery. This showcases a pathway toward broader machine-assisted chemical research and provides an open-source platform for future development and application.

title: Rebalancing Token Importance in Language Models with TF-IDF Weighted Cross-Entropy Loss
summary: Large language models are typically trained under uniform token weighting, which allows frequent and low-information tokens to dominate learning and can increase the tendency to memorize surface-level text spans. To address this, we present an information-weighted cross-entropy loss that rescales token-level contributions using TF-IDF statistics, emphasizing semantically informative tokens while down-weighting ubiquitous ones. Experiments on five decoder-only LLMs ranging from 1.1B to 13B parameters show consistent reductions in memorized substring length while preserving perplexity and downstream task performance. Under LoRA fine-tuning, TF-IDF reduces average substring memorization length by 14% across all five models. Under full-weight fine-tuning on TinyLLaMA 1.1B, the reduction reaches 58%. Our approach is architecture-agnostic and can be incorporated into existing training pipelines with less than 3% computational overhead, offering a lightweight and principled way to mitigate memorization without disrupting standard training dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an information-weighted cross-entropy loss using TF-IDF so that training focuses more on informative tokens, reducing memorization in large language models while maintaining performance.
AI.motivation: Standard LLM training uses uniform token weighting in the loss, causing frequent, low-information tokens to dominate the gradient signal and encouraging memorization of surface text rather than underlying semantics. There is a need for a simple, principled modification to training that can curb memorization without hurting perplexity or downstream capabilities.
AI.method: Introduce an information-weighted cross-entropy loss where each token’s loss contribution is rescaled based on its TF-IDF score computed over the training corpus. High-information (rare and contextually important) tokens are up-weighted, while ubiquitous tokens are down-weighted. This reweighting is applied during fine-tuning or full training of decoder-only LLMs, and evaluated under both LoRA and full-weight fine-tuning settings. The method is designed to be architecture-agnostic and adds less than 3% computational overhead.
AI.result: Across five decoder-only LLMs (1.1B–13B parameters), using the TF-IDF-weighted loss consistently shortens memorized substrings while keeping perplexity and downstream task performance essentially unchanged. With LoRA fine-tuning, average memorized substring length drops by 14%. With full-weight fine-tuning on TinyLLaMA 1.1B, memorized substring length drops by 58%.
AI.conclusion: Information-weighted cross-entropy using TF-IDF is an effective and efficient way to reduce memorization in LLMs without sacrificing standard metrics. It is simple to integrate into existing training pipelines, architecture-agnostic, and incurs minimal computational cost, making it a practical tool for mitigating unwanted memorization in language model training.

title: DRG-MAPPO: Hierarchical Dynamic Role-Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Air Combat
summary: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) has emerged as a pivotal paradigm for complex decision-making in autonomous systems and air combat. While MARL has demonstrated significant potential in air combat, achieving sophisticated tactical coordination remains a non-trivial challenge.
