English and German benefit from long traditions of dictionaries and linguistic description that help identify wrong pronunciations; Kurdish has far less such support, so software choices can go unchecked. The voices sound fluent, but they represent the reading styles of their speakers rather than Kurdish as a whole. Most of these issues can be fixed using information the team already has, without changing the reported results. Better records would mainly make the work easier for others, especially community linguists, to check and reuse. The license is the main exception: whether audiobook owners allow corrected versions to be shared will affect whether future Kurdish voices can build on this work or must start again.

AI.tldr: Review of a Kurdish text-to-speech resource finds mismatches between the paper and released files, practical data and documentation flaws, overstated public claims, and licensing limits that may restrict reuse, while noting that most technical issues are fixable without changing the reported scientific results.
AI.motivation: Kurdish has millions of speakers but very limited text-to-speech technology, and a new open release of voices and data is potentially important. However, for such resources to be trustworthy and reusable—especially in under-resourced languages without strong lexicographic or linguistic infrastructures—the released materials must accurately reflect the described methods and results. This paper is motivated by the need to audit the consistency, quality, and openness of this influential Kurdish TTS release, and to understand its implications for future work and for community linguists.
AI.method: The author systematically compares the public release (three synthetic voices, 35 hours of speech data, configuration and settings files, and documentation, including the download page) against the methods and results described in the original research paper. They inspect metadata, configuration details, dataset composition (training vs. test splits), and software behavior (e.g., number handling), and evaluate the claims and recommendations made on the project’s website. The analysis also situates the resource within the broader sociolinguistic context of Kurdish variation and language technology support.
AI.result: The review finds several concrete discrepancies and issues: (1) a configuration/settings file lists recording equipment that was never actually used; (2) test recordings are mixed in with training data and not clearly labeled; (3) a coding error leads to incorrect handling of long numbers; (4) the public download page makes a stronger performance claim than what is reported in the paper; and (5) the page recommends one voice as suitable for general use, despite being based on limited, prepared-speech recordings from just three speakers. The study also observes that the voices, while fluent, largely capture the reading styles of the specific speakers rather than the broader range of Kurdish speech, especially given the language’s significant regional and orthographic variation and the scarcity of lexicographic resources to detect pronunciation errors.
AI.conclusion: The author concludes that the Kurdish TTS resource, while valuable and generally careful about acknowledging its limits, suffers from documentation and data-management shortcomings and some overstatements in its public presentation. Most technical and documentation issues could be corrected using information already available to the original team, without altering the validity of the published results. Improving records and metadata would primarily enhance transparency, verifiability, and reusability for other researchers and community linguists. However, the licensing constraints around the source audiobooks may limit the ability to redistribute corrected versions; this in turn will shape whether future Kurdish TTS projects can build directly on this work or will need to recreate similar resources from scratch.

title: AI-Powered Flare Combustion Efficiency Estimation
comment: Accepted at the 4th International Conference on Machine Learning and Data Engineering (ICMLDE 2025). 5 pages
summary: Achieving high combustion efficiency in flare stacks is crucial for adhering to regulatory standards and controlling the release of hydrocarbons into the environment. Traditional instruments like gas analyzers and hyperspectral cameras are expensive, fragile, and require frequent calibration, which makes them impractical for remote or budget constrained industrial sites. We propose an innovative solution that combines a lightweight vision-language encoder with a compact multi-layer perceptron to predict combustion efficiency directly from low-cost thermal video footage. The fully trained model is integrated into an easy-to-deploy graphical user interface. This interface overlays predicted combustion efficiency values on each video frame, displays real-time trends in combustion efficiency, shows the distribution of combustion efficiency across all frames in the video, and allows users to export CSV reports. Over a six-month period, the system achieved 99% uptime and required less than 15 minutes of maintenance per week.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a low-cost, vision-based system to estimate flare stack combustion efficiency from thermal video, providing a practical, deployable alternative to expensive instruments.
AI.motivation: High combustion efficiency in flare stacks is required to meet regulations and minimize hydrocarbon emissions, but conventional measurement tools (gas analyzers, hyperspectral cameras) are too costly, delicate, and maintenance-heavy for many remote or budget-limited industrial sites. There is a need for a robust, low-cost, easy-to-deploy monitoring solution.
AI.method: The authors design a system that uses low-cost thermal video as input and processes it with a lightweight vision-language encoder paired with a compact multi-layer perceptron to predict combustion efficiency. They fully train this model and embed it into a graphical user interface that overlays predicted efficiency on each frame, shows real-time efficiency trends, visualizes the distribution of efficiency over the video, and supports CSV report export.
AI.result: Deployed over six months, the system demonstrated 99% uptime and demanded under 15 minutes of weekly maintenance, indicating strong reliability and low operational overhead in real-world conditions.
AI.conclusion: A compact, learning-based system using inexpensive thermal cameras can reliably estimate flare stack combustion efficiency in real time, offering a practical and maintainable alternative to traditional, high-cost measurement instruments for industrial sites.

title: The Illusion of Balanced Multimodal Sentiment Analysis: Beyond the Limits of Optimization-Based Methods
summary: Multimodal Sentiment Analysis (MSA) remains constrained by modality imbalance, yet the field continues to rely on optimization-based balancing methods that promise more than they deliver. We provide three contributions: 1) a unified evaluation framework testing gradient and loss-based balancing strategies under controlled settings; 2) a theoretical diagnosis explaining why these methods fail, as they conflate fitting speed with discriminative contribution; and 3) a research agenda toward held-out discriminative modality valuation. Experiments on CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI reveal three shortcomings: no strategy reliably outperforms Late Concatenation; performance is sensitive to hyperparameters; and even ratio calibration fails to yield consistent gains. The core issue is fundamental: loss is not utility, and gradients are not importance. Modality imbalance remains unresolved, motivating utility estimation from held-out performance.

AI.tldr: The paper critically evaluates existing optimization-based methods for balancing modalities in multimodal sentiment analysis and shows they largely fail, arguing for new approaches based on held-out utility estimation.
AI.motivation: In multimodal sentiment analysis, different modalities (e.g., text, audio, video) contribute unequally to performance, causing modality imbalance. Current methods try to fix this by re-weighting losses or gradients during training, but their real effectiveness is unclear and often overclaimed. The authors aim to rigorously test these strategies, understand why they fail, and propose a better research direction.
AI.method: The authors build a unified and controlled evaluation framework to systematically compare gradient-based and loss-based balancing strategies for multimodal sentiment analysis. They theoretically analyze these approaches to show that they incorrectly equate faster loss reduction or larger gradients with higher modality importance. They then empirically test various strategies, including ratio calibration, against a simple Late Concatenation baseline on CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI datasets.
AI.result: Across experiments on CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI, no evaluated balancing strategy consistently outperforms the simple Late Concatenation baseline. The performance of these methods is highly sensitive to hyperparameter choices, and even more refined techniques like ratio calibration fail to provide stable improvements. This empirically supports the theoretical claim that optimization signals such as loss values and gradient magnitudes are not reliable indicators of modality utility.
AI.conclusion: The work concludes that existing optimization-based balancing methods do not solve modality imbalance in multimodal sentiment analysis. The central insight is that loss and gradient information reflect optimization dynamics rather than true discriminative utility of each modality. The authors argue that progress requires new methods that estimate modality importance via held-out performance (utility estimation) rather than training-time optimization signals, and they outline this as a future research agenda.

title: Predicting Train Delays in Finland Using Machine Learning and Weather Data
comment: 6 pages, 3 Figures, 4 tables, presented at Wireless Europe 2026, Rimini, Italy, June 2026
summary: Reliable railway operations depend increasingly on real-time environmental intelligence delivered through wireless sensor infrastructures, a capability that 6G networks will substantially enhance through integrated sensing and edge computing. Adverse weather, particularly in Arctic regions with extreme temperatures and heavy precipitation, remains a leading cause of train delays, yet most prediction approaches rely on raw meteorological inputs without exploiting domain-informed feature engineering. This paper investigates machine learning for train delay prediction using the Finland Integrated Train-Weather (FI-TW) dataset, which fuses railway operational records with observations from the Finnish Meteorological Institute's nationwide sensor network of approximately 200 stations communicating over wireless links. We evaluate three feature configurations using XGBoost at Oulu central station (101,146 observations): full weather features, instant weather observations only, and derived weather category scenarios. The category-based approach, employing hierarchical classifications such as Blizzard, Heavy Snow, and Extreme Cold, achieved an R^2 of 0.78, root mean squared error of 8.5 minutes, and mean absolute error of 3.7 minutes, representing an 11% R^2 improvement and 10% error reduction over alternative configurations. These results demonstrate that compact, domain-informed features derived from sensor streams outperform raw meteorological observations, offering bandwidth-efficient representations suitable for edge deployment over current and emerging wireless infrastructures.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that engineered, category-based weather features from a nationwide wireless sensor network significantly improve train delay prediction versus raw weather data, enabling more efficient edge deployment in 6G-ready railway systems.
AI.motivation: Railway operations, especially in harsh Arctic weather, suffer from delays driven by complex weather impacts. Existing prediction models mostly use raw meteorological variables and do not capitalize on domain knowledge or bandwidth constraints of wireless sensor networks and future 6G infrastructures. There is a need to understand whether compact, domain-informed features can improve both prediction accuracy and communication efficiency.
AI.method: Using the Finland Integrated Train-Weather (FI-TW) dataset, which links train operation records with weather station observations from about 200 wireless-connected stations, the authors focus on Oulu central station (101,146 samples). They train XGBoost regression models under three feature configurations: (1) full raw weather feature set, (2) only instantaneous weather observations, and (3) engineered categorical weather scenarios derived via hierarchical labels (e.g., Blizzard, Heavy Snow, Extreme Cold). They compare model performance using R^2, RMSE, and MAE.
AI.result: The feature configuration using derived weather categories performs best, achieving R^2 = 0.78, RMSE = 8.5 minutes, and MAE = 3.7 minutes. This corresponds to about an 11% R^2 gain and 10% reduction in prediction error compared with models using raw or instant-only weather features. Thus, structured categorical representations of weather impacts yield more accurate train delay predictions.
AI.conclusion: Domain-aware, compact weather scenario categories derived from rich sensor data can outperform models that rely on raw meteorological variables for train delay prediction. Such representations reduce bandwidth needs and are suitable for deployment on edge devices within current and future 6G wireless sensor infrastructures, enhancing real-time railway resilience, especially in challenging Arctic environments.

title: Automatic Lyric Transcription for Greek Songs: Scaling and Task Composition Effects in Whisper Adaptation
summary: Automatic Lyric Transcription (ALT) remains substantially more challenging than speech recognition due to melodic variability, rhythmic irregularity, and accompaniment interference. This is heightened in low-resource languages like Greek, where no prior benchmark for ALT exists. We present the first controlled study of Whisper adaptation for Greek ALT, investigating model scaling effects, task composition via multitask training in transcribe-translate ratios, and two-stage speech-to-singing adaptation. We also curate a segment-level aligned singing dataset based on the Greek Audio Dataset (GAD) using source separation and CTC forced alignment. Results show that scaling consistently improves performance, while multitask learning acts as a beneficial regularizer primarily for smaller-capacity models. The 2-stage adaptation in Whisper Large-v3 achieves a Word Error Rate (WER) of 27.2%, a significant improvement over zero-shot baselines, establishing the first Greek ALT benchmark.

AI.tldr: First controlled adaptation of OpenAI Whisper for Greek automatic lyric transcription (ALT), creating a new benchmark and showing that larger models and a 2-stage adaptation significantly reduce word error rate.
AI.motivation: ALT is much harder than normal speech recognition and is especially underdeveloped for low-resource languages like Greek, where no benchmark existed. The authors aim to understand how to best adapt a strong speech model (Whisper) to this setting and to provide data and baselines for future research.
AI.method: They adapt various sizes of Whisper models to Greek ALT, systematically studying: (1) model scaling; (2) different mixtures of transcription and translation tasks via multitask learning; and (3) a two-stage adaptation path from speech to singing. They also construct a segment-level aligned singing dataset from the Greek Audio Dataset using source separation and CTC-based forced alignment.
AI.result: Larger Whisper models consistently perform better. Multitask training with transcription and translation offers regularization benefits, especially for smaller models. The best system, a two-stage adapted Whisper Large-v3, reaches a WER of 27.2% on Greek ALT, clearly outperforming zero-shot Whisper baselines.
AI.conclusion: Scaling and carefully designed adaptation strategies are crucial for effective ALT in low-resource languages. The curated Greek singing dataset and the reported 27.2% WER result establish the first concrete benchmark for Greek ALT, providing a foundation for subsequent work in this area.

title: Bio-inspired Learning and Decision-Making with Probabilistic In-Memory Computing Hardware: Part 1
summary: Learning and decision-making in animals are often modeled as Bayesian processes, where sensory evidence is integrated with prior beliefs to guide behavior in the face of uncertainty. But what are the inherent neural dynamics that give rise to this ability, and how could they be replicated in computing systems? This abstract discusses a biologically grounded framework in which noisy neural and synaptic dynamics perform inference and learning via stochastic sampling from an internal energy function, capturing uncertainty over latent states and model parameters through neural and synaptic variability, respectively. This enables approaches such as predictive coding networks to account for epistemic uncertainty via Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. Drawing a parallel between intrinsic noise in biological systems and electrical noise in emerging probabilistic analogue memory technologies, we highlight how analogue in-memory computing hardware naturally emerges as the solution for massively scalable and energy-efficient probabilistic inference.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a biologically inspired framework where noisy neural and synaptic dynamics implement Bayesian inference and learning via stochastic sampling, and argues that analogue in‑memory computing hardware is naturally suited for scalable, energy‑efficient probabilistic inference.
AI.motivation: To understand how animals perform Bayesian-like learning and decision-making under uncertainty at the neural level, and to leverage these principles to design more efficient computing systems for probabilistic inference. Specifically, the authors seek a mechanistic link between neural/synaptic noise, Bayesian computation, and suitable hardware implementations.
AI.method: They frame neural activity and synaptic plasticity as stochastic sampling processes from an internal energy (or probability) function. Neural variability encodes uncertainty over latent states, while synaptic variability encodes uncertainty over model parameters. They apply this view to architectures such as predictive coding networks, interpreting their operation as Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. They then map these computational principles onto analogue in‑memory computing hardware by exploiting intrinsic electrical noise in probabilistic analogue memory devices.
AI.result: Conceptually, they show that common neural and synaptic noise can be reinterpreted as a computational resource that naturally implements Bayesian inference and learning by sampling. Predictive coding networks can, within this framework, represent epistemic uncertainty using Markov chain Monte Carlo dynamics. On the hardware side, they identify a close correspondence between biological noise and device-level electrical noise in analogue memories, showing that such hardware can natively support massively parallel, low-energy probabilistic computation.
AI.conclusion: Neural and synaptic noise need not be treated as a nuisance but as the basis of a principled sampling-based implementation of Bayesian inference and learning. This perspective unifies biological computation and probabilistic machine learning and points to analogue in‑memory computing hardware as a particularly well-matched platform for scalable, energy-efficient probabilistic inference, inspired by the brain’s own mechanisms.

title: MultiHuSE: A Multimodal Dataset for Humour Styles and Emotions
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at IEEE CBMI 2025 (International Conference on Content-Based Multimedia Indexing), Dublin, Ireland
summary: Computational recognition of verbal humour remains a challenging task, requiring an understanding of language, delivery style, emotions, and cultural context. Most existing approaches focus on binary classification and lack datasets that capture psychological dimensions of humour alongside variations in expression. We introduce MultiHuSE, a multimodal dataset comprising 2,407 high-definition videos of 50 demographically diverse actors performing 1,463 text samples across four psychological humour styles (affiliative, aggressive, self-enhancing, and self-deprecating), as well as neutral content. A subset is additionally annotated for underlying emotions. The dataset uniquely captures multiple actor interpretations of the same texts, enabling systematic analysis of expressive diversity. Baseline experiments show that multimodal fusion outperforms unimodal approaches (80.1% vs. 77.4% accuracy) in humour style classification, with particularly strong gains for affiliative humour (66% to 74%). While text provides the strongest individual signal, fusion models deliver meaningful improvements. We hope that MultiHuSE provides empirical support for psychological theories linking humour and emotion, while also opening new avenues for research in human communication, well-being, and AI-driven interaction. The dataset is available for academic use under an End-User Licence Agreement.

AI.tldr: MultiHuSE is a new multimodal dataset for recognizing different psychological humour styles, showing that combining text, audio, and video improves classification over single modalities.
AI.motivation: Existing humour recognition work mostly does simple binary funny/non-funny classification and lacks resources that reflect psychological humour styles, emotional underpinnings, and expressive variability across speakers. This limits both theoretical study of humour and the development of richer AI systems that can understand nuanced, context-dependent humour in realistic interactions.
AI.method: The authors collected 2,407 HD videos of 50 demographically diverse actors performing 1,463 text samples designed to represent four psychological humour styles (affiliative, aggressive, self-enhancing, self-deprecating) plus neutral text. Some samples are additionally annotated with underlying emotions. Multiple actors perform the same texts, capturing diverse expressive realizations. They then train and evaluate unimodal (text, audio, visual) and multimodal fusion models on humour style classification to establish baselines.
AI.result: The dataset exhibits multiple expressive interpretations of the same humorous texts and includes labels for humour style and, for a subset, emotions. Baseline classification experiments show that text alone is the strongest single modality, but multimodal fusion (combining modalities) achieves higher overall accuracy (80.1%) than the best unimodal model (77.4%), with notable gains for affiliative humour classification (from 66% to 74%).
AI.conclusion: MultiHuSE provides a rich, multimodal, psychologically grounded dataset for studying humour styles and their emotional and expressive correlates. The initial experiments demonstrate that integrating text with audiovisual signals improves humour style recognition, highlighting the importance of multimodal cues. The authors argue that this resource can support research on humour, emotion, and human communication, and help build more socially aware, humour-sensitive AI systems; the dataset is released for academic use under an EULA.

title: When Does Text Inform? Benchmarking Information-Theoretic Metrics for Multimodal Time-Series Forecasting
summary: Multimodal forecasting models that combine time series with text annotations promise richer prediction through textual context, but how do we know whether a text annotation meaningfully contributes to the forecasters prediction? This is an information-theoretic question, but to evaluate whether information-theoretic metrics can reliably measure the predictive value an annotation provides, a ground truth benchmark is needed, and none currently exist. We create a synthetic time series signal with annotations in three categories: semantically correct, incorrect, and irrelevant. Because the data generation process is fully controlled, ground-truth information content is known exactly, enabling principled evaluation of six complementary mutual information estimators (KSG, MINE, InfoNCE, CCA, PID and V-information). We show that all six estimators identify correct annotations as most informative, and are able to audit the quality of mixed text corpora, choosing the annotations that result in the best downstream forecasting results without the need for model training. Our benchmark identifies limitations of each estimator, and these are validated on seven real-world datasets, which show how estimator performance differs on weak signals. Finally, we establish practical rules for implementing these metrics for annotation auditing and fusion selection.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a synthetic benchmark to test whether information-theoretic metrics can reliably measure how informative text annotations are for time-series forecasting, and evaluates six mutual-information-style estimators for auditing annotation quality and guiding multimodal fusion.
AI.motivation: Multimodal time-series forecasters often use text annotations, but it is unclear how to quantify whether a specific annotation actually helps prediction. Information-theoretic measures seem natural, yet their reliability is unknown because there is no dataset with known ground-truth information content. A controlled benchmark is required to systematically test and compare such estimators and derive practical guidance for annotation auditing and fusion choices.
AI.method: The authors construct a synthetic time-series generation process with text annotations that fall into three precisely defined categories: semantically correct (informative about the signal), incorrect (misleading), and irrelevant (noise). Because the data-generating process is known, the true information content of each annotation type is analytically available. Using this benchmark, they evaluate six information-theoretic or mutual-information-based estimators—KSG, MINE, InfoNCE, CCA-based measures, partial information decomposition (PID), and V-information—in terms of their ability to rank annotation categories by informativeness and to assess mixed-quality annotation corpora without training forecasting models. They then validate the observed behaviors and limitations on seven real-world multimodal forecasting datasets.
AI.result: All six estimators consistently identify the semantically correct annotations as the most informative and can be used to audit mixed annotation sets, selecting subsets that yield superior downstream forecasting performance, all without training forecasters. The benchmark also reveals distinct failure modes and limitations of each estimator, particularly in weak-signal or noisy settings, and these qualitative findings are corroborated on seven real-world datasets, where estimator performance diverges when predictive signals are subtle.
AI.conclusion: Information-theoretic estimators can be effectively used to quantify the predictive value of text annotations in multimodal time-series forecasting and to audit annotation corpora prior to model training. The proposed synthetic benchmark, with known ground-truth information content, exposes strengths and weaknesses of various estimators and is validated against real-world data. From these analyses, the authors distill practical implementation rules for applying such metrics to annotation auditing and fusion selection in multimodal forecasting pipelines.

title: E-CONAN (Entailment, CONtradition And Neutral) Benchmarks: Arabic Textual Entailment and Natural Inference Datasets
summary: Natural Language Inference processes pairs of sentences to extract their semantic relations. NLI has been a hot research topic, integrated as a main component in other NLP applications. Despite significant advancements in textual inference across various languages all around the world, Arabic language still suffers from limited resources in this domain. To address this gap, this paper introduces E-CONAN benchmarks that are composed of sentences pairs from various sources: (1) automatically-translated pairs, (2) human-validated machine-translated pairs, (3) hand-crafted pairs from teaching Arabic as foreign language books, and (4) headlines pairs from different news channels containing rumors. E-CONAN contains two benchmark datasets, E-CONAN-2, a 2-way dataset (RTE) and E-CONAN-3, a 3-way dataset (NLI). Additionally, we have used E-CONAN benchmarks to evaluate 9 state-of-the-art multilingual pretrained models using zero-shot classification. Models were evaluated across the ArNLI, XNLI, and E-CONAN datasets. Results show that E-CONAN is a potentially valuable resource for evaluating model generalization and even for fine-tuning pre-trained models. Its diverse composition, derived from a combination of sources, offers a broader and more robust assessment compared to XNLI and ArNLI. In addition, we have evaluated 5 LLMs on E-CONAN-3 dataset. Moreover, we incorporated MARBERT as a representative Arabic-specific baseline and conducted performance evaluation comparison to demonstrate how Arabic-specific models scale against cross-lingual and LLM-based approaches on the E-CONAN benchmarks. Furthermore, we conducted detailed qualitative and quantitative error analysis to analyze frequent error patterns. E-CONAN benchmarks will be publicly available, we hope that it will enrich research community in Arabic textual entailment and natural language inference.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces E-CONAN, new Arabic Natural Language Inference (NLI) benchmarks, and uses them to evaluate multilingual, Arabic-specific, and LLM models, showing E-CONAN’s value for assessing and improving Arabic NLI.
AI.motivation: Natural Language Inference is crucial in NLP and widely studied in many languages, but Arabic lacks high-quality, diverse NLI resources. Existing benchmarks like XNLI and ArNLI do not fully capture Arabic phenomena or provide broad coverage across different text sources and label formats (2-way and 3-way). This resource gap limits training, evaluation, and generalization analysis of modern multilingual and Arabic-specific models on Arabic NLI.
AI.method: The authors construct E-CONAN from four sources of Arabic sentence pairs: (1) automatically translated pairs, (2) human-validated machine-translated pairs, (3) hand-crafted pairs from teaching Arabic as a foreign language textbooks, and (4) headline pairs from diverse news channels that include rumors. They create two benchmarks: E-CONAN-2 with 2-way labels (RTE-style) and E-CONAN-3 with 3-way labels (NLI-style). They then evaluate nine state-of-the-art multilingual pretrained models in a zero-shot setting across ArNLI, XNLI, and E-CONAN. They further evaluate five large language models (LLMs) on E-CONAN-3 and include MARBERT as an Arabic-specific baseline. Finally, they perform detailed quantitative and qualitative error analyses to characterize common failure patterns.
AI.result: Experiments show that E-CONAN is a challenging and informative benchmark that reveals differences in how models generalize to diverse Arabic NLI scenarios. The resource provides a broader and more robust assessment than XNLI and ArNLI alone, and can also be effectively used for fine-tuning. Arabic-specific models like MARBERT are directly compared to multilingual and LLM-based models, highlighting how each category scales and where they succeed or fail. Error analysis identifies frequent error types and systematic weaknesses across models.
AI.conclusion: E-CONAN is a valuable new Arabic NLI resource consisting of two benchmarks (2-way and 3-way) built from multiple heterogeneous sources, including educational materials and rumor-related news headlines. It enables richer evaluation of multilingual, Arabic-specific, and LLM models, supports both zero-shot and fine-tuning scenarios, and provides insights into model error patterns. The authors will release E-CONAN publicly to facilitate further research in Arabic textual entailment and NLI.

title: Generating a Consistent Enterprise: Synthesis and Reference-Free Evaluation of Multi-System Business Data
summary: Synthetic relational data is normally produced by a model trained on a real dataset, and its quality is measured as the distance to that dataset. This paper describes a generator that has no real dataset at either end. Given an industry, a company size, a business model, a set of business applications, and a random seed, it produces a complete fictional enterprise: a workforce, a customer base, sales deals, support tickets, recorded calls, chat messages, and documents, all consistent with one another. One entity graph is projected into the native formats of 66 business products, so the same customer appears in the CRM, the support desk, and the call system under one identity. Because no real counterpart exists, realism is built in from cited reference statistics and verified by reference-free measurement: a five-axis scorecard of 28 statistical checks, an adversarial detector that hunts for the marks of synthetic generation, and a set of soundness checks that include a classifier test against an independently shuffled copy of the data. Because these instruments existed before the generator was tuned, progress is measured under a fixed yardstick: over 23 generated companies, mean realism climbed from 60.3 to 99.1, the weakest company from 41.1 to 94.9, and the detector, which initially flagged 55.2% of all records, now flags none. The scores hold on a seed never used during development. A second generator builds relational databases from a list of business questions. It forces qualifying rows for each answerable question, adds controlled near misses, and computes exact labels from the finished tables. The generator runs as a hosted service at https://console.era.eon.io. A company built there to a specification is served through its simulators over MCP and REST, and the simulators are also published as container images for offline use

AI.tldr: Paper introduces a system to generate fully synthetic, realistic enterprise relational datasets without using real source data, and methods to evaluate and iteratively improve their realism.
AI.motivation: Address the need for high-quality, privacy-safe synthetic enterprise data that spans many business systems and remains internally consistent, without relying on real datasets as training input or ground truth for evaluation.
AI.method: Design a generator that takes high-level business descriptors (industry, size, model, apps, seed) and creates an underlying entity graph representing a fictional enterprise, then projects this graph into 66 product-specific schemas (CRM, support, calls, etc.). Realism is enforced through reference statistics from public sources and validated using a fixed, reference-free evaluation toolkit: a five-axis scorecard with 28 statistical checks, an adversarial detector for synthetic artifacts, and soundness checks like classification against shuffled copies. A second generator builds task-focused relational databases from a set of business questions, ensuring presence of qualifying rows, near misses, and exact labels.
AI.result: Across 23 generated companies, the realism score improved from an initial mean of 60.3 to 99.1, and the weakest instance improved from 41.1 to 94.9; an adversarial detector’s synthetic flags fell from 55.2% of records to zero. These results generalize to an unseen random seed. The question-driven database generator can reliably produce labeled relational datasets tailored to specified analytical questions.
AI.conclusion: It is feasible to generate highly realistic, fully synthetic enterprise relational data without real training data, and to measure and drive improvements using a fixed, reference-free evaluation framework. The approach supports practical deployment as a hosted service and containerized simulators for offline use, enabling safe, realistic data for development, testing, and research.

title: On the Impact of Anonymization on the Performance of Large Language Models
summary: As large language models are increasingly deployed in sensitive domains, anonymizing input data to protect personally identifiable information has become a critical practice. However, the impact of this anonymization on model utility is not well understood. This paper presents a systematic empirical study of the trade-off between privacy and performance. We evaluate five prominent language models across eleven diverse benchmarks, comparing their performance on original versus pseudonymized inputs. Our results reveal that while anonymization generally degrades performance, the effect is highly nuanced. We find that more capable models, such as Qwen2.5-72B and GPT-4o mini, suffer the largest performance drops, suggesting a stronger reliance on specific entity information. The impact is also task-dependent: performance on TruthfulQA improves with anonymization, while retrieval-focused tasks like RGB experience a catastrophic decline. Further experiments show that reversible anonymization techniques that preserve entity uniqueness significantly outperform irreversible ones like redaction, and that explicitly prompting models about anonymization offers no discernible benefit. We conclude that anonymization is not a one-size-fits-all solution and must be co-designed with the model and task in mind to balance privacy and utility effectively. Our findings provide a crucial baseline for developing more robust, privacy-aware AI systems.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically studies how anonymizing inputs (to protect personal data) affects the performance of large language models, finding nuanced, task- and model-dependent trade-offs between privacy and utility.
AI.motivation: As large language models are increasingly used on sensitive, personally identifiable data, practitioners anonymize inputs to protect privacy. Yet it is unclear how different anonymization strategies affect model utility across tasks and model scales. There is a need for a systematic, quantitative understanding of the privacy–performance trade-off to guide the design of privacy-preserving, high-performing AI systems.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic empirical evaluation of five prominent language models on eleven diverse benchmarks. They compare model performance on original inputs versus pseudonymized variants, exploring multiple anonymization strategies, including reversible techniques that preserve entity uniqueness and irreversible ones like redaction. They also test whether explicitly prompting models about anonymization changes performance.
AI.result: Anonymization generally degrades model performance, but the magnitude and direction of effects are nuanced. Larger, more capable models (e.g., Qwen2.5-72B, GPT-4o mini) suffer the largest performance drops, suggesting heavy reliance on specific entity information. The impact varies by task: some, like TruthfulQA, see improved performance, whereas retrieval-heavy tasks such as RGB show catastrophic declines. Reversible anonymization that maintains entity uniqueness substantially outperforms irreversible redaction. Prompting models about anonymization yields no clear performance benefit.
AI.conclusion: Anonymization introduces non-trivial, context-dependent trade-offs between privacy and utility. It is not a universal, plug-and-play solution: effective privacy protection must be co-designed with the particular model, task, and anonymization technique. The study establishes baseline evidence and guidelines for constructing more robust, privacy-aware AI systems that better balance data protection with task performance.

title: Off-Target Effects of Response-Style Alignment in a Korean 27B Language Model
comment: 19 pages. Korean-language evaluation (KoBBQ); all uncertainty estimates over KoBBQ items are clustered on the benchmark template
summary:
We post-train Qwen3.8-27B for Korean response style -- verbosity, list and markdown usage, discourse structure and register -- and measure two behaviours the objective never targets: abstention on ambiguous social questions in KoBBQ, where the benchmark-correct answer is UNKNOWN, and unprompted disclosure in securities guidance. Both move, and the changes are expressed primarily through the model's emission policy: how often it answers and how much it says.
  Matched target-form controls show that answer propensity depends on the training target, not the prompt set or recipe alone. Holding prompts, recipe, data volume and serving fixed and changing only the target text, three style seeds give positive answer-rate point estimates (mean +0.82 pp) and three neutral seeds negative ones (mean -1.53 pp); the observed seed ranges do not overlap and the means differ by 2.34 pp. A length-matched arm lies between them, and a fourth arm that stays short while preserving hedging is unstable across seeds, so which feature of the form is responsible is unresolved.
  For absolute stereotyped exposure the decomposition into an answer-propensity term and a conditional-composition term is an algebraic identity, not a finding; its empirical content is where the movement went. Across the trained checkpoints the changes are dominated by answer propensity while the composition term stays small, and because that term is evaluated on treatment-dependent answered subsets we do not read it as evidence about latent preference.
  Two measurement results follow. A between-arm contrast in conditional stereotyped share does not identify a change in conditional content preference when answer status is treatment-dependent. And agreement between two rule detectors for the same construct runs from 0.44 to 0.99 depending on which checkpoint produced the text -- observable without any reference labels.

AI.tldr: They fine-tune a large language model for Korean stylistic traits and show that this unintentionally changes how often it answers or abstains, which in turn drives changes in measured behaviors like stereotyped exposure and safety judgments, more than changes in conditional content.
AI.motivation: To understand how post-training on seemingly harmless stylistic targets (verbosity, markdown, discourse structure, register) can unintentionally alter a model’s answer/abstention behavior and measured safety-related outcomes, especially in cases where the training objective never directly mentions those behaviors. They also want to clarify what can and cannot be inferred from benchmark metrics that conflate answer propensity with conditional content, and to highlight that detector agreement itself can depend strongly on the generating model.
AI.method: They start with Qwen3.8-27B and perform post-training (instruction-style finetuning) for Korean response style only. They systematically vary the target text across several “style seeds”: three that tend to promote more answering, three that are more neutral, a length-matched condition, and another condition that keeps answers short but maintains hedging. They hold prompts, training recipe, data volume, and serving fixed, changing only the target form. They then evaluate on (1) KoBBQ ambiguous social questions where UNKNOWN is the correct benchmark answer to measure abstention, and (2) securities guidance tasks where unprompted disclosure is measured. They decompose stereotyped exposure into an answer-propensity term and a conditional-composition term and analyze how these terms move across checkpoints. They also run two rule-based detectors for the same construct on generated text and measure their agreement across checkpoints, without needing ground-truth labels.
AI.result: Post-training for style significantly changes the model’s emission policy: how often it chooses to answer and how long or verbose the answers are, even though those behaviors were not explicit targets. Matching for target-form shows that answer propensity is determined by the specific training target text rather than prompt set or training recipe alone: three “style seed” variants yield positive shifts in answer rate (mean +0.82 percentage points), while three neutral variants yield negative shifts (mean −1.53 percentage points), with non-overlapping seed ranges and a 2.34 pp gap between their means. A length-matched condition falls between these, and a condition that preserves hedging while staying short shows unstable results across seeds, so the exact form feature driving the effect is unresolved. In decomposed stereotyped exposure, most of the change across checkpoints is attributed to answer propensity, while the conditional-composition component remains small; because composition is computed only on subsets where the model answered (which are treatment-dependent), it cannot be cleanly interpreted as revealing latent content preference. Empirically, (1) differences in conditional stereotyped share between arms do not identify changes in conditional content preference when answering probability itself changes with treatment, and (2) the agreement between two detectors for the same rule-based construct varies widely (0.44–0.99) depending solely on which checkpoint generated the text, a phenomenon visible even without reference labels.
AI.conclusion: Post-training an LLM for seemingly superficial style properties can materially alter its propensity to answer, abstain, or elaborate, which then dominates changes in downstream behavioral metrics such as stereotyped exposure and safety benchmarks. Therefore, naïve interpretations of changes in conditional content metrics (e.g., conditional stereotyped rates) as shifts in underlying preference are invalid when answer propensity is treatment-dependent. Evaluation and safety analysis must explicitly account for emission policy and recognize that detector behavior and agreement can depend strongly on the generating model itself.

title: SEAR: Segment-Evidence-Aware Routing for Weak-to-Strong Multilingual Speech MCQ
summary: This paper describes our system for Task~2 of the second Multilingual Conversational Speech Language Model (MLC-SLM) Challenge. We adapt Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct with a segment-evidence-aware data and post-training pipeline. A language model converts timestamped ASR into coherent event spans, which are expanded by a boundary margin and cropped from the original recording. We then synthesize complementary semantic MCQs with Qwen3.6-27B and acoustic MCQs with Gemini~3.1 Flash-Lite, followed by structural, grounding, answer-consistency, and target-model trainability checks, yielding 359,825 verified MCQs across 21 language and accent variants. A text-only probe partitions the data into weak, text-answerable items used for supervised fine-tuning and strong, audio-dependent items used for reinforcement learning with Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO), stabilized by debiased advantages, sequence-level importance correction, and dynamic filtering. Our system obtains 90.92% accuracy on the final official evaluation set.

AI.tldr: They built a multilingual conversational speech LM system for the MLC-SLM Challenge by generating and filtering large-scale audio-grounded MCQs and training Qwen3-based models with both supervised fine-tuning and RL, achieving 90.92% accuracy.
AI.motivation: Improve multilingual conversational speech understanding by making LMs actually rely on audio evidence rather than just transcripts, and to compete in the MLC-SLM Task 2 setting.
AI.method: Start from Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct. Convert timestamped ASR into coherent event spans, expand with margins, and crop audio segments. Auto-generate two types of multiple-choice questions: semantic ones with Qwen3.6-27B and acoustic ones with Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite. Apply multiple filters (structural validity, grounding in audio, answer consistency, and trainability for the target model) to obtain a high-quality MCQ set. Use a text-only probe to separate weak (text-answerable) vs strong (audio-dependent) items. Train with supervised fine-tuning on weak items and reinforcement learning with Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) on strong items, plus stabilization tricks (debiased advantages, importance correction, dynamic filtering).
AI.result: They obtain a curated dataset of 359,825 verified MCQs across 21 language and accent variants and reach 90.92% accuracy on the official MLC-SLM Task 2 evaluation set.
AI.conclusion: Segment-evidence-aware data construction plus a combination of supervised learning on text-answerable items and RL on audio-dependent items can effectively train a multilingual conversational speech LM that strongly leverages audio signals, as shown by high challenge accuracy.

title: Memory Compression for High-Fanout Agent Sandboxes
summary:
High-fanout agent workloads create a growing memory bottleneck because a single task may spawn many concurrent sandbox sessions. Yet these sandboxes are far from independent: they originate from a shared template and execute related trajectories, exposing substantial template-relative and cross-sandbox memory redundancy. Conventional memory compression is poorly matched to this setting in three fundamental dimensions: how to compress, because they fail to exploit similarity across non-identical sandbox pages; what to compress, because they control page-fault overhead through conservative page selection; and when to compress, because compression is either triggered by memory pressure or performed without awareness of agent execution phases.
  We present AgentZip, the first memory compression system designed specifically for AI-agent sandboxes. AgentZip introduces compression mechanisms that exploit both the template-relative and cross-sandbox redundancy. It broadens the compression scope to any page with a profitable representation and shifts overhead control from compression-time page selection to restore-time prefetching. It further aligns expensive compression with LLM waiting periods to avoid interfering with foreground tool execution. Across LLM training and inference workloads, AgentZip reduces sandbox-owned memory by up to 8.7x, compared with 2.1x for the Linux configuration. Restore prefetching and agent-execution-aware scheduling reduce the slowdown of aggressive compression from as high as 3.1x to 1.40x while retaining nearly all of its memory-saving benefit.

AI.tldr: AgentZip is a memory compression system specialized for high-fanout AI agent sandboxes, exploiting cross-sandbox and template-relative redundancy to greatly reduce memory while keeping performance overhead low via smart prefetching and phase-aware scheduling.
AI.motivation: High-fanout AI-agent workloads spawn many concurrent sandboxes, causing a memory bottleneck. Existing memory compression is ill-suited because it: (1) cannot effectively exploit similarity across related but non-identical pages, (2) compresses only a conservative subset of pages to limit page-fault overhead, and (3) triggers compression based on generic memory pressure rather than agent execution phases. A specialized approach is needed to leverage cross-sandbox redundancy and coordinate with LLM/tool timing.
AI.method: Design and implement AgentZip, a memory compression system tailored to AI-agent sandboxes that: (1) introduces compression mechanisms to exploit both template-relative redundancy (pages derived from a common template) and cross-sandbox redundancy (similarities among concurrent sandboxes); (2) expands the set of compressible pages to any page with a net-profitable compressed representation, shifting overhead management from which pages to compress to how and when to restore them via prefetching; and (3) schedules compression work during LLM waiting periods so it does not interfere with active tool execution. It also employs restore-time prefetching to hide page-fault latency under agent execution patterns.
AI.result: On LLM training and inference workloads, AgentZip reduces sandbox-owned memory usage by up to 8.7x, compared to 2.1x for a tuned Linux configuration. With restore prefetching and agent-execution-aware scheduling, the runtime overhead of aggressive compression is cut from up to 3.1x slowdown to 1.40x, while preserving nearly all of the memory savings.
AI.conclusion: Specializing memory compression to AI-agent sandboxes and exploiting both template-relative and cross-sandbox redundancy can dramatically reduce memory usage with acceptable overhead. By broadening the compression scope and shifting overhead control to restore-time prefetching, and by aligning compression with LLM idle periods, AgentZip achieves much higher memory savings than conventional OS compression while keeping performance slowdowns modest.

title: TransClean: A Benchmark for Detecting and Extracting Clean Translations from Large Language Model Outputs
comment: Accepted to the Eleventh Conference on Machine Translation (WMT26)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for machine translation, yet their outputs often contain additional text beyond the translation itself, such as language labels, explanations or bilingual repetitions, which we term translation noise. Despite its prevalence, this problem lacks dedicated benchmarks and systematic study. We analyze over 790,000 translation outputs from 12 LLMs across 22 language pairs (LPs) and identify 12 recurring noise patterns, which we group into formatting and content noise. Building on the observed patterns, we construct TransClean, a controlled benchmark of 9,900 pairs of noisy and clean translation outputs, comprising 8,800 synthetically generated instances and 1,100 manually curated authentic instances. We evaluate two extraction approaches on the TransClean benchmark: 1) a span-based extraction method leveraging translation quality estimation models for span detection, and 2) an LLM-based extraction method that prompts an LLM to isolate the translation. Our benchmark and analysis provide the first systematic framework to evaluate and improve the cleanliness of LLM translation outputs.

AI.tldr: The paper defines and studies “translation noise” in LLM-based machine translation, builds a benchmark called TransClean with noisy/clean pairs, and evaluates methods to extract clean translations from noisy outputs.
AI.motivation: LLMs used for machine translation often produce extra, unwanted text (labels, explanations, repetitions) in addition to the translation, but there is no dedicated benchmark or systematic analysis for this issue, making it hard to measure or improve output cleanliness.
AI.method: The authors collect over 790k translations from 12 LLMs across 22 language pairs and manually categorize 12 recurring noise patterns into formatting and content noise. Using these patterns, they build TransClean, a benchmark of 9,900 noisy/clean translation pairs (8,800 synthetic, 1,100 authentic). They then test two extraction approaches: (1) a span-based method that uses translation quality estimation models to detect and extract the translation spans; and (2) an LLM-based method where another LLM is prompted to return only the translation portion.
AI.result: They obtain a taxonomy of 12 translation noise patterns and a large, controlled dataset (TransClean) reflecting them. On this benchmark, they demonstrate and compare the effectiveness of span-based extraction and LLM-based extraction methods for isolating clean translations, quantifying their performance across varied noise types.
AI.conclusion: Translation noise is a systematic and measurable problem in LLM-based MT. The TransClean benchmark and the proposed extraction methods form a first structured framework to study, evaluate, and improve the cleanliness of LLM translation outputs, enabling future research on more robust and clean MT generation from LLMs.

title: Routing by Reasoning Need: Trajectory-Aware Decoding Control for Diffusion Vision-Language Models
comment: 17 pages, 9 figures. Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026
summary: Diffusion vision-language models generate answers through iterative refinement, exposing intermediate answer trajectories that can be inspected and controlled at inference time. However, this controllability creates a reasoning-need mismatch, where a universal generation length is applied to questions with different reasoning demands. Visually closed questions may be harmed by continued refinement after a stable answer has formed, whereas reasoning-sensitive questions may be harmed by premature commitment. We formulate this problem as reasoning-budget mismatch and study it in LLaDA-V. Rather than choosing a universal generation length, our training-free controller routes each example to early commitment, baseline preservation, or reasoning-supportive decoding using trajectory signals from answer closure, commitment evidence, and representation revision pressure, without using ground-truth answers. Across answer-focused, mixed-reasoning, and CoT-sensitive benchmarks, routed control improves robustness over fixed long decoding, pure short decoding, and single-rule interventions. The gains are not explained by shorter outputs alone. Answer-closed examples often benefit from commitment, whereas CoT-sensitive examples require preserving or supporting intermediate reasoning. Taken together, these results suggest diffusion VLM decoding should route inference-time control by the state suggested by the observed trajectory instead of relying on a universal decoding length.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to dynamically decide when to stop or extend diffusion-based vision-language model decoding instead of using a fixed number of refinement steps.
AI.motivation: Diffusion vision-language models refine answers over multiple steps, exposing intermediate trajectories that allow inference-time control. Current practice typically uses a fixed, universal generation length for all questions, regardless of their reasoning complexity. This leads to a reasoning-budget mismatch: simple, visually closed questions can be damaged by excessive refinement after the answer is already stable, while complex, reasoning-intensive questions can be harmed by stopping too early. The authors aim to better match the decoding process to the actual reasoning needs of each input.
AI.method: Using the LLaDA-V diffusion VLM, the authors design a training-free controller that dynamically routes each example among three decoding regimes: (1) early commitment (stop once an answer is clearly formed), (2) baseline preservation (follow the standard decoding schedule), and (3) reasoning-supportive decoding (allow extended refinement for hard questions). The routing decision is made online during decoding based on trajectory signals: answer closure (how stable the emerging answer is), commitment evidence (confidence that the current answer should be fixed), and representation revision pressure (indications that the internal representation is still changing). The controller does not rely on ground-truth labels.
AI.result: On a range of benchmarks spanning answer-focused tasks, mixed-reasoning tasks, and chain-of-thought (CoT)-sensitive evaluations, the routed controller improves robustness and accuracy compared with using a fixed long decoding schedule, a uniformly short decoding schedule, or single-rule heuristics. Performance gains cannot be attributed simply to shorter outputs, indicating that trajectory-aware routing is capturing genuine improvements in reasoning allocation.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion-based VLMs benefit from adaptive, trajectory-aware decoding rather than a one-size-fits-all refinement length. By monitoring answer trajectories and routing each example to early commitment, baseline, or reasoning-supportive decoding, models better match their reasoning budget to task demands. This suggests that future diffusion VLM systems should incorporate inference-time controllers that condition on observed decoding dynamics instead of relying on a universal number of refinement steps.

title: SWRouter: Similarity-Contractive Window Routing for Multi-Turn Large Language Model Conversations
summary: Large language models exhibit complementary strengths, motivating routing methods that dispatch each query to the most suitable model. Although existing routers are effective in single-turn settings, they do not directly transfer to multi-turn dialogue, where routing performance critically depends on how historical context is segmented, retained, and incorporated into the current prompt. This introduces two fundamental challenges: preventing information loss and information confusion during context construction, and evaluating routing quality without conflating model selection with prompt construction quality. In this paper, we propose SWRouter, a Similarity-Contractive Window Router for multi-turn large language model routing. SWRouter combines a similarity-based context segmentation mechanism for prompt construction with a dual-metric evaluation framework that decouples construction accuracy from router performance. Experiments on multi-turn dialogue benchmarks demonstrate that SWRouter consistently surpasses strong baselines, achieving a 16.26% improvement in evaluation accuracy over the best individual large language model and an additional 8.22% gain over the Conv-ID Context baseline. Our results highlight that multi-turn large language model routing requires a joint design of context construction and evaluation, rather than a direct extension of single-turn routing methods.

AI.tldr: Proposes SWRouter, a routing method for multi-turn LLM dialogues that jointly designs context construction and router evaluation, outperforming strong baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM routers work well for single-turn queries but fail to directly extend to multi-turn dialogues, where effective routing depends on how conversation history is segmented and included in the prompt. This setting faces two major challenges: avoiding loss of important information and avoiding confusion from irrelevant or redundant context, as well as fairly evaluating routing quality without mixing it with prompt construction quality.
AI.method: Introduce SWRouter, a Similarity-Contractive Window Router that uses similarity-based context segmentation to decide which parts of the dialogue history to include when forming the prompt for each turn. It also proposes a dual-metric evaluation framework that separately measures the accuracy of context construction and the routing performance, thus decoupling model selection quality from prompt-building quality.
AI.result: On multi-turn dialogue benchmarks, SWRouter outperforms strong baseline routing and prompting methods, improving evaluation accuracy by 16.26% over the best single LLM used alone and by an additional 8.22% over the Conv-ID Context baseline approach.
AI.conclusion: Multi-turn LLM routing cannot be treated as a simple extension of single-turn routing. Instead, effective multi-turn routing requires jointly designing how dialogue context is constructed and how routing is evaluated, and SWRouter provides an approach that addresses both aspects while delivering superior performance.

title: Mr.LHDR: A Benchmark for Multimodal Real-World Long-Horizon Deep Research Agents
comment: Code and data are available at https://github.com/minghaoguo20/Mr-LHDR-eval
summary: Deep research agents are increasingly capable of web search, tool use, multimodal evidence analysis, and information synthesis. However, existing benchmarks mainly evaluate medium-horizon exploration and rarely test whether agents can sustain long, dependency-heavy research processes. We introduce Mr.LHDR (Multimodal real-world Long-Horizon Deep Research), a benchmark for evaluating real-world deep research over long, irreducible chains of interdependent evidence across eight categories. Each question is constructed from a hidden Node-Relation graph and requires an average of 12.1 necessary intermediate conclusions with a mean dependency depth of 10.4 before reaching a short, unique, and verifiable answer. Questions incorporate multimodal evidence, including images, maps, PDFs, logos, charts, tables, and video frames, with at least one non-text element that changes the reasoning state. Mr.LHDR evaluates both final answers and the correctness of intermediate conclusions under annotated dependencies. We evaluate general models, deep research systems, and agent frameworks using Overall Accuracy (OA), Strict Accuracy (SA), Checklist Score (CS), and Dependency-Aware Checklist Score (DACS). Results show that even the strongest system achieves only 43.1% OA and 34.3% SA, indicating that final-answer accuracy substantially overestimates complete research success. Removing images reduces DACS by 12.6 points, demonstrating the importance of multimodal evidence, while SA consistently declines as reasoning chains become longer. These findings reveal sustained, dependency-consistent evidence integration, rather than isolated fact retrieval, as a key bottleneck for current deep research agents.

AI.tldr: Introduces Mr.LHDR, a benchmark for evaluating long-horizon, multimodal deep research agents using complex evidence-dependency graphs; finds current systems perform poorly, especially on dependency-consistent reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks focus on short- to medium-horizon tasks and do not adequately test whether research agents can maintain long, dependency-heavy reasoning chains that reflect real-world research complexity. The authors want to measure sustained, structured evidence integration rather than simple fact retrieval.
AI.method: They construct Mr.LHDR, a benchmark built from hidden Node-Relation graphs where each question requires many interdependent intermediate conclusions (average 12.1, depth 10.4) to reach a verifiable answer. Questions span eight categories and include multimodal evidence (text plus images, maps, PDFs, logos, charts, tables, video frames), with at least one non-text element that changes the reasoning state. The benchmark evaluates systems on both final answers and intermediate conclusions using metrics such as Overall Accuracy, Strict Accuracy, Checklist Score, and Dependency-Aware Checklist Score. They test general models, deep research systems, and agent frameworks under these metrics and ablate image information to study the impact of multimodality.
AI.result: Even the strongest evaluated system achieves only 43.1% Overall Accuracy and 34.3% Strict Accuracy, showing a large gap between final-answer correctness and fully correct research processes. Removing images reduces the Dependency-Aware Checklist Score by 12.6 points, underscoring the importance of multimodal evidence. Strict Accuracy declines as reasoning chains lengthen, indicating difficulty with long-horizon, dependency-heavy reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Current deep research agents struggle with sustained, dependency-consistent integration of multimodal evidence, particularly over long chains of interdependent steps. Final-answer accuracy alone significantly overestimates true research success. The Mr.LHDR benchmark exposes long-horizon, multimodal dependency reasoning as a key bottleneck and provides a more rigorous, process-aware way to evaluate and improve deep research systems.

title: Cross-Lingual Clinical Annotation Projection as Constrained Text Generation: A Six-Language Study
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables, submitted to journal
summary: Background: To determine whether cross-lingual clinical annotation projection can be formulated as a text-preserving, document-level generative task that produces verifiable character-level annotations for multilingual clinical corpus construction, and to characterize its robustness and computational trade-offs relative to candidate-based projection pipelines. Methods: We developed a constrained LLM projection workflow that inserts entity tags directly into immutable target-language text, followed by deterministic validation and character-offset reconstruction. We evaluated it alongside supervised candidate-span projection and hybrid ML-LLM refinement for transferring Spanish Disease, Symptom, and Procedure annotations into six languages. Evaluation used MultiClinAI gold standard with strict span matching and character-overlap F1 Results: Direct LLM projection achieved the strongest and most consistent performance. GLM 5.2 obtained a mean Strict F1 of 0.9201 across 18 language-entity combinations, while locally deployable Gemma4:31B achieved 0.9133. The best LLM configuration improved Strict F1 over the previous state of the art in all 18 settings, by 0.0564-0.1512, yielding 55,416 grounded mentions with reconstructed offsets. Conclusions: Direct LLM-based projection enables high-quality multilingual clinical annotation transfer and provides a practical approach for extending clinical NLP resources to languages with fewer annotated datasets and language-specific tools. Combined with local inference and deterministic validation, it can substantially reduce expert time and cost for multilingual clinical corpus construction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and evaluates a direct, document-level LLM-based method to project clinical entity annotations across languages by inserting tags into fixed target text and reconstructing character offsets, outperforming earlier candidate-based projection pipelines in both accuracy and robustness.
AI.motivation: Multilingual clinical NLP is limited by the scarcity of annotated corpora and language-specific tools, especially outside high-resource languages. Existing cross-lingual annotation projection methods often rely on candidate spans, alignment heuristics, or complex pipelines that can be brittle, less accurate, and hard to validate at character level. There is a need for a method that can reliably transfer clinical entity annotations across languages in a way that preserves the original text, yields verifiable character-level offsets, and can be practically used to build large, high-quality multilingual clinical corpora with reduced expert effort.
AI.method: The authors formulate cross-lingual clinical annotation projection as a constrained, text-preserving, document-level generative task. Large language models are prompted to insert entity tags for diseases, symptoms, and procedures directly into immutable target-language clinical text. After generation, a deterministic validation step enforces formatting constraints and filters errors, and then the system reconstructs character-level entity offsets from the tagged text. This direct LLM projection workflow is compared against two baselines: supervised candidate-span projection and a hybrid ML–LLM refinement approach. Experiments transfer Spanish clinical entity annotations into six target languages using different LLMs (including GLM 5.2 and Gemma 4:31B) and evaluate performance with strict span matching and character-overlap F1 on the MultiClinAI gold standard.
AI.result: Direct LLM-based projection achieved the best and most consistent performance across all evaluated settings. GLM 5.2 reached a mean Strict F1 of 0.9201 across 18 combinations of languages and entity types, while the locally deployable Gemma 4:31B model achieved a similar mean Strict F1 of 0.9133. For every one of the 18 evaluated scenarios, the best LLM configuration outperformed the previous state-of-the-art candidate-based approach, with absolute Strict F1 gains ranging from 0.0564 to 0.1512. Using this workflow, the authors produced 55,416 grounded entity mentions with reconstructed character offsets in the target languages.
AI.conclusion: Formulating cross-lingual clinical annotation projection as a constrained, document-level LLM generation task that preserves target text and yields deterministic character-level offsets is both feasible and effective. The proposed direct LLM-based workflow consistently outperforms candidate-based and hybrid pipelines, enabling high-quality transfer of disease, symptom, and procedure annotations from Spanish into multiple languages. When combined with local model deployment and deterministic validation, this approach offers a scalable, cost-efficient way to build multilingual clinical corpora, particularly for languages with limited annotated resources and tools, thereby reducing expert annotation time and supporting broader multilingual clinical NLP development.

title: Magenta: Closing the Loop Between Mathematical Reasoning and Lean Verification
summary: Most of mathematical knowledge has been communicated through so-called informal use of mathematics and natural language. With large language models (LLMs) being highly adept in using natural language, they achieve strong performance, yet not perfect, in informal mathematical reasoning. Restraining LLMs to informal reasoning misses out on the opportunity to use the discrete verification abilities that machines offer through machine-checkable proofs. In this paper, we bridge the gap between informal and formal reasoning by integrating Lean signals into the informal reasoning process. We introduce Magenta, a training-free agentic pipeline that, given only a natural-language problem, produces an answer, expresses it as a Lean 4 statement, and constructs a machine-checked proof. A statement judge verifies whether the formalisation preserves the original problem, while an error-attribution judge routes failed attempts either to mathematical re-derivation or local Lean repair. Magenta achieves 100% accuracy across all evaluated olympiad benchmarks, including AIME 2025, AIME 2026, and HMMT February 2026. When paired with the open-weight K2-Horizon-7B reasoner, it solves all six IMO 2026 problems. Our analysis shows that statement adjudication is essential for preventing false certificates and that feedback-guided correction outperforms independent resampling on difficult problems.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Magenta, a training-free agentic pipeline that turns natural-language math problems into Lean 4 formal statements and machine-checked proofs, achieving perfect accuracy on several competition benchmarks by tightly integrating informal reasoning with formal verification and feedback-guided repair.
AI.motivation: Most mathematical work is written informally in natural language, and LLMs are already good but imperfect at such informal reasoning. However, informal reasoning alone cannot exploit computers’ ability to perform strict, discrete verification via proof assistants like Lean, nor does it prevent confidently wrong answers. The authors want to close the gap between informal, natural-language mathematics and fully formal, machine-checkable proofs, so that LLM-based systems can produce both correct answers and certified proofs, avoiding false "proof certificates" while still leveraging strong natural-language reasoning.
AI.method: The authors design Magenta, a training-free, modular agentic pipeline that starts from a purely natural-language math problem. First, an LLM-based reasoner derives a solution and simultaneously proposes a Lean 4 formal statement that encodes the problem and its answer. A dedicated statement-judging component checks whether this Lean statement faithfully represents the original natural-language problem. If the formalisation is judged valid, a proof-generation component attempts to construct a Lean 4 proof to be checked by the Lean kernel. When proofs fail, an error-attribution judge decides whether the failure is due to mathematical mistakes (triggering re-derivation of the reasoning/solution) or due to local formalisation/proof issues (triggering targeted Lean-level repair). The pipeline iterates this process, using feedback-guided correction instead of naive resampling, until it obtains a machine-verified proof or exhausts its budget.
AI.result: On olympiad-style benchmarks, Magenta attains 100% accuracy, including on AIME 2025, AIME 2026, and HMMT February 2026, indicating that every solved problem has both a correct answer and a matching Lean 4 proof. In combination with the open-weight K2-Horizon-7B model serving as the mathematical reasoner, Magenta successfully solves all six problems from IMO 2026. Ablation and analysis show that the statement adjudication module is crucial to avoid cases where an incorrect or mismatched formal statement could lead to a misleading "verified" proof, and that feedback-guided correction strategies are more effective than independent resampling, especially on harder problems.
AI.conclusion: Integrating formal Lean 4 signals directly into the informal reasoning loop enables LLM-based systems to go beyond high but imperfect answer accuracy and reach fully verified mathematical solutions for challenging olympiad problems. The authors conclude that (1) statement-level adjudication is key to ensuring that formal proofs actually certify the intended natural-language problems, and (2) iterative, feedback-driven repair mechanisms significantly enhance robustness compared to naive resampling. This demonstrates a viable path for bridging informal natural-language mathematics with formal proof assistants, suggesting that future mathematical AI systems should tightly couple natural-language reasoning with formal verification rather than treating them as separate tasks.

title: ReGround: Grounding Reviewer Comments in Multimodal Evidence
summary: Reviewer comments naturally relate to specific parts of the reviewed paper, yet grounding these comments to the underlying evidence is difficult due to long multimodal documents. Existing benchmarks do not capture this setting and largely focus on explicit, information-seeking queries. We introduce ReGround, a large-scale dataset for reviewer comment grounding that links 10,267 reviewer comments to 16,274 evidence in the original anonymous submission of 3,656 papers. We build on a simple observation: author rebuttals often include explicit references to content of the submission used to address reviewer comments, providing a high-precision annotation source. We cast grounding as a retrieval task and evaluate a wide range of retrieval methods. Results show that retrieval over the entire paper content performs poorly, evidence-type inference is a major bottleneck, and multimodal evidence provides complementary signals that text alone misses. Our dataset exposes grounding reviewer comments as a difficult and practically important problem for scientific document understanding.

AI.tldr: ReGround is a new large-scale dataset that links reviewer comments to specific evidence spans (including multimodal content) in scientific papers, enabling the study and benchmarking of reviewer comment grounding as a retrieval task.
AI.motivation: Reviewer comments typically refer to specific parts of a paper, but automatically grounding these comments to the right passages/figures/tables is hard because papers are long, multimodal, and existing benchmarks mainly cover short, explicit, information-seeking queries rather than realistic peer-review scenarios. There is a need for realistic data and benchmarks focused on this grounding problem in scientific document understanding.
