AI.method: The authors construct ReGround by leveraging author rebuttals in peer review, which often explicitly quote or reference parts of the original anonymous submissions when responding to reviewer comments. These references are used as high-precision annotations that link 10,267 reviewer comments to 16,274 evidence items across 3,656 papers. They formulate comment grounding as a retrieval problem and benchmark a broad set of retrieval approaches, including methods that use full-paper retrieval, evidence-type inference, and multimodal (text + non-text) evidence sources.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows that naïvely retrieving over the entire paper content yields poor grounding performance. Correctly inferring the type of evidence (e.g., text section, figure, table) is a key challenge limiting performance. Additionally, incorporating multimodal evidence (such as figures and other non-text elements) substantially improves grounding because it offers complementary information beyond text-only approaches.
AI.conclusion: ReGround establishes reviewer comment grounding as a challenging, realistic benchmark task for scientific document understanding. The findings highlight the limitations of current retrieval systems on long multimodal documents, underscore the importance of evidence-type inference, and demonstrate that multimodal evidence is crucial for accurately grounding reviewer comments. This dataset and benchmark open avenues for developing more advanced models for peer-review and scientific-document tools.

title: AI Exposure and AI Resilience: A Two-Dimensional Assessment Framework for Software and Software-Based Business Model
summary: Artificial intelligence is changing both software production and the economics of software-based business models. Classical technology due diligence mainly examines technical properties such as architecture, scalability, and technical debt. These criteria do not fully capture how AI can affect a company's value proposition, competitive position, margins, or access to customers. This paper develops Artificial Intelligence Exposure and Resilience (AI-ER) as a two-dimensional assessment framework. AI exposure describes the pressure for change that AI creates for a business model. AI resilience describes the company's ability to absorb that pressure, adapt to changed conditions, and use AI in an economically viable way. Metrics for both dimensions are derived from current AI capabilities, their deployment conditions, and relevant research on business models and organizational adaptability. The model keeps exposure and resilience separate and adds an explicit assessment of evidence quality and confidence. It can be applied first with public information and later refined with internal evidence. The result is a traceable company profile that supports comparison without concealing uncertainty in the underlying evidence. The paper also specifies an initial score logic and a procedure for empirical validation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a two-dimensional framework, AI Exposure and Resilience (AI-ER), to systematically assess how AI affects a company's business model and its ability to adapt.
AI.motivation: Traditional technology due diligence focuses on technical aspects (architecture, scalability, technical debt) and overlooks how AI changes value propositions, competitive dynamics, margins, and customer access. Investors and managers need a structured way to evaluate how vulnerable or robust a business model is to AI-driven change.
AI.method: The authors conceptualize a two-dimensional framework: (1) AI exposure, measuring the pressure for change that AI exerts on a business model, and (2) AI resilience, measuring the firm's capacity to absorb that pressure, adapt, and deploy AI profitably. They derive concrete metrics for both dimensions from current AI capabilities, deployment conditions, and literature on business models and organizational adaptability. They separate exposure from resilience, incorporate explicit evidence quality/confidence ratings, define an initial scoring logic, and outline how assessments can begin with public data and then be refined with internal information. They also propose a procedure for empirical validation of the framework.
AI.result: The outcome is a structured AI-ER assessment model that yields a transparent, traceable profile of a company's AI exposure and resilience, including explicit uncertainty indicators. It supports comparison across companies or cases without masking the limitations of the underlying evidence and provides an initial scoring scheme and validation plan.
AI.conclusion: AI-ER offers a more complete and rigorous approach to technology due diligence in the age of AI by capturing both how strongly AI threatens or transforms a business model and how capable a company is of adapting and leveraging AI. The framework is suitable for staged use (public to internal data), supports comparative analysis, and is designed to be empirically refined and validated over time.

title: Structural priors for data-efficient language learning
summary: Efficient language learning requires methods to reduce the reliance on large data and computational resources. We investigate structural transfer: First training models on non-language data to induce useful priors for natural language. This approach is a form of weight initialization for multilingual language modeling. We evaluate transfer via next-token-prediction loss, weight shifts in the model, and downstream linguistic benchmarks. Several symbolic data types - notably music, probabilistic grammars, and cellular automata - yield lower language-modeling loss than random initialization. These gains coincide with smaller weight shifts during subsequent language training, suggesting that structural transfer positions models in a more favorable region of the parameter space. However, a lower loss does not translate consistently into better downstream linguistic performance, and transfer from non-language data is less efficient than additional language data. We conclude that non-language data can serve as a partial substitute for language data for the training objective of next-token prediction but does not reliably support broader linguistic generalization.

AI.tldr: They test whether pretraining language models on structured non-language data (like music or grammars) can partially replace language data by acting as a good weight initialization for multilingual language modeling.
AI.motivation: Training large language models requires massive language datasets and compute. The authors want to know if we can reduce this dependence by first training on cheaper or more available non-language but structured data, in order to induce general structural priors that could help with later language learning.
AI.method: They introduce “structural transfer”: pretrain models on various symbolic, non-linguistic datasets (music, probabilistic grammars, cellular automata, etc.), then fine-tune on multilingual language modeling. They compare this against random initialization and against simply using more language data. Evaluation covers (1) next-token prediction loss, (2) how much the model weights move during language fine-tuning, and (3) performance on downstream linguistic benchmarks.
AI.result: Pretraining on several structured non-language domains (especially music, probabilistic grammars, and cellular automata) leads to lower language-modeling loss than starting from random initialization. These models also require smaller weight updates during subsequent language training, indicating they start from a better region of parameter space. However, they do not consistently outperform baselines on downstream linguistic tasks, and using non-language data is still less effective than just adding more language data.
AI.conclusion: Non-language, structurally rich data can partially substitute for language data for the narrow goal of optimizing next-token prediction: it provides a useful inductive prior and a better starting point in parameter space. Nonetheless, this structural transfer does not reliably yield stronger general linguistic capabilities, so non-language data cannot yet be considered an efficient or robust replacement for additional language data in building broadly capable language models.

title: Exploring Diffusion Transformers for Cross-Modal Augmentation in Multimodal Brain State Decoding
comment: CoMA-DiT, a cross-modal augmentation framework built on Diffusion Transformer, extends multimodal learning beyond fusion by leveraging paired modalities as mutual generative supervision to enrich training data and improve brain state decoding
summary: Multimodal brain state decoding has largely focused on fusing paired modalities for prediction, but has rarely explored how their correspondence can be further exploited to enrich training data and improve multimodal representation learning. To address this gap, we propose CoMA-DiT, a bidirectional cross-modal Diffusion Transformer for latent augmentation that treats paired modalities as sources of mutual generative supervision rather than merely as inputs to be fused. CoMA-DiT conditions velocity prediction on the paired modality through cross-modal attention and adaptively injects the resulting variation via a reliability-gated residual mechanism. Experiments on multimodal auditory attention decoding and emotion recognition showed that CoMA-DiT consistently outperformed 20 representative baselines, achieving absolute gains of 4.28% and 6.70% in accuracy and macro-F1 over the no-augmentation baseline, respectively. Extensive ablation, sensitivity, visualization, and interpretability analyses further demonstrated its robustness, generalizability, and ability to capture functionally relevant cross-modal interactions. These findings support a broader view of multimodal learning: Paired modalities can serve not only as inputs for fusion but also as supervision sources that augment one another.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CoMA-DiT, a cross-modal diffusion transformer that uses paired brain-signal modalities to generate augmented latent representations for each other, improving multimodal brain state decoding.
AI.motivation: Most multimodal brain state decoding methods only fuse paired modalities for direct prediction and ignore the potential of using their correspondence to generate additional, informative training data. The authors want to leverage each modality as a generative supervision source for the other, enhancing representation learning and model robustness.
AI.method: They design CoMA-DiT, a bidirectional cross-modal Diffusion Transformer for latent augmentation. The model performs diffusion-based velocity prediction in latent space and conditions this prediction on the paired modality via cross-modal attention. A reliability-gated residual mechanism adaptively injects cross-modal variation into the target modality’s latent representation. This is done in both directions between modalities, effectively augmenting each modality’s latent space using the other.
AI.result: On multimodal auditory attention decoding and emotion recognition tasks, CoMA-DiT outperforms 20 strong baselines. It yields absolute improvements of 4.28% in accuracy and 6.70% in macro-F1 compared with a no-augmentation baseline. Additional ablation, sensitivity, visualization, and interpretability analyses show that the method is robust, generalizes well, and captures meaningful cross-modal interactions.
AI.conclusion: Treating paired modalities as mutual generative supervision sources—rather than only as inputs to be fused—can significantly improve multimodal brain state decoding. CoMA-DiT demonstrates that cross-modal diffusion-based latent augmentation is an effective and robust way to exploit multimodal correspondence, supporting a broader paradigm for multimodal learning where modalities augment one another.

title: Complex-Text Robustness Evaluation and Failure Diagnosis for Low-Resource Multilingual Text-to-Speech
summary: Low-resource multilingual text-to-speech (TTS) systems have expanded language coverage, but their robustness under complex text inputs remains insufficiently diagnosed. Existing evaluations mainly focus on naturalness, speaker similarity, and content consistency using regular test sentences, while providing limited insight into how multilingual TTS systems fail when handling challenging inputs such as numbers, dates, named entities, long sentences, code-switched expressions, and punctuation-related structures. This paper proposes a complex-text robustness diagnosis framework for low-resource multilingual TTS. We evaluate robustness from three dimensions: content consistency, language consistency, and generation stability. A multilingual robustness testing scheme is designed for Thai, Vietnamese, Swahili, and Indonesian, covering ordinary sentences and multiple types of complex text inputs. We further introduce automatic diagnostic metrics, including character error rate, language identification accuracy, and duration abnormal rate. To support input-level risk analysis before speech generation, we propose a lightweight Text Risk Score (TRS), which estimates synthesis risk from interpretable text features without manual annotation or model training. Experiments on three representative multilingual TTS systems, including OmniVoice, VoxCPM2, and MMS-TTS, show that complex text inputs expose systematic failure patterns that are not fully reflected by ordinary short-sentence evaluation. Different systems exhibit distinct vulnerabilities in number normalization, named entity handling, long-text generation, and code-switched input processing. Furthermore, TRS shows a positive correlation with content errors and duration abnormalities, demonstrating its usefulness as a low-cost pre-synthesis indicator for complex-text risk diagnosis in low-resource multilingual TTS.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a diagnostic framework to evaluate how robust low-resource multilingual TTS systems are to complex text inputs and proposes an automatic Text Risk Score to predict risky inputs before synthesis.
AI.motivation: Multilingual TTS systems in low-resource languages are increasingly available, but current evaluations mostly use simple, regular sentences and only assess naturalness, speaker similarity, and basic content correctness. This leaves a gap in understanding how these systems behave on real-world, complex text such as numbers, dates, named entities, long sentences, and code-switching, where failures are likely to be more severe and systematic. The authors aim to systematically characterize these failure modes and provide tools to anticipate problematic inputs.
AI.method: The authors design a complex-text robustness diagnosis framework with three evaluation dimensions: content consistency, language consistency, and generation stability. They create a multilingual robustness test set for Thai, Vietnamese, Swahili, and Indonesian that includes ordinary sentences as well as challenging categories like numbers, dates, named entities, long sentences, code-switched inputs, and punctuation-heavy structures. They define automatic diagnostic metrics—character error rate (CER), language identification accuracy, and duration abnormal rate—to quantify system behavior. Additionally, they propose a lightweight Text Risk Score (TRS) that uses interpretable textual features to estimate how risky an input is, without extra annotation or training. They then evaluate three representative multilingual TTS systems (OmniVoice, VoxCPM2, and MMS-TTS) under this framework.
AI.result: The experiments reveal that complex text inputs uncover systematic and category-specific failure patterns in multilingual TTS systems that are not captured by evaluations on ordinary, short sentences. The three tested systems show different weaknesses, e.g., in number normalization, named entity pronunciation, long-text stability, and code-switched input handling. The proposed automatic metrics effectively quantify these issues. The Text Risk Score correlates positively with observed content errors and duration abnormalities, indicating that it can serve as a useful, low-cost predictor of synthesis risk for a given text input.
AI.conclusion: Robustness evaluation of low-resource multilingual TTS requires going beyond simple sentence tests and standard perceptual metrics. The proposed framework and test sets make it possible to systematically diagnose robustness to complex text across languages. The study shows that current systems have distinct, systematic vulnerabilities that only appear under challenging inputs. The Text Risk Score offers a practical tool for pre-synthesis risk assessment and can help developers identify and mitigate problematic inputs in low-resource multilingual TTS applications.

title: Portable Semantics, Private Dialects: Reuse and Negative Transfer in Latent Communication Between Language-Model Cells
comment: 17 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Companion to arXiv:2608.20054. Code and evaluation records: https://github.com/tokenosopher/populus-evidence-partitioning ; checkpoints and fitted alignment maps: https://huggingface.co/tokenosopher/populus-evidence-partitioning-checkpoints
summary: In shared-genome language-model societies, restricted evidence visibility favors reusable, value-indexed latent packet interfaces, whereas the sole high-performing globally visible model in the parent study learned an episode-entangled code. This companion study asks whether independently trained societies share one packet language, where strict zero-shot transfer fails, and whether inherited interface state helps or harms later learning. First, a leakage-controlled causal interoperability audit over all 30 ordered pairs of six independently trained restricted societies -- under sealed held-out structure and a preregistered raw/orthogonal/linear/nonlinear alignment ladder -- shows the six semantically similar interfaces do not form one raw language: one same-initialization pair is exactly interoperable in both directions, a second shows asymmetric partial compatibility, and all 26 cross-initialization directions fail every frozen alignment rung. Second, within the tested decomposition and a single sealed source formulation, a source-span control localizes strict zero-shot failure to interpretation and execution of the new operator instructions. Third, in a matched adaptation factorial, the globally trained communication interface acts as a severe negative-transfer prior: reinitializing only the packet reader, writer, and mouth raises final depth-three accuracy from 0.169 to 0.857. Fourth, across two restricted checkpoints and two independently frozen target streams each, inherited interfaces never exceeded fresh-interface controls by the preregistered 0.10 margin. All primary conclusions are bounded to a near-transfer 17-state setting; the negative-transfer factorial concerns one globally visible parent-cohort checkpoint, while an appendix adds a post hoc tagged-global twin case study.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how different language-model-based agent societies develop and (fail to) share internal communication codes (“packet interfaces”), showing that independently trained societies do not share a common language and that reusing a globally trained interface can hurt later learning.
AI.motivation: To understand whether internal communication codes learned by language-model societies are reusable across independently trained groups, whether they form a shared “language,” and how inheriting an existing interface affects future learning performance.
AI.method: They train several “restricted evidence visibility” societies of language models that communicate via latent packets, then perform (1) a causal interoperability audit across all ordered pairs of six societies using a preregistered alignment ladder (raw/orthogonal/linear/nonlinear) under held-out structures; (2) source-span control experiments to localize where zero-shot transfer fails; (3) a factorial adaptation experiment comparing performance when reusing vs reinitializing parts of a globally trained interface; and (4) tests across multiple checkpoints and target streams to compare inherited vs fresh interfaces against a preregistered performance margin.
AI.result: (1) The six interfaces are semantically similar but not one shared raw language: only one same-seed pair is fully interoperable, another shows asymmetric partial compatibility, and all cross-seed directions fail all alignment levels. (2) Zero-shot failure is localized to interpreting and executing novel operator instructions. (3) Reusing the globally trained interface creates strong negative transfer, with reinitializing packet I/O and the “mouth” boosting accuracy from 0.169 to 0.857. (4) Inherited interfaces never beat fresh ones by more than the 0.10 preregistered margin across tested checkpoints and targets. Conclusions are limited to the near-transfer 17-state configuration and specific checkpoints studied.
AI.conclusion: Independently trained language-model societies with restricted evidence visibility do not converge to a single interoperable internal packet language, and strict zero-shot transfer of interfaces largely fails, especially for new operator instructions. Moreover, inheriting a globally trained communication interface can significantly hinder later learning (negative transfer), and across tested conditions, inherited interfaces do not systematically outperform freshly initialized ones. These findings, in a constrained 17-state near-transfer setting, caution against assuming that internal communication codes are universal or that reusing them will aid downstream learning.

title: A Training-Free, Alignment-Free Approach to Corporate Intelligence: Application to SEC Filings
summary: High-dimensional dense text embeddings and large language models face real obstacles in financial-disclosure analysis: context-window limits, hallucination risk, high computational cost, and the arbitrary rotation of vector spaces across independently trained models. We present a training-free, alignment-free framework for corporate intelligence built on deterministic sparse seed vectors. Hashing word strings into a fixed high-dimensional basis places all documents and all temporal epochs in a common coordinate system by construction, removing any need for training or alignment. Accumulating these seed vectors across sentence contexts yields corpus-specific semantic signatures that compose linearly, supporting sub-second document comparison, issuer fingerprinting, tracking of how an issuer's vocabulary shifts between filings, and thematic sentence extraction, all on ordinary CPU hardware. Demonstrating the approach on a multi-year corpus of SEC filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K), we show how material corporate events, among them Boeing's 737 MAX crisis, Intel's supply-chain disruptions, and Bunge's acquisition of Viterra, emerge as distinct, interpretable semantic profiles, each traceable to the exact source sentences that produced it, with no domain-specific training and no LLM inference.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a training-free, alignment-free method for analyzing financial disclosures using deterministic sparse seed vectors instead of dense embeddings or LLMs.
AI.motivation: Conventional high-dimensional dense text embeddings and LLM-based methods struggle in financial-disclosure analysis due to context-window limits, hallucinations, high computational costs, and the problem that vector spaces from separately trained models are arbitrarily rotated and thus not directly comparable over time or across models. The authors seek a method that avoids training, reduces compute, and yields stable, comparable document representations across time.
AI.method: They hash word strings into a fixed high-dimensional sparse basis, generating deterministic seed vectors for tokens. These seed vectors place all documents and time periods into a single common coordinate system by construction. By accumulating seed vectors at the sentence and document level, they build corpus-specific semantic signatures. These signatures are linearly composable and allow efficient comparison of documents and sentences using simple vector operations on CPUs, without any training or alignment procedures.
AI.result: On a multi-year corpus of SEC filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K), the framework supports sub-second document comparison, issuer fingerprinting, monitoring of how an issuer’s vocabulary and focus change over time, and thematic sentence extraction. The method identifies distinct and interpretable semantic profiles associated with specific material corporate events, such as Boeing’s 737 MAX crisis, Intel’s supply-chain disruptions, and Bunge’s acquisition of Viterra.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic sparse seed-vector representations provide a practical, training-free, and alignment-free alternative to dense embeddings and LLMs for financial-disclosure analysis. They enable fast, interpretable, and temporally stable semantic analysis on standard CPU hardware, making it possible to track corporate events and issuer behavior directly from filings without domain-specific training or LLM inference.

title: RAMamba-Net: A Reliability-Aware and Mamba-Based Multimodal Fusion Network for Auditory Attention Detection
comment: RAMamba-Net, a reliability-aware Mamba-based multimodal fusion network for auditory attention decoding
summary: Auditory attention decoding (AAD) identifies the attended speaker from physiological signals, supporting neuro-steered hearing devices and natural human-machine interaction. Electroencephalography (EEG) is the dominant modality for AAD but provides incomplete evidence in naturalistic audio-visual scenes, motivating EEG and electrooculography (EOG) fusion. Existing approaches remain limited by weak cross-modal interaction, inefficient temporal modeling, and low robustness to sample variations. To address the limitations, we propose RAMamba-Net, a reliability-aware Mamba-based multimodal fusion network for AAD. RAMamba-Net employs a Mamba-enhanced band-aware convolutional Transformer to capture band-specific EEG patterns and long-range temporal dynamics. A dual-branch temporal-spatial encoder models EOG temporal and inter-channel dependencies. Cross-modal attention enables explicit modality interaction. Then, a reliability-aware module is introduced to estimate sample-wise modality weights for feature and prediction consistency, thereby enhancing multimodal fusion. Experiments on two AAD benchmarks demonstrate that RAMamba-Net effectively exploits complementary EEG-EOG information, yielding accuracy gains of 5.76% over unimodal baselines, together with more robust decoding and discriminative representations. Further analyses show that explicit cross-modal interaction improves multimodal alignment, while the reliability-aware module suppresses unreliable modality evidence and is robust to signal perturbation and parameter variation.

AI.tldr: A paper proposing RAMamba-Net, a reliability-aware multimodal fusion network combining EEG and EOG using Mamba-based temporal modeling to improve auditory attention decoding accuracy and robustness.
AI.motivation: Auditory attention decoding is key for neuro-steered hearing aids and natural human-machine interaction. Existing methods rely mostly on EEG, which is incomplete in realistic audio-visual environments, and current multimodal (EEG+EOG) fusion approaches suffer from weak cross-modal interaction, poor temporal modeling, and low robustness to variations. There is a need for a more powerful, robust, and interactively fused multimodal model.
AI.method: RAMamba-Net introduces a Mamba-enhanced band-aware convolutional Transformer to extract frequency-band-specific EEG features and long-range temporal dependencies. For EOG, it uses a dual-branch temporal-spatial encoder to learn both temporal patterns and inter-channel relationships. Cross-modal attention layers are used to explicitly model interactions between EEG and EOG features. Additionally, a reliability-aware module estimates per-sample modality weights and enforces consistency at the feature and prediction level, down-weighting unreliable modalities during fusion.
AI.result: On two standard AAD benchmarks, RAMamba-Net significantly outperforms unimodal baselines by about 5.76% accuracy and shows improved robustness in decoding performance and more discriminative feature representations. Analyses demonstrate better multimodal alignment from cross-modal attention and that the reliability-aware module effectively suppresses noisy or unreliable modality information, maintaining performance under signal and parameter perturbations.
AI.conclusion: RAMamba-Net effectively leverages complementary EEG and EOG information via advanced temporal modeling, cross-modal attention, and reliability-aware fusion, leading to higher AAD accuracy and robustness than unimodal or less integrated multimodal methods. The framework provides a promising direction for robust neuro-steered hearing devices and other multimodal neural decoding applications.

title: Structured Transforms for Low-Overhead Quantization of Language Models
summary: We revisit Kashin-decomposition-based weight quantization for large language models and propose an improved algorithm with stronger convergence properties and structured, efficient orthogonal transforms. The method retains the core factorization of each weight into two components -- one with bounded infinity norm and the other with bounded infinity norm after an orthogonal transformation -- but replaces the dense random orthogonal matrix with a sign-randomized Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT), reducing the per-iteration cost from $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ to $\mathcal{O}(N \log N)$. The proposed greedy algorithm with alternating updates guarantees the four-peak distribution required for stable 2-bit clustering of each factor and admits closed-form initialization of cluster centers, removing the multi-restart k-means bottleneck of prior work. Composed with OPTQ-style sequential error compensation and QuIP-style incoherence preprocessing, the resulting JAX pipeline is competitive with OPTQ, QuIP, QuIP-RG and a fine-tuning- and vector-quantization-free variant of QuIP# at 4-bit per channel on OPT, Llama-2 and Pythia, with favorable wall-clock scaling. The bounded-$\ell_\infty$ factorization is also notably robust: on stress configurations where QuIP variants diverge to four-digit perplexity (Pythia-6.9B) or abort with NaNs in LDL back-substitution (Mistral-7B), Kashin-DCT remains numerically stable and stays close to FP16 baseline. At inference time, each weight decomposes into two 2-bit factor codes per channel that are structurally suited to native-2-bit hardware.

AI.tldr: The paper improves Kashin-decomposition-based 2-bit weight quantization for LLMs using a fast structured transform and a better optimization algorithm, achieving stable, competitive 4-bit-per-channel performance with good scaling and robustness.
AI.motivation: Existing Kashin-based quantization methods for LLMs have strong theoretical motivation but are impractical due to expensive dense orthogonal transforms (O(N^2)) and reliance on multi-restart k-means, and can suffer from numerical instability on some models. The authors want an efficient, stable, hardware-friendly 2-bit factorization that remains competitive with state-of-the-art 4-bit quantization methods across modern LLMs.
AI.method: They keep the Kashin-style factorization of each weight into two components with bounded infinity norm constraints (one directly, one after an orthogonal transform) and replace the dense random orthogonal matrix with a sign-randomized DCT to get an O(N log N) transform. They design a greedy alternating-update algorithm that enforces a four-peak weight distribution suitable for 2-bit clustering of each factor and supports closed-form initialization of cluster centers, avoiding costly multi-restart k-means. They integrate this factorization into a JAX pipeline with OPTQ-style sequential error compensation and QuIP-style incoherence preprocessing, and quantize LLMs without extra fine-tuning or vector quantization.
AI.result: The resulting Kashin-DCT quantization pipeline matches or closely tracks the accuracy of competitive 4-bit-per-channel schemes like OPTQ, QuIP, QuIP-RG, and a simplified QuIP# variant on models such as OPT, Llama-2, and Pythia, while having better wall-clock scaling due to the fast structured transform and simpler clustering. It remains numerically stable and near FP16 perplexity even on stress-test configurations (e.g., Pythia-6.9B, Mistral-7B) where QuIP-based methods diverge or fail numerically.
AI.conclusion: A structured Kashin-style decomposition with a sign-randomized DCT and a tailored greedy alternating algorithm provides an efficient, robust, and hardware-aligned 2-bit factorization for LLM weights. This approach yields competitive 4-bit-per-channel performance versus strong baselines, scales better computationally, and shows improved numerical robustness, making it a promising direction for practical low-precision LLM deployment, especially on hardware with native 2-bit support.

title: Beyond Confidence: Stability-Aware Test-Time Adaptation for LLM Reasoning
summary: Test-time adaptation has emerged as a lightweight alternative to costly post-training for improving the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) on downstream tasks. Predictive entropy provides a model-derived signal for such adaptation, guiding models toward higher-confidence reasoning states without external verifiers or reward models. However, higher confidence does not necessarily imply correctness, as LLMs may remain highly confident along incorrect reasoning trajectories. We observe that high-confidence reasoning is more likely to be correct when confidence remains stable under local perturbations. Based on this observation, we propose Test-Time Adaptation via Stability-Aware Confidence Optimization (TASCO), a framework that incorporates local stability into confidence-based test-time adaptation while keeping the LLM frozen. TASCO operationalizes local stability by optimizing a lightweight task-level prefix under two alternative perturbation strategies: Random Perturbation promotes distributional stability across trajectories induced by nearby perturbed prefixes, whereas Sharpness-Aware Perturbation targets worst-case local sensitivity. Experiments demonstrate that TASCO improves reasoning accuracy and token efficiency across diverse LLMs and reasoning benchmarks, while behavioral analyses show that it maintains stable confidence under local perturbations without prematurely concentrating the model's predictive distribution.

AI.tldr: They propose TASCO, a test-time adaptation method that optimizes a small prefix to encourage both high and locally stable confidence, improving LLM reasoning accuracy and token efficiency without updating model weights.
AI.motivation: Existing test-time adaptation methods rely on predictive entropy (confidence) to improve LLM reasoning, but LLMs can be confidently wrong. The authors observe that correctness correlates better with confidence that is stable under small perturbations, motivating a confidence signal that accounts for local stability rather than raw entropy alone.
AI.method: They keep the LLM weights frozen and introduce TASCO, which optimizes a lightweight task-level prefix at test time. Local stability is enforced via two perturbation strategies: (1) Random Perturbation, which samples nearby perturbed prefixes and promotes distributional similarity in their induced trajectories; and (2) Sharpness-Aware Perturbation, which explicitly seeks worst-case local perturbations to minimize sensitivity of the predictive distribution. The optimization objective combines confidence maximization with stability regularization across these perturbations.
AI.result: Across several LLMs and reasoning benchmarks, TASCO yields higher reasoning accuracy and better token efficiency than baselines. Behavioral analyses show the method produces confidence that is robust to local perturbations and avoids prematurely over-concentrating the predictive distribution.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating local stability into confidence-based test-time adaptation provides a more reliable signal than raw entropy alone. TASCO, implemented as a prefix optimization framework with random and sharpness-aware perturbations, can systematically improve LLM reasoning performance and efficiency without fine-tuning core model parameters.

title: Negative Self-Distillation: Learning to Reason by Avoiding Flaws
summary: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) has emerged as a popular paradigm for large language model (LLM) self-improvement, allowing models to act as their own teachers by leveraging privileged information such as ground-truth solutions. However, recent findings indicate that OPSD can severely degrade the performance of LLMs on complex reasoning tasks: By forcing the student to imitate an artificially confident reasoning trace conditioned on privileged information, OPSD inadvertently suppresses expressions of uncertainty and penalizes the exploratory, self-corrective behaviors required to solve challenging problems. To address this, we introduce Negative Self-Distillation (NSD), a new framework that optimizes LLMs by diverging from flawed reasoning rather than imitating privileged solutions. Instead of relying on ground-truth answers or external supervision, NSD uses the model itself to generate a question-specific negative condition (eg, acting as a ``careless reasoner'') and pushes the student's distribution away from this self-generated negative teacher. Naively applying unlearning objectives to achieve this divergence is problematic, as flawed reasoning tokens are confounded with basic linguistic tokens; indiscriminately penalizing both risks catastrophically degrading the model's foundational language capabilities. We resolve this by designing a dynamic gating mechanism that automatically identifies and isolates reasoning-critical tokens, ensuring gradient updates target only behavioral flaws while preserving the model's linguistic priors. Empirically, NSD consistently outperforms OPSD and other label-free, self-bootstrapping reinforcement learning (RL) baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Negative Self-Distillation (NSD), a self-improvement method for large language models that learns by diverging from model-generated flawed reasoning, outperforming standard on-policy self-distillation and other label-free RL baselines.
AI.motivation: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), where a model learns from its own privileged, confident reasoning traces, has become popular for LLM self-improvement. However, new evidence shows OPSD can worsen performance on complex reasoning because it suppresses uncertainty and exploratory, self-corrective behaviors that are crucial for solving difficult tasks. There is a need for a self-improvement framework that avoids these issues without relying on external labels or supervision.
AI.method: The authors introduce Negative Self-Distillation (NSD). Instead of imitating privileged, correct reasoning, the model generates a question-specific negative condition, such as a "careless reasoner" persona, and then trains a student model to diverge from this negative teacher distribution. To avoid catastrophic forgetting of basic language skills, they design a dynamic gating mechanism that identifies reasoning-critical tokens within the flawed trace and restricts gradient updates to these tokens, preventing penalization of generic linguistic tokens.
AI.result: Across experiments, NSD consistently yields better performance than OPSD and other label-free, self-bootstrapping RL baselines on complex reasoning benchmarks, indicating more effective self-improvement without external labels.
AI.conclusion: Moving from imitating confident, privileged reasoning (OPSD) to actively diverging from self-generated flawed reasoning (NSD), coupled with careful token-level gating, produces more robust improvements in LLM reasoning. NSD preserves linguistic competence while enhancing exploratory, self-corrective behavior, offering a promising alternative paradigm for label-free LLM self-training.

title: From Queries to Narratives: Cultural Heritage Data Stories for Knowledge Graph Exploration and Quality Assessment
summary: Cultural-heritage KGs such as the NFDI4Culture-KG contain millions of triples about artworks, music, inscriptions, historical events, and the people and places connected to them. For many users, however, discovering this knowledge can be difficult. While SPARQL can be learned, writing meaningful queries first requires an in-depth understanding of the graph's data model, an investment many domain researchers and practitioners are unwilling to make. Even with existing user interfaces, a starting point and some guidance are usually needed, because the data contained in the graph is highly specialized, heterogeneous, and constantly growing, making it challenging to know what it contains or which questions it can answer. In this paper, we present data stories as a way not only to lower this barrier, but also to turn exploration into data-quality assessment, and thus combine accessible querying with the discovery of issues that remain hidden in aggregate statistics. In this contribution, a data story is understood as a narrative document that integrates explanatory text and images with executable SPARQL queries and their visualized results. It is described how they are authored against the graph and how they serve several purposes: guiding users through an unfamiliar graph, creating reproducible narratives, and surfacing data-quality issues previously hidden in aggregate statistics. The authoring platform LODEON including its Sparnatural and AI-supported authoring assistants is introduced as a proof-of-concept. Within the authoring environment, every claim made about the data can be backed by an explicit query, making these narratives transparent and reproducible. This paper also reflects on lessons learned from hands-on seminars and workshops. Early experience suggests that such data stories make cultural-heritage knowledge graphs more accessible for both exploration and quality assessment.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes "data stories"—narrative documents combining text, images, and executable SPARQL queries—to make large, complex cultural-heritage knowledge graphs easier to explore while simultaneously supporting data-quality assessment.
AI.motivation: Cultural-heritage knowledge graphs like NFDI4Culture-KG have millions of heterogeneous triples, but are difficult for most users to explore because SPARQL requires deep understanding of the underlying data model and existing interfaces still need a good starting point and domain knowledge. There is also a need to better surface data-quality issues that remain hidden in aggregate statistics.
AI.method: The authors define and implement "data stories" as narrative documents that interleave explanatory text and images with embedded, executable SPARQL queries whose results are visualized. They design an authoring workflow and implement it in the LODEON platform, which incorporates tools like Sparnatural and AI-supported authoring assistants to help users formulate queries and construct stories. Each narrative claim must be backed by an explicit query, ensuring transparency and reproducibility. They then apply this approach in seminars and workshops to gather early feedback.
AI.result: The proof-of-concept platform LODEON demonstrates that users can author and consume data stories over cultural-heritage KGs. The stories successfully guide users through unfamiliar graphs, enable reproducible narratives linked directly to data, and reveal specific data-quality problems that were not evident from high-level statistics. Early hands-on use shows that participants can more easily explore and understand the KG contents while also noticing quality issues.
AI.conclusion: Data stories are an effective means to lower the entry barrier for exploring complex cultural-heritage knowledge graphs and to turn exploration activities into opportunities for data-quality assessment. By tightly coupling narrative explanations with executable queries in the LODEON environment, the approach supports transparent, reproducible, and guided exploration. Early experiences from workshops indicate that this method improves both accessibility and quality-awareness, suggesting its promise for broader adoption in cultural-heritage KG projects.

title: The Eloquence submission for Task 2 of the Interspeech 2026 MLC-SLM challenge
summary: This paper details the Eloquence team's approach to Task 2 of the 2nd MLC-SLM challenge at Interspeech 2026, which involves multilingual Multiple-Choice Question Answering (MCQA) across 21 languages. Three approaches are explored. First, we fine-tune Voxtral-Mini-3B via LoRA with cross-lingual data augmentation, ASR transcript augmentation and timestamp-aware audio cropping, achieving 0.72 macro-accuracy on evaluation Phase 2. Second, we apply multimodal in-context learning (ICL) to the frozen Voxtral-24B model to correct a strong label bias, reaching 0.81, our best result. Third, a training-free retrieval system based on a three-layer voice-anchored memory combining acoustic identity, semantic content, and a knowledge graph achieves 0.68. All three systems substantially outperform the official baseline.

AI.tldr: Eloquence team explores three systems for multilingual speech-based MCQA in 21 languages, achieving up to 0.81 macro-accuracy and outperforming the challenge baseline.
AI.motivation: To build effective multilingual multiple-choice QA systems over speech in 21 languages for the MLC-SLM challenge, addressing issues like label bias, data scarcity, and the need to leverage both audio and text without expensive retraining.
AI.method: They propose three approaches: (1) Fine-tuning a 3B speech-language model (Voxtral-Mini-3B) with LoRA using cross-lingual data augmentation, ASR transcript augmentation, and timestamp-aware audio cropping. (2) Using multimodal in-context learning on a larger frozen model (Voxtral-24B) to mitigate strong label bias and improve MCQA performance. (3) Designing a training-free retrieval system with a three-layer voice-anchored memory that encodes acoustic speaker identity, semantic content, and external knowledge via a knowledge graph.
AI.result: Fine-tuned Voxtral-Mini-3B achieves 0.72 macro-accuracy in Phase 2 evaluation. Multimodal ICL with Voxtral-24B achieves 0.81 macro-accuracy, the best among their methods. The training-free retrieval system with voice-anchored memory achieves 0.68 macro-accuracy. All three surpass the official baseline system's performance.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal in-context learning over a large frozen model is most effective for multilingual speech MCQA, but lightweight LoRA fine-tuning and training-free retrieval with structured voice-anchored memory also bring sizable gains. Combining cross-lingual augmentation, transcript-based enhancements, and multimodal prompting is a powerful strategy to outperform the challenge baseline across 21 languages.

title: LLMs as Post-hoc Auditors of Physiological Plausibility in Symbolic Regression: A Clinician-Evaluated Case Study
summary: Genetic Programming and its variants, such as grammatical evolution, are widely used in Symbolic Regression to derive mathematical expressions from multivariate data. In addition to predictive accuracy, models are appreciated for their potential to provide interpretability, offering explicit equations that relate input variables to outcomes. However, achieving interpretability and plausibility remains challenging, as evolved models may be complex or scientifically inconsistent. In this study, we explore whether Large Language Models, can assist in improving the explainability of Symbolic Regression models generated by evolutionary computation methods. Building upon our previous work on estimating body fat percentage using grammar-based Genetic Programming , we investigate the use of LLMs as post-processing tools to analyze and rank evolved expressions according to their interpretability and medical plausibility. Four symbolic expressions are analysed by three LLMs over three repeated runs, and the resulting interpretations and rankings are assessed by a panel of three clinicians. Across the three LLMs, comparative model-ranking outputs received more favorable clinician assessments than isolated term-level interpretations. However, the LLMs also produced physiologically and mathematically questionable explanations, indicating that they are better suited to comparative auditing under expert oversight than to autonomous validation.\blfootnote{The present work is an extended version of a paper submitted into a journal.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether large language models can help make symbolic regression models from genetic programming more interpretable and medically plausible, using body fat estimation as a case study.
AI.motivation: Symbolic regression via genetic programming can produce accurate but complex and scientifically dubious formulas, limiting their interpretability and usefulness in domains like medicine. There is a need for tools that can assess and improve the explainability and plausibility of such evolved expressions.
AI.method: Using prior work on body fat percentage estimation with grammar-based genetic programming, the authors select four evolved symbolic expressions and analyze them with three different large language models across three runs each. The LLMs are tasked with interpreting, explaining, and ranking the expressions by interpretability and medical plausibility. A panel of three clinicians then evaluates the LLMs' explanations and rankings.
AI.result: Clinicians judged that LLM outputs providing comparative rankings of the models were more useful and favorably assessed than outputs focused on isolated term-by-term interpretations. Nonetheless, clinicians also identified multiple physiological and mathematical inaccuracies in the LLM-generated explanations.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can assist as comparative auditing tools to rank and discuss symbolic regression models, especially under expert supervision, but they are unreliable for autonomous validation due to their tendency to generate questionable or incorrect scientific explanations.

title: LOCUS: Task-Aware Low-Rank Post-Training for Token-Efficient Language Generation
summary: Large language model serving costs scale directly with output sequence length, yet standard preference alignment often inflates response verbosity without improving utility. We study whether the parameterization of post-training updates affects generation length: low-rank subspaces alter sequence length without modifying the alignment loss. We present LOCUS, a method that selects a task-aware low-rank adaptation subspace to minimize output-token cost subject to a utility constraint. Within this subspace, post-training retains the native preference objective with a frozen backbone. Across Anthropic HH-RLHF dialogue preferences, we evaluate two $\sim$3B decoder backbones, Pythia-2.8B and Qwen2.5-3B, against protocol-matched full-parameter DPO and DrDPO branches and the released SamPO checkpoint. LOCUS reduces continuation length by up to 39.84\% on Pythia-2.8B and by 14.87--17.58\% on Qwen2.5-3B while updating only 0.24--0.28\% of model parameters, with no material change in the internal preference diagnostic.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LOCUS, a post-training method that makes LLM responses shorter (cheaper) without hurting alignment quality, by restricting training to a task-aware low-rank subspace.
AI.motivation: Serving large language models is expensive because cost scales with output length. Standard alignment tuning often makes models more verbose without increasing usefulness. The authors want a way to keep or improve alignment utility while explicitly controlling and reducing response length and cost.
AI.method: They propose LOCUS, which chooses a task-aware low-rank adaptation subspace where only a small fraction of parameters are updated. The backbone model is frozen and the usual preference alignment objective (e.g., DPO/DrDPO on Anthropic HH-RLHF data) is kept, but optimization is constrained to this subspace. This design lets them manipulate sequence length behavior while preserving the alignment loss. They test LOCUS on ~3B-parameter decoder models (Pythia-2.8B and Qwen2.5-3B) and compare against full-parameter post-training methods like DPO, DrDPO, and SamPO under matched protocols.
AI.result: On Anthropic HH-RLHF dialogue preferences, LOCUS reduces continuation length by up to about 40% for Pythia-2.8B and about 15–18% for Qwen2.5-3B, while touching only about 0.24–0.28% of parameters. Importantly, preference diagnostics (alignment metrics) show no material degradation compared to full-parameter baselines.
AI.conclusion: Constrained, low-rank post-training (LOCUS) can significantly cut LLM output length and thus serving cost while preserving alignment utility, outperforming or matching standard full-parameter preference tuning in terms of alignment, but with far fewer trainable parameters and shorter generations.

title: Calibration-Aware Uncertainty Cascades for Efficient Heterogeneous Model Collaboration
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables, including appendix. Under review
summary: Heterogeneous model collaboration seeks to exploit the complementary strengths of different models to balance predictive performance and inference cost. Existing approaches typically rely either on trained routers, which tie routing decisions to a fixed task and model pool, or on raw-confidence cascades, whose thresholds lack consistent reliability semantics across heterogeneous models. Consequently, these approaches adapt poorly to changing model pools and deployment budgets. We propose Calibration-Aware Uncertainty Cascades (CAUC), a simple post-hoc framework that independently calibrates each model's confidence and selects deployment policies using validation data. The resulting calibrated confidence scores establish a common reliability scale for accepting an early prediction, invoking a stronger model, or selectively combining model outputs. This unified decision criterion decouples deployment policies from any particular model pool or operating budget. We further show theoretically that calibration gives confidence thresholds an explicit selective-risk interpretation, whereas uncalibrated scores offer no comparable reliability guarantee. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, across six language benchmarks, CAUC achieves an average relative accuracy improvement of 1.9% over strong-model-only inference while avoiding approximately 47% of strong-model calls. On image classification benchmarks, it maintains or improves predictive performance while reducing measured GFLOPs by up to 57%.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CAUC, a calibration-based framework that lets multiple heterogeneous models collaborate efficiently by using comparable, well-calibrated confidence scores to decide when to accept, escalate, or combine predictions.
AI.motivation: Existing heterogeneous model collaboration methods either use trained routers that are tied to a specific task and fixed model set, or rely on raw confidence thresholds whose values are not comparable across different models. As a result, these methods are brittle when the available models or deployment budgets change, and their confidence thresholds lack clear reliability or risk interpretations. There is a need for a simple, post-hoc approach that can flexibly adapt to changing model pools and budgets while providing sound reliability semantics.
AI.method: The authors propose Calibration-Aware Uncertainty Cascades (CAUC), a post-hoc framework in which each model in a pool is independently calibrated using validation data, converting its raw confidence outputs into calibrated confidence scores. These calibrated scores live on a shared reliability scale and are used to define deployment policies: when to accept a prediction from a cheaper/weaker model, when to invoke a stronger/more expensive model, and when to combine model outputs. The framework uses these calibrated confidences as a unified decision criterion, decoupling routing logic from any specific task, model pool, or inference budget. Theoretical analysis shows that under calibration, confidence thresholds correspond to explicit selective-risk guarantees, unlike uncalibrated scores.
AI.result: On six language benchmarks, CAUC yields an average relative accuracy gain of 1.9% compared to always using the strongest model, while avoiding about 47% of calls to that strong model (reducing cost). On image classification benchmarks, CAUC maintains or improves accuracy while reducing computational cost—measured in GFLOPs—by up to 57%. These results indicate that CAUC can improve the accuracy-cost tradeoff over both strong-model-only baselines and traditional cascades without sacrificing reliability.
AI.conclusion: Calibration-Aware Uncertainty Cascades provide a simple, post-hoc way to make heterogeneous models collaborate based on a common, reliability-grounded confidence scale. By calibrating each model and using calibrated scores to control when to accept, escalate, or combine predictions, CAUC decouples deployment policies from specific model pools and budgets, and gives confidence thresholds a principled selective-risk interpretation. Empirical results across language and vision tasks show that this approach can significantly reduce inference cost while maintaining or improving predictive performance.

title: RAG-Safety-Bench: Reliable Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented LLM Safety
summary: Allowing large language models (LLMs) to retrieve information from a set of trusted documents can increase reliability and reduce hallucination. However, recent work has demonstrated that retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can have unintended side effects on the overall safety of the generated responses, when prompted for harmful or dangerous content. A clearer understanding of the mechanisms leading to this result is needed, as increasing numbers of end users turn to RAG to incorporate corporate documents and knowledge bases into LLM-based systems. We introduce RAG-Safety-Bench, a benchmark to measure the safety impact of RAG on LLM models. By removing the confounding effect of retriever quality, and cleanly separating the problem into four conditions -- non-RAG, RAG with an oracle document containing the answer to the harmful request, RAG with documents related to the harmful request but without the specific answer, and RAG with random, safe documents -- the benchmark isolates the impacts of different factors in the observed safety degradation. We report results across five open-source LLMs, showing an inverse relationship between benign and unsafe capability, strong evidence that baseline safety guardrails do not lead to downstream safety guarantees in the RAG case, and model-specific support for previous findings that even benign documents can lead to unsafe generation in retrieval-enabled systems.

AI.tldr: The paper presents RAG-Safety-Bench, a benchmark to evaluate how retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) affects the safety of LLM outputs, showing that RAG can degrade safety even with benign documents.
AI.motivation: While RAG improves reliability and reduces hallucinations by grounding LLMs in trusted documents, recent work shows it can unintentionally worsen safety when models are prompted for harmful content. As more systems integrate proprietary or corporate knowledge via RAG, there is a need to understand when and how retrieval changes safety behavior, and to disentangle the effect of document content from retriever quality and model guardrails.
AI.method: The authors design RAG-Safety-Bench, a controlled benchmark that evaluates LLM safety under four conditions: (1) non-RAG (no retrieval), (2) RAG with an oracle document that directly answers the harmful query, (3) RAG with documents related to the harmful topic but lacking the specific harmful answer, and (4) RAG with random, safe documents. By fixing or removing the retriever as a confounder and systematically varying document conditions, they probe how different retrieval contexts affect safety. They then test five open-source LLMs under these conditions and measure both benign and unsafe capabilities.
AI.result: Experiments on five open-source LLMs show: (a) an inverse relationship between benign capability (ability to answer helpfully) and unsafe capability (propensity to give harmful answers), (b) existing baseline safety guardrails in the base models do not ensure safety once RAG is enabled, and (c) even benign or random safe documents can, in some cases, lead to unsafe generations when used in a retrieval-augmented setup.
AI.conclusion: RAG-Safety-Bench reveals that retrieval can systematically weaken safety guardrails in LLMs, and that safety in non-RAG settings does not automatically transfer to retrieval-augmented deployments. Even benign documents can contribute to unsafe behavior, implying that both document curation and model-level defenses must be reconsidered for RAG systems. The benchmark provides a structured way to study and improve safety in retrieval-enabled LLM applications.

title: RouteRepair: Instance-Level Failure Diagnosis and Targeted Repair in LLM-Based Automated Heuristic Design for Routing Optimization
summary: Efficient routing optimization is essential to freight transportation, urban logistics, and shared mobility, where high-quality heuristics are often required under limited computational budgets. Recent large language model (LLM)-based automated heuristic design methods can generate effective routing rules, but aggregate evaluation may mask recurrent failures on particular instance structures. To address this limitation, this study develops RouteRepair, which diagnoses parent-specific weaknesses from instance-level performance and applies targeted modifications to the corresponding heuristic components while protecting behavior that already performs well. Routing evidence, solver behavior, and program context are combined to define bounded repair objectives, and each intervention is validated through matched parent-child evaluation of failure recovery and collateral degradation. Experiments on the traveling salesman problem (TSP) and capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) span constructive search, guided local search, and ant colony optimization. RouteRepair-GLS reduces the mean TSP optimality gap from 1.7476% to 0.7587%, while the constructive CVRP heuristic lowers average route cost by 1.91% relative to the savings heuristic; the generated ACO priors also outperform matched hand-designed priors. These results show that failure-aware, evidence-constrained refinement can improve routing heuristics on difficult instances while preserving performance on cases they already solve well.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RouteRepair, a method that refines LLM-designed routing heuristics by diagnosing and fixing their instance-specific failures without harming existing strengths, achieving significantly better performance on TSP and CVRP benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based automated heuristic design can create strong routing heuristics, but their evaluation is usually aggregated over many instances. This can hide systematic failures on particular instance types or structures, which is problematic in real-world routing where robust performance is required under limited compute. There is a need for a principled way to detect where a heuristic fails and to selectively improve those weak spots while preserving behavior that already works well.
AI.method: The authors introduce RouteRepair, a framework that analyzes instance-level performance of a given heuristic (the parent) to identify where and how it fails. It combines routing evidence, solver behavior, and program context to define localized, bounded repair objectives for specific components of the heuristic. Using an LLM, it proposes targeted modifications (children heuristics) to those components rather than redesigning the whole heuristic. Each candidate repair is evaluated through matched parent-child comparisons focusing on two aspects: whether failures on the targeted instances are fixed and whether performance degrades elsewhere. The process is applied to several routing paradigms: constructive search, guided local search (GLS), and ant colony optimization (ACO), on TSP and CVRP instances.
AI.result: In experiments on TSP and CVRP, RouteRepair produces refined heuristics that outperform their parent versions and standard baselines. For TSP with guided local search, RouteRepair-GLS cuts the mean optimality gap from 1.7476% to 0.7587%. For CVRP, a constructive heuristic improved by RouteRepair achieves an average route cost 1.91% lower than the classical savings heuristic. For ACO, LLM-generated priors refined via RouteRepair outperform carefully hand-designed priors. Across tasks, the method improves performance on difficult instances specifically targeted for repair while maintaining or minimally affecting performance on instances the parent heuristic already solved well.
AI.conclusion: RouteRepair demonstrates that a failure-aware, evidence-constrained refinement strategy can systematically strengthen LLM-generated routing heuristics. By focusing on instance-level weaknesses and bounding the scope of modifications, the approach recovers from recurrent failures without sacrificing robustness on easy or already well-handled cases. This suggests a promising direction for iterative, data-driven improvement of automated heuristic design in routing and potentially other combinatorial optimization domains.

title: Component-Aware Differential Privacy for Federated Multilingual Speech-LLMs
summary: Per-layer differential privacy (DP) clipping improves gradient fidelity in federated learning by allocating per-matrix clipping budgets proportional to parameter count. We show that this recipe breaks for speech large language models (speech-LLMs), when the acoustic encoder and the language decoder differ by an order of magnitude in update norm. Single-pool per-layer methods suffer \emph{cross-component budget collapse}, dragging word error rate (WER) far from flat global clipping or collapsing training entirely. When the norm imbalance is milder, adaptive single-pool methods partially recover, confirming that collapse severity scales with the inter-component norm ratio. We empirically diagnose the root cause across six per-layer methods and three speech-LLM architectures. We then propose \emph{$α$-split}, a two-pool allocation that normalises encoder and LLM parameters into independent pools, and show that joint $\ell_2$ sensitivity and the original $(\varepsilon,δ)$-DP guarantee are unchanged. At architecture-calibrated $α$, our method recovers WER utility compared to flat DP, while granting the encoder $4.47{\times}$ tighter per-component noise protection against speaker voice-based gradient-inversion attacks at only $+2.6\%$ LLM noise overhead.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a failure mode of standard per-layer DP clipping in speech-LLMs due to large norm imbalance between encoder and decoder, analyzes why it happens, and proposes a two-pool clipping scheme (α-split) that restores model utility while strengthening privacy for the acoustic encoder.
AI.motivation: Federated training of speech-LLMs requires differential privacy to protect users, but naive global clipping hurts utility, so per-layer clipping is used. However, speech models have highly imbalanced gradient norms between the speech encoder and text LLM decoder, which may invalidate existing per-layer DP recipes and compromise either model quality or privacy. The authors are motivated to understand and fix this issue specifically for speech-LLMs.
AI.method: 1) Empirically study gradient norm distributions in speech-LLMs and evaluate multiple existing per-layer DP clipping/allocation methods under these conditions. 2) Identify and characterize the phenomenon of cross-component budget collapse, where a single clipping pool shared by encoder and decoder causes one component to dominate the clipping budget. 3) Propose α-split, a DP clipping scheme that partitions parameters into two pools (encoder vs LLM) and allocates clipping budgets separately while keeping the joint ℓ2 sensitivity and (ε, δ)-DP guarantees unchanged. 4) Tune α based on model architecture and compare against flat DP and single-pool per-layer methods on WER and privacy metrics, including robustness to gradient inversion attacks on speaker identity.
AI.result: Experiments on three speech-LLM architectures and six per-layer DP methods show that standard single-pool per-layer clipping can significantly degrade or even collapse training when encoder-decoder norm imbalance is large, pushing WER far from flat clipping baselines. Adaptive per-layer methods only help when norm imbalance is moderate, confirming that performance collapse severity scales with the inter-component norm ratio. The proposed α-split two-pool scheme recovers WER utility comparable to or better than flat DP while providing substantially stronger privacy for the encoder, achieving a 4.47× reduction in effective noise exposure for encoder parameters with only a 2.6% overhead in noise for the LLM decoder.
AI.conclusion: Standard per-layer DP clipping is unsafe to apply naively in speech-LLMs with strongly imbalanced encoder/decoder update norms, due to cross-component budget collapse. Carefully separating encoder and decoder into distinct clipping pools via α-split preserves the overall DP guarantee while restoring training stability and accuracy. This two-pool approach yields much better protection for voice-related encoder parameters against gradient inversion, with negligible additional noise cost on the language model, and should be preferred over single-pool per-layer methods for such architectures.

title: Flexible and Interpretable Accent Distance Measurements
summary: Determining the differences between two speakers' accents is a fundamental task in linguistics and speech technology research. The methodology used to measure these differences depends on the specific research area. A phonetics researcher may demonstrate accent variation by comparing vowel formants in paired recordings of individual words. These results will be interpretable, but the recordings will be time-consuming to collect and may not be representative of connected speech. Accented Text-to-Speech (TTS) research has pushed towards using accent embeddings derived from accent classification tasks. These embeddings can be produced from any speech recording, but are not readily interpretable. In this paper, we demonstrate that articulatory representations created through articulatory inversion can be used as an interpretable basis for accent comparison and that optimal transport provides a framework for accent comparison across arbitrary recording types.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an interpretable method to compare accents using articulatory representations and optimal transport.
AI.motivation: Existing accent comparison methods either use phonetic measurements that are interpretable but limited and time‑consuming to collect, or accent embeddings from TTS research that are easy to obtain but not interpretable. There is a need for a method that is both widely applicable to arbitrary speech recordings and linguistically interpretable.
AI.method: The authors use articulatory inversion to estimate articulatory trajectories (articulatory representations) from speech audio. They then apply optimal transport as a mathematical framework to compare the distributions of these articulatory representations across different speakers and recording types, thereby quantifying accent differences.
AI.result: They show that articulatory representations derived from articulatory inversion can serve as a meaningful, interpretable basis for comparing accents, and that optimal transport can effectively compare accent differences across varied types of recordings, such as isolated words and connected speech.
AI.conclusion: Articulatory inversion-based representations provide an interpretable representation for accent comparison, and optimal transport offers a flexible framework for comparing accents across arbitrary recording types, bridging the gap between traditional phonetic analysis and modern embedding-based approaches.

title: Recognizing Is Not Reversing: A Controlled Inversion Test of Fact-Preserving News Framing
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to analyze and rewrite news, yet current framing studies mainly evaluate generation, detection, or whether rewritten text appears more neutral. They do not directly show whether a model can undo a known framing transformation while keeping the facts fixed. We introduce a controlled inversion test over three established textual realizations of framing: evaluative lexis, agency realization, and information salience. Across 60 news articles and three intervention strengths, this yields 540 paired variants with preserved atomic facts and recorded edits. Across Qwen, DeepSeek, and Kimi, factual preservation remains near 0.84, whereas intervention reversal is 0.044--0.068. Even when both framing type and direction are recognized correctly, pooled reversal reaches 0.071. These results reveal a clear separation between factual fidelity, framing recognition, and framing inversion: recognizing how an article is framed does not imply that the framing can be undone.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether large language models can actively undo known framing in news articles while keeping facts unchanged, and finds that models preserve facts reasonably well but largely fail to invert framing.
AI.motivation: While LLMs are widely used to analyze and rewrite news, existing framing research mostly checks if models can generate, detect, or superficially neutralize framing. There is a gap in understanding whether models can actually reverse a known framing transformation (e.g., from positive to negative framing) without altering underlying facts. This capability is crucial if LLMs are to be trusted for bias mitigation and fair news rewriting.
AI.method: The authors design a controlled inversion test focused on three textual realizations of framing: evaluative lexis (value-laden word choice), agency realization (how responsibility and actors are expressed), and information salience (which facts are foregrounded or backgrounded). They collect 60 news articles and systematically apply three levels of intervention strength to create 540 paired variants with preserved atomic facts and logged edits. They then evaluate several LLMs—Qwen, DeepSeek, and Kimi—on their ability to preserve facts and to invert the framing, measuring factual preservation and successful intervention reversal, and analyzing performance even when the models correctly recognize the framing type and direction.
AI.result: Across Qwen, DeepSeek, and Kimi, factual preservation scores stay relatively high at about 0.84, indicating that models usually maintain core facts. However, successful framing inversion scores are very low, around 0.044–0.068 overall. Even in the subset of cases where the models correctly identify both the framing type and its direction, pooled reversal performance only rises slightly to 0.071, showing that recognizing framing does not translate into reliably undoing it.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates a clear separation between three capacities of LLMs in news rewriting: maintaining factual content, recognizing how an article is framed, and effectively inverting that framing. Although models can largely preserve facts and can sometimes detect framing, they are currently poor at actually reversing framing while keeping facts fixed. This highlights a significant limitation of current LLMs for tasks involving bias mitigation and controlled reframing of news content.

title: The Convention Gap: Towards Measuring Implicit Communication in Cooperative AI Evaluation
summary: Cooperative AI agents are evaluated against other AIs, yet human cooperation relies on implicit conventions---shared protocols for reading meaning beyond the literal message---which AI-AI benchmarks may not capture. We propose the \emph{convention gap}, the difference between the failure probability predicted from the literal content of communication and the observed failure rate, as a metric of implicit communication. In the card game Hanabi, the finite deck and deterministic hint constraints make this posterior exactly computable. We replayed about 101,000 play actions from three public datasets of human-human (hanab.live), AI-AI (HOAD), and human-AI (HanabiData) games. The gap was +26.2 percentage points (pp) in human pairs, $-$0.7~pp in AI pairs, and +16.4~pp in human-AI pairs, and was concentrated on plays of cards that had received no hints (+46~pp in human pairs). Within human-AI play, the literal information available to humans was similar across the three AI partners (mean predicted failure 38--41\%), but human failure rates ranged from 14.4\% to 34.4\% and the gap from +24.1 to +6.2~pp; the partner eliciting the largest gap produced the fewest human failures. Game score carried different information: it depended on each corpus's roster composition, whereas the gap separated human from AI play at the agent level. As a known-answer check, Off-Belief Learning agents, whose convention content is controlled by construction, gave a gap of +1.6~pp at the convention-free level, rising monotonically to +21.7~pp. These results suggest that convention compatibility, rather than AI-AI performance, may predict an AI's effectiveness with human partners.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a quantitative metric (the "convention gap") to measure how much of successful cooperation in Hanabi relies on implicit conventions beyond literal communication, and uses it to compare humans and AIs.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of cooperative AI agents focus on AI-AI performance and typically assume that all relevant information is captured by the literal content of messages. However, human cooperation heavily depends on implicit conventions and shared pragmatic inferences. There is a need for a measurable way to quantify such implicit communication and to understand whether AI agents that perform well with other AIs are also effective partners for humans.
AI.method: The authors define the "convention gap" as the difference between (1) the failure probability of a play inferred purely from literal communication and game state, and (2) the actual empirical failure rate of that play. In the game Hanabi, they can compute the literal failure probability exactly thanks to a finite deck and deterministic hint rules. They then replay around 101,000 historical play actions from three public datasets: human-human games (hanab.live), AI-AI games (HOAD), and human-AI games (HanabiData). They compute the convention gap for each setting, analyze how it varies by card hints and partner type, compare it with game score, and validate the metric using Off-Belief Learning agents with systematically varied levels of convention content.
